nodes.label: Platinum-based chemotherapy
nodes.description: A type of chemotherapy recommended for ovarian cancer, containing the metal platinum. Examples include carboplatin, cisplatin, and oxaliplatin. A type of chemotherapy that uses platinum-based drugs, with cisplatin as a common example. If cisplatin is too harsh or cannot be given for other reasons, a different platinum drug called carboplatin may be used instead. A type of chemotherapy using platinum-based drugs, recommended as first-line therapy for metastatic anal cancer.

nodes.label: Ovary
nodes.description: One of the two female reproductive organs that produce eggs for sexual reproduction and release hormones that affect breast growth, body shape, and the menstrual cycle. Each ovary is about the size and shape of a grape, and is located on one side of the uterus. Ovarian cancers can start in the surface layer of tissue surrounding the ovaries, called the epithelium, or in the fallopian tube.

nodes.label: Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)
nodes.description: A type of skin cancer that can develop from skin damage caused by exposure to pollutants. It can form in scars or chronic wounds and is more difficult to treat if it starts in damaged, inflamed, or scarred skin. It is also associated with actinic keratoses and certain genetic syndromes. A type of mouth cancer that starts in the surface (epithelium) lining the inside of the mouth, made up of squamous cells.

nodes.label: Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP)
nodes.description: Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is a hereditary condition linked to an increased risk of developing an adrenal tumor. A rare inherited cancer syndrome that can cause hundreds to thousands of polyps to form in the colon and rectum, which over time can become invasive rectal cancer. Individuals with FAP should be referred to a genetic counselor for testing related to rectal cancer. An inherited cancer syndrome causing hundreds to thousands of polyps to form in the colon and rectum, which can become invasive colon cancer over time. FAP is one of the two such conditions associated with Lynch syndrome and MMR gene mutations. A genetic disorder that causes hundreds to thousands of polyps to form in the colon and rectum, which over time can become invasive colon cancer. It is characterized by the formation of benign growths that can progress to cancer. There are two forms: classic FAP, which often develops cancer by age 50, and attenuated FAP, which causes fewer polyps and usually starts later in life. Genetic testing is recommended if an inherited syndrome is suspected, and a genetic counselor can provide guidance on testing for syndromes related to colon cancer.

nodes.label: NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app
nodes.description: A mobile application developed by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) that provides patient guides for various types of cancer, including information on fertility preservation, managing chemotherapy side effects, and acute lymphoblastic leukemia treatment. It also offers guidelines for patients with adolescent and young adult cancer, as well as resources for those seeking treatment at adult cancer centers.

nodes.label: Chemoradiation
nodes.description: A treatment strategy used for cervical cancer that combines chemotherapy and external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) given concurrently (during the same time period). It is recommended for most locally advanced cervical cancers that have grown beyond the cervix but have not spread to the liver, lungs, or bones. A combination treatment involving chemotherapy and radiation, potentially used after surgery for certain stages of cancer.

nodes.label: Hypomethylating agents (HMAs)
nodes.description: Hypomethylating agents (HMAs) are a class of drugs that block methyl groups from binding to DNA, turning silenced genes back on, which allows leukemic blasts to mature into normal cells. Azacitidine (Vidaza) and decitabine (Dacogen) are examples of HMAs. Hypomethylating agents (HMAs) are a class of drugs that block methyl groups from binding to DNA, allowing silenced genes to be turned back on and leukemic blasts to mature into normal cells. Azacitidine (Vidaza) and decitabine (Dacogen) are examples of HMAs.

nodes.label: Cirrhosis
nodes.description: Cirrhosis is a type of long-term (chronic) liver disease where liver cells are replaced by scar tissue. It is a risk factor for liver cancer, and those with cirrhosis should be screened for liver cancer. Cirrhosis is a scarring of the liver, a type of long-term (chronic) liver disease where liver cells are replaced by scar tissue. It can be caused by hepatitis B virus or infection, hepatitis C virus or infection, alcohol use, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), genetic hemochromatosis, stage 4 primary biliary cholangitis, alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency, or other causes. Individuals with cirrhosis should be screened for liver cancer.

nodes.label: Total thyroidectomy
nodes.description: A surgical procedure where the entire thyroid gland is removed. It is recommended for papillary cancers that have grown or spread beyond the thyroid, tumors larger than 4 cm, high-risk types of papillary cancer, and when nearby lymph nodes with cancer are present.

nodes.label: Study drug
nodes.description: A medication used in a clinical trial as part of the search-related costs. The medication being tested in a clinical trial, whose costs are covered by the study sponsor. A medication or therapy being tested in a clinical trial, often the new drug component in combination with a standard treatment. The new drug that is part of a clinical trial and is usually paid for by the study sponsor, along with other research-related costs. The medication or treatment being tested in a clinical trial, which is funded and overseen by the study sponsor.

nodes.label: Germline testing
nodes.description: Germline testing is a type of genetic test used for prostate cancer care that looks for inherited mutations that occur in every cell in the body. It is done using a sample of blood, urine, or saliva and can detect characteristic changes in genes like BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, CHEK2, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PALB2, PMS2, and others. Germline mutations in genes like BRCA1 or BRCA2 are also related to breast cancer, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, and skin cancer (melanoma).

nodes.label: Breast Cancer Staging
nodes.description: A process used to determine the extent of breast cancer at the time of diagnosis, involving the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) staging system. It includes anatomic TNM staging, tumor grade, and biomarker status like HER2, ER, and PR. Staging helps predict prognosis and inform treatment decisions. It is often done twice, before and after surgery, with clinical stage (c) given before any treatment.

nodes.label: Chest
nodes.description: A body part, typically the area of the body containing the heart and lungs, that may be imaged using MRI or CT scan to check for cancer spread. A body part that may be imaged using a CT scan to help determine the extent of cancer. A region of the body where cancer may be present beyond the pelvis, and where a CT scan with contrast is recommended to look for areas of cancer, such as the liver or lungs.

nodes.label: Metastatic anal cancer
nodes.description: Metastatic anal cancer refers to the spread of anal cancer to areas far from the pelvis. Treatment for metastatic anal cancer is not specified in the text, but it is mentioned that information on its treatment can be found on page 26. A type of anal cancer that has spread beyond the pelvis. Treatment recommendations include platinum-based chemotherapy as first-line therapy, with options such as carboplatin and paclitaxel, 5-FU, leucovorin, and oxaliplatin (FOLFOX), 5-FU, leucovorin, and cisplatin (FOLFCIS), modified docetaxel, cisplatin, fluorouracil (DCF), or 5-FU and cisplatin. A type of cancer that has spread from the anal region to other parts of the body and is treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors like pembrolizumab.

nodes.label: Cervical Cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer that affects the cervix, the lower part of the uterus that connects to the vagina. It can spread to nearby lymph nodes and may require surgical staging before treatment. Risk factors for cervical cancer include a history of smoking, multiple childbirths, oral contraceptive use, early sexual activity, a high number of sexual partners, a history of sexually transmitted infection, certain autoimmune diseases, and a weakened immune system due to HIV or AIDS. Imaging is recommended for stages 2, 3, and 4A, and metastatic imaging is used to learn how the cancer is responding to systemic therapy for stage 4B or distant recurrences. Treatment options include chemotherapy combinations, immunotherapy, and targeted therapy, depending on the biomarkers present. Radiation therapy for cervical cancer can have long-term and serious side effects on fertility, sexual health, and bowel and bladder function.

nodes.label: Titian
nodes.description: Titian was an Italian Renaissance painter known for his contributions to the art of the Venetian school, though the text does not provide a detailed description of his life or work.

nodes.label: Age
nodes.description: A demographic factor that affects the risk of various diseases, including skin cancer and prostate cancer, with risk increasing with age due to cumulative sun exposure and other factors. It is also a significant factor in determining the need for further testing after a digital rectal exam and influences PSA levels. Age is the leading risk factor for prostate cancer, and the risk of developing the disease increases with age. For bladder cancer, the risk also increases with age, with a higher likelihood of menstruation returning within 2 years after treatment for individuals 35 years of age and under.

nodes.label: Standard treatment
nodes.description: The conventional or usual treatment used in combination with a placebo or a new drug in cancer clinical trials. The standard treatment used in conjunction with placebos or new drugs in cancer clinical trials, which participants continue to receive during the trial. This care is billed to insurance and participants are responsible for copayments. The conventional or established treatment for cancer that is often used in combination with a placebo or a new drug in clinical trials. The conventional cancer care that patients typically receive, which may continue while participating in certain clinical trials. It is billed to—and often covered by—insurance. The conventional treatment used in conjunction with a placebo or a new drug in cancer clinical trials. It provides a baseline for comparison and helps determine the efficacy of the new treatment or drug.

nodes.label: Pathologist
nodes.description: A medical professional who examines tissue samples, including those from sentinel lymph nodes, to determine the presence or absence of cancer cells. They analyze cells and tissues removed during a biopsy to provide cancer diagnosis, staging, and information about biomarker testing. Pathologists assess the grade and type of cancer, including the subtype, and may use techniques such as immunohistochemistry to measure the number of cells with estrogen and/or progesterone receptors. They are members of multidisciplinary teams involved in the planning and implementing of treatment for various types of cancer, such as breast, pancreatic, and prostate cancer. Pathologists may also examine removed tissues under a microscope to determine the extent of cancer and identify concerning or high-risk features. Additionally, they can use microscopes to analyze urine samples for abnormal cells that may indicate cancer, and review biopsy samples under a microscope to determine if a thyroid nodule is cancerous and, if so, the cancer type.

nodes.label: Pancreatic cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer that starts in the pancreas, a large gland in the digestive system that produces enzymes and hormones like insulin and glucagon. Pancreatic cancer is one of the most common cancers and is challenging to treat, but experts are studying new treatments and improving existing ones. A type of cancer that affects the pancreas, with risk factors including smoking tobacco, heavy alcohol use, a less healthy diet, major contact with cancer-causing chemicals, health conditions like diabetes and chronic inflammation of the pancreas, and having close blood relatives with pancreatic, breast, ovarian, or colorectal cancers or melanoma. Approximately 1 in 10 pancreatic cancers are hereditary, with known hereditary health conditions including Hereditary breast-ovarian cancer syndrome (HBOC), Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, Lynch syndrome, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Familial malignant melanoma syndrome, and hereditary pancreatitis. Genetic tests can detect the genes linked to these hereditary conditions. A type of cancer that affects the pancreas, with various stages ranging from stage 0 to stage 4, and can spread to lymph nodes and nearby arteries. Treatment options include surgery and drug treatment, with ongoing research assessing the best timing for these interventions. Some people with stage 1, 2, or 3 pancreatic cancer have surgery to remove cancer from the body, while drug treatment is most often used to control cancer’s growth and reduce symptoms. Clinical trials are also available for people with pancreatic cancer. A type of cancer that affects the pancreas, with five stages ranging from stage 0 to stage 4. It requires a multidisciplinary team of experts for treatment and can benefit from seeking a second opinion on treatment options. A type of cancer that affects the pancreas, with an increased risk associated with BRCA mutations in genes BRCA1 and BRCA2.

nodes.label: Clinical Trials
nodes.description: Research studies that test new drugs or treatment approaches on people with cancer, involving human participants that test new treatments or medical procedures. They have eligibility criteria based on age, cancer type and stage, treatment history, or general health to ensure participant safety and similarity. Participants can leave and seek treatment outside of the clinical trial at any time. The possible benefits and risks are not well understood by many with cancer. These studies provide access to investigational treatments that may, in time, be approved by the U.S. FDA for various types of cancer, including thyroid, bladder, anal, and glioma cancer. They are managed by a research team, involving eligibility criteria and informed consent forms.

nodes.label: BRCA mutation
nodes.description: A specific genetic mutation that can be found in the BRCA genes, associated with an increased risk of ovarian cancer, breast cancer, and other hereditary cancers. Genetic testing can determine if an individual has a BRCA mutation. It is recommended for everyone diagnosed with ovarian cancer, and BRCA status plays a significant role in guiding maintenance therapy decisions. A genetic mutation that can increase the risk of developing certain types of cancer, particularly ovarian cancer, and may make cancers more responsive to PARP inhibitors like Olaparib (Lynparza), Niraparib (Zejula), and Rucaparib (Rubraca). A specific genetic mutation that, if present, can influence the recommendation for maintenance therapy with a PARP inhibitor.

nodes.label: CT Scan
nodes.description: A medical imaging technique that uses x-rays and computer technology to generate detailed images of the body's internal structures. It involves taking multiple x-ray images from various angles and combining them into a single picture. Often uses contrast for better visualization. A CT scan can be used to look for bleeding in the brain, monitor for signs of cancer in nearby lymph nodes or in other parts of the body, guide a lymph node biopsy, or check for cancer spread to the liver, lungs, or other organs. It is often combined with PET to form a PET/CT scan, providing more detailed images. A CT scan is usually completed in less than 30 minutes and may involve lying face-up on a table that moves through a tunnel-like machine and using a contrast agent. It is also used in the simulation process before EBRT begins to obtain pictures of the cancer site(s).

nodes.label: Imaging
nodes.description: A medical procedure that uses technology to create images of the inside of the body to help diagnose and monitor diseases. In the context of basal cell skin cancer, imaging may be used as one of the tests to diagnose the condition. A medical procedure that can be conducted before, during, or after a biopsy, and after cancer treatment to assess its effectiveness and recurrence. Imaging methods for prostate cancer include MRI, CT, PET, ultrasound, bone scan, or a combination of these. A medical procedure used to determine the extent of the cancer. A diagnostic procedure used in surveillance, typically ordered if new or worsening symptoms occur or if other findings suggest recurrence or spread. The frequency and specific types of imaging tests vary depending on the cancer stage. A general term for medical imaging tests used to learn how cervical cancer is responding to systemic therapy for stage 4B or distant recurrences. The use of tests to create images of the body's internal structures, used to locate, size, and characterize brain tumors and other conditions.

nodes.label: HER2
nodes.description: HER2 is a protein involved in normal cell growth. Higher amounts of HER2 may be present in breast cancer, leading to the classification of the cancer as HER2-positive. A cell protein targeted by certain therapies, such as ADCs, to deliver chemotherapy. It is involved in the growth and division of cells.

nodes.label: Clinical Stage
nodes.description: A rating given before any treatment for cancer, based on a physical exam, biopsy, and imaging tests, such as cN1 or cMIn mouth cancer. The rating given before any treatment for cancer, based on a physical exam, biopsy, and imaging tests. It is denoted by the letter 'c' and provides an initial assessment of the cancer stage before any treatment is administered. A rating given before any treatment for breast cancer, based on a physical exam, biopsy, and imaging tests. Examples include cN2 or cM. The rating given before any treatment for cancer staging, based on a physical exam, biopsy, and imaging tests. An example is cN2 for nasopharyngeal cancer, indicating imaging and biopsy results before any treatment as part of an initial diagnosis.

nodes.label: lymph nodes
nodes.description: Small, bean-shaped structures that catch and filter out foreign particles and harmful cells, including cancer cells. Found in high numbers in the neck, groin, and armpits. Small, bean-shaped structures that are part of the lymphatic system, which helps to filter and remove waste from the body. In the context of rectal cancer, the presence or absence of cancer in removed lymph nodes is assessed by the pathologist as part of the surgical staging process. If cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes, it is classified as stage 3. Organs of the lymphatic system where B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma typically grows, as opposed to the bone marrow. A part of the body where cancer can be diagnosed using an FDG PET-CT scan, which can help find cancer in distant sites.

nodes.label: Cervical Cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer that affects the cervix, a part of the female reproductive system. Chemoradiation is often used to treat this condition, especially for locally advanced cases that have not spread to the liver, lungs, or bones. A type of cancer involving the cervix, for which brachytherapy can be used as a treatment. It can be treated using high dose-rate (HDR) or low dose-rate (LDR) brachytherapy, with most centers currently using HDR. Treatment is typically given in 3 to 5 sessions over 2 weeks.

nodes.label: Radiation therapy
nodes.description: A medical treatment that uses high-energy rays or particles to kill cancer cells or shrink tumors, involving two main types: external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) and brachytherapy. It can also be used to treat pain caused by cancer and is one of the many treatment options available for advanced-stage prostate cancer, along with hormone therapy, chemotherapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, radiopharmaceuticals, surgery, and other therapies. Radiation therapy can cause side effects such as skin rash or redness, problems swallowing, dry mouth, thick saliva, changes in taste, and tiredness, which typically start during treatment and stop shortly after, but some can occur years later. Fertility and family planning risks may be discussed with the patient, and they may be referred for counseling about fertility preservation options.

nodes.label: Systemic Therapy
nodes.description: A type of cancer treatment that affects the entire body, often involving substances traveling in the bloodstream to reach cells throughout the body. It includes chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy, and is typically given intravenously in cycles of treatment days followed by days of rest. Systemic therapy can be used alone or in combination with other treatments like radiation therapy, chemotherapy, or immunotherapy, and is particularly useful for treating high-risk or very high-risk Squamous Cell Skin Cancer, metastatic CSCC, or when surgery and radiation therapy cannot remove cancer. Immunotherapy with an immune checkpoint inhibitor is a recommended treatment option if eligible and if surgery, radiation therapy, or platinum-based chemotherapy are not possible or were not successful. Certain herbal supplements might need to be avoided or stopped due to potential drug interactions.

nodes.label: Doctor Visits
nodes.description: In-person medical appointments with healthcare professionals, as mentioned in the text. Medical appointments with a healthcare professional, where questions can be asked and notes taken. Medical appointments with healthcare professionals for diagnosis, treatment, or follow-up. It is recommended to bring someone along for support or have someone join by phone or in person for telehealth visits. Appointments with healthcare professionals for discussing diagnosis, treatment, and other aspects of breast cancer management. Regular appointments with a healthcare provider where patients can discuss their health, symptoms, and treatment options.

nodes.label: Progenitor Cells
nodes.description: Intermediary cells formed from blood stem cells that will become red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. They are also known as precursor cells. Cells that develop from blood stem cells and eventually mature into specific types of blood cells such as red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. They are also known as precursor cells. Intermediary cells that develop from blood stem cells and eventually become red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. They are also known as precursor cells.

nodes.label: Open MRI
nodes.description: A type of MRI scan with a magnetic top and bottom, allowing for an opening on each end. It has a larger, more open space compared to closed MRIs and is less common than closed MRIs. Open MRIs are often used for imaging the brain and can help reduce claustrophobia.

nodes.label: Closed MRI
nodes.description: A type of MRI scan with a capsule-like design where the magnet surrounds the patient, often used for imaging the brain and taking longer to perform than CT scans. It has a smaller, enclosed space and is more common than open MRIs, potentially causing claustrophobia in some patients. Contrast is often used in closed MRIs.

nodes.label: Adrenocortical carcinoma
nodes.description: A type of adrenal cancer that originates in the adrenal glands, affecting children ages 5 and under and adults in their 40s and 50s. It can be cured if caught early, but the chances of cure decrease if the cancer has spread beyond the adrenal glands. Symptoms may include weight gain, muscle weakness, hormonal changes, nausea, vomiting, abdominal bloating, back pain, fever, loss of appetite, and loss of weight without trying. Risk factors include certain genetic conditions such as Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, Carney complex, Familial adenomatous polyposis, Hereditary paraganglioma-pheochromocytoma syndrome, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Lynch syndrome, Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1, Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2, Neurofibromatosis type 1, and Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, which can also increase the risk of developing a kidney tumor.

nodes.label: MSH6
nodes.description: MSH6 is a gene that, when mutated, can increase the risk of different types of cancer, including prostate, breast, ovarian, pancreatic, and skin cancer (melanoma). Germline mutations in this gene are associated with an increased risk of cancer in general. A gene associated with germline mutations that can put an individual at risk for prostate cancer, colorectal and uterine cancers, and skin cancer (melanoma). MSH6 is a gene that, when mutated, can increase the risk of different types of cancer. It is one of the genes typically looked at in hereditary gene testing for prostate cancer. A gene associated with inherited mutations that can increase the risk of developing certain cancers, including prostate cancer, colorectal cancer, and other cancers.

nodes.label: Antimetabolites
nodes.description: A type of chemotherapy that prevents the building blocks of DNA from being used, with examples including Cladribine (Mavenclad), Clofarabine (Clolar), Cytarabine (Ara-C), and Fludarabine, each causing different side effects.

nodes.label: T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma
nodes.description: A type of cancer mentioned in the text, characterized by the growth of T-cell lymphoblasts in the thymus rather than the bone marrow. A type of lymphoma where cancer cells grow primarily in the thymus rather than the bone marrow, often associated with T-cell lymphoblastic leukemia (T-LL) or T-LBL. A type of cancer that occurs when T-cell lymphoblasts grow mostly in the thymus rather than in the bone marrow.

nodes.label: Surgery
nodes.description: A medical procedure involving the incision and manipulation of body tissues, often used to treat various types of cancer, including basal cell skin cancer, squamous cell skin cancer, ovarian cancer, and bladder cancer. It may involve the removal of cancerous tissue, nearby lymph nodes, or even entire organs, and can be followed by radiation therapy or systemic therapy. Smoking can increase the risk of side effects and complications during and after surgery.

nodes.label: Ureters
nodes.description: Tube-like structures that transport urine from the kidneys to the bladder. Two tubes that carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder. Tube-like structures in the urinary system that carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder. Cancer can start in the ureters, although bladder is the most common site for urothelial carcinoma. The anatomical structures examined during a ureteroscopy, which goes a little farther than a cystoscopy to look at the upper parts of the urinary tract. Tube-like structures that carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder. In an ileal conduit procedure, one end of the ileal conduit tube is connected to the ureters to allow urine to flow into the conduit.

nodes.label: Cryotherapy
nodes.description: A superficial treatment that freezes and destroys precancerous and cancerous cells using a very cold liquid or tool, often involving liquid nitrogen. It can cause a burning sensation during treatment, form a blister and scab that heals over 2 to 3 weeks, and may result in skin darkening or lightening while healing. A treatment option for actinic keratoses, which are pre-cancerous lesions. It involves the use of extreme cold to destroy abnormal cells. A treatment option for actinic keratoses, a type of pre-cancerous lesion.

nodes.label: MRI
nodes.description: An abbreviation for Magnetic Resonance Imaging, an imaging technique that uses strong magnetic fields and radio waves to make pictures of areas inside the body without using radiation, especially good at making clear pictures of areas of soft tissue.

nodes.label: Contrast
nodes.description: Substances used to enhance and improve the images of several organs and structures in the body during imaging tests, not permanent and leaving the body in urine after the test. Different types of contrast are used for CT than for MRI. May cause allergic reactions and might not be used if the patient has a serious allergy or kidney issues. Used in medical imaging procedures such as CT and MRI scans to enhance the visibility of internal body structures.

nodes.label: Small Intestine
nodes.description: A part of the digestive tract where food enters after being broken down into a liquid by the stomach. A part of the digestive system that follows the stomach. Food and drink enter the stomach and move into the small intestine where nutrients are absorbed into the bloodstream. The small intestine is part of the digestive or gastrointestinal (GI) tract.

nodes.label: Biopsy
nodes.description: A medical procedure involving the removal and examination of a small sample of tissue or fluid for diagnostic purposes, often used to confirm the presence of cancer. Biopsies can be performed on various parts of the body, including the skin, lungs, prostate, breast, cervix, thyroid, bones, and lymph nodes. They may involve the use of special tools, needles, or surgical techniques, and can provide important information for guiding treatment plans and determining cancer stage.

nodes.label: NCCN
nodes.description: A nonprofit organization that provides patient guidelines and resources for cancer, including information on adolescent and young adult cancer, fertility preservation, and follow-up exams after skin cancer treatment. It is a group of 27 comprehensive cancer centers in the United States that collaborate to improve and standardize cancer care, and it offers guidelines for patients on immunotherapy side effects. The NCCN also provides recommendations for chemotherapy regimens and has a website and app for patient resources and feedback.

nodes.label: Rituximab
nodes.description: A main immunotherapy drug used for primary CNS lymphoma. It is a monoclonal antibody that hunts for specific proteins on the surface of cancer cells, particularly the CD20 protein. The main immunotherapy drug for primary CNS lymphoma. It is used to treat the cancer by utilizing the body’s immune system. An immunotherapy drug used in the treatment of primary CNS lymphoma, often given in combination with chemotherapy. It can be given on its own but usually works better when given with chemotherapy.

nodes.label: Oropharynx
nodes.description: One of the three parts of the pharynx, located in the throat, includes the back of the roof of the mouth, tonsils, side and back walls of the throat, and the base of the tongue. A part of the pharynx that includes the back of the roof of the mouth (soft palate), the tonsils, the side and back walls of the throat, and the base of the tongue found in the throat. The middle part of the throat near the mouth, one of the three parts of the pharynx, is the area where oropharyngeal cancer occurs and is the focus of the book. A part of the anatomy mentioned in relation to throat cancer, along with the nasal cavity, hypopharynx, base of the skull, jaw, and roof of the mouth.

nodes.label: Carcinoma
nodes.description: A type of cancer that starts in cells that line the inner or outer surfaces of the body. In the kidneys, carcinomas most often start in the cells that line the renal tubules, leading to renal cell carcinoma (RCC). RCC is the most common type of kidney cancer, accounting for about 9 out of 10 cases. Carcinoma is a type of cancer that starts in the cells that line the inner or outer surfaces of the body. Almost all breast cancers are a subtype of carcinoma, which arise in cells that make up the lining (epithelial cells) in the terminal duct lobular units (TDLUs) of the breast, specifically as either ductal or lobular carcinomas. A type of cancer that starts in the cells that line the inner or outer surfaces of the body. Carcinomas are the most common type of breast cancer, and they can be either ductal or lobular, arising in cells that make up the lining (epithelial cells) in the terminal duct lobular units (TDLUs) of the breast. Carcinoma is a type of cancer that starts in the cells that line the inner or outer surfaces of the body. The most common types of breast carcinoma are ductal, starting in the cells that line the milk ducts, and lobular, starting in the lobules of the breast. Carcinoma is a type of cancer that starts in the cells that line the inner or outer surfaces of the body. It is the most common type of breast cancer, and includes subtypes such as ductal and lobular carcinoma.

nodes.label: B-ALL
nodes.description: A type of cancer mentioned in the text, characterized by the growth of B-cell lymphoblasts in the lymph nodes rather than the bone marrow. A type of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) that is more common than T-ALL. B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, a type of ALL that starts in B-cell lymphocytes. It is more common than T-ALL and has a subtype called mature B-cell ALL (also called Burkitt leukemia), which is essentially the same as Burkitt lymphoma but treated differently. In some cases, B-cell lymphoblasts grow mostly in the lymph nodes instead of the bone marrow, leading to B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma (B-LL or B-LBL).

nodes.label: AML
nodes.description: AML, or Acute Myeloid Leukemia, is a type of blood cancer that starts in the stem cells of bone marrow, characterized by abnormal changes in very immature white blood cells called myeloid blasts or myeloblasts. This leads to a buildup of blasts in the bone marrow and blood, causing a deficiency of healthy red blood cells, platelets, and white blood cells. AML does not have stages like other cancers and is diagnosed based on the number of blasts and the presence of certain gene mutations or abnormal chromosomes. Accurate testing is essential for diagnosing and treating AML. Treatment for AML is described as being in phases and involving a multidisciplinary team approach, with the goal of putting the cancer in remission. Results from blood tests, bone marrow aspirate and biopsy, and imaging studies guide treatment decisions. AML is treated with chemotherapy as the standard of care based on past clinical trials, and specific treatment regimens may be based on cancer features or health circumstances. Certain FLT3 mutations such as FLT3-ITD and FLT3-TKD may be targeted in treatment with dostaurin, sorafenib, or quizartinib in conjunction with chemotherapy.

nodes.label: Advanced-stage prostate cancer
nodes.description: Advanced-stage prostate cancer is a form of prostate cancer that has grown outside the prostate and may have spread to other areas in the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or organs like the liver or lungs. It can be separated into two types: regional prostate cancer, where cancer grows from the prostate gland to nearby lymph nodes, and metastatic prostate cancer, where cancer spreads to distant organs. A more severe form of prostate cancer that has grown outside the prostate gland and may have spread to other areas of the body such as lymph nodes, bones, or organs like the liver or lungs, also known as metastatic prostate cancer. Advanced-stage prostate cancer is a type of prostate cancer that has grown outside the prostate and spread to other areas in the body such as lymph nodes, bones, liver, lungs, or other organs. It is also called metastatic prostate cancer. Advanced-stage prostate cancer is a severe form of prostate cancer where cells in the prostate gland grow out of control at an advanced rate, leading to potential fatal outcomes for some patients. Improved detection methods and better treatments have been reducing the number of deaths from prostate cancer in patients of all races and ethnicities. Many people with advanced-stage prostate cancer continue to live with the cancer and, in the end, may die from something else.

nodes.label: MRI
nodes.description: A medical imaging technique that uses radio waves and powerful magnets to take pictures of the inside of the body without using x-rays and radiation. It can be used to visualize the primary tumor and neck, detect cancer spread, stage cancer, and plan treatment. MRI scans can take longer than CT scans and may require contrast agents. They are safe for most people but not for those with certain medical devices or conditions. MRI scans can be either closed or open, with closed MRIs being more common and having a capsule-like design where the magnet surrounds the patient. Open MRIs have a magnetic top and bottom with openings on each end. MRI scans are often used as an alternative to CT scans when contrast agent use is not possible, especially for looking at the abdomen, liver, or spine. They can provide a more detailed view of the cancer within the prostate and can be used to check for cancer recurrence after treatment. MRI scans can take 1 to 2 hours, including 30 to 60 minutes of actual scanning time, and require patients to remain motionless during each scan. They may require a gel and a light coil device or blanket for patient comfort. MRI scans can be used in conjunction with a computerized navigation system for targeting and removing a brain tumor sample with precision. They can also be used to find out if there are any lesions in the spine when cancer cells are found in the spinal fluid or if symptoms are present. MRI scans can be used to learn the extent of anal cancer in the pelvis, involving a magnetic field and radio waves to make pictures of areas inside the body. Unlike a CT scan, MRI does not use radiation and may be combined with positron emission tomography (PET). PET involves injecting radioactive glucose into the body and detecting it with a special camera during the scan. Cancer cells appear brighter than normal cells because they use sugar more quickly. MRI scans are recommended for surveillance after recurrence treatment, involving a magnetic resonance imaging scan of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast.

nodes.label: Lungs
nodes.description: A pair of spongy, air-filled organs located in the chest cavity, responsible for the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide between the air and the bloodstream. During a physical exam, a healthcare provider listens to the lungs to assess their function and detect any abnormalities. The lungs are surrounded by a thin layer of tissue called the pleural membrane and connected to the windpipe (trachea) by two large breathing tubes called bronchi. Inside the lungs are small tubes (bronchioles) and small air sacs (alveoli). The left lung has 2 lobes and the right lung has 3 lobes. Lungs are an organ that can be affected by the spread of cancer cells from various primary tumors, including throat, breast, prostate, nasopharynx, cervical, thyroid, stomach, bladder, anal, and lung cancer.

nodes.label: Urethra
nodes.description: A tube that carries urine from the bladder to the outside of the body, and through which semen is released during ejaculation. It is part of the urinary tract and is involved in the elimination of urine from the body. The prostate surrounds the urethra just beneath the bladder. Cancer can start in the urethra, although bladder is the most common site for urothelial carcinoma. The proximal urethra is the part of the urethra that goes through the prostate. A flexible tube called a catheter is inserted into the urethra to reach the bladder for intravesical therapy.

nodes.label: glioma
nodes.description: A type of brain tumor, which can be low-grade or high-grade. Low-grade gliomas generally grow slowly and can develop for years before diagnosis, while high-grade gliomas can grow quickly, developing in months or weeks. Symptoms of gliomas can include headaches, seizures, fatigue, nausea, and vomiting.

nodes.label: Computed Tomography (CT)
nodes.description: A type of imaging that takes many x-rays of the same body part from different angles and combines them to make a single detailed image. The main imaging test used to see colon cancer in the body, involving lying face-up on a table that moves through a tunnel-like machine, with the use of contrast to make the pictures clearer. The contrast is injected into the vein and mixed with a liquid to drink. A medical imaging technique that uses x-rays to create cross-sectional images of the body, often used to look for cancer that has spread beyond the bladder. A medical imaging technique that takes many pictures of areas inside the body using x-rays, combines them using a computer to make one detailed picture, and may use contrast to make the pictures clearer. It is used to learn the extent of anal cancer in the anus and nearby areas, and to look for areas of cancer beyond the pelvis. CT scans may be combined with positron emission tomography (PET). CT scans use x-rays and may cause allergic reactions to contrast agents. They require the patient to lie face-up on a table that moves through a tunnel-like machine and may involve drinking oral contrast or receiving an injected contrast agent.

nodes.label: Blood Stem Cells
nodes.description: The cells that give rise to increased amounts of myeloid progenitor cells in CML. They are the origin of the disease. Early blood-forming cells found in bone marrow that give rise to all types of blood cells, including red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Also known as hematopoietic stem cells. Specialized cells that can develop into different types of blood cells. They are grown and restored through stem cell rescue procedures to help the body's immune response and blood production.

nodes.label: Germline Testing
nodes.description: A type of genetic testing done using a sample of blood, urine, or saliva to look for characteristic changes in genes associated with cancer risk. It is recommended for those with prostate cancer and certain family history or high-risk factors. A type of genetic testing used to identify inherited risks for cancer.

nodes.label: Lymph Nodes
nodes.description: Small, bean-shaped structures found throughout the body that are part of the lymphatic system, involved in the filtering and storage of lymphatic fluid and white blood cells. They filter lymph fluid, trap pathogens, and are involved in the production and storage of lymphocytes. Lymph nodes are a crucial component of the immune system's defense against pathogens and can be affected by various types of cancer, including anal, bladder, esophageal, gastric, ovarian, and skin cancer. They can be removed, tested, or monitored using imaging techniques such as MRI to determine cancer spread and staging decisions.

nodes.label: Epithelium
nodes.description: The innermost lining of the esophagus wall, normally made up of flat, thin cells called squamous cells. The innermost layer of cells that covers the inside of the gallbladder and bile ducts. The lamina propria is a type of connective tissue found under the epithelium. A type of tissue covering the inside of the gallbladder and bile ducts, with the lamina propria found under it. The surface layer of the oral mucosa containing stratified squamous cells, which are thin, flat cells. It may be nonkeratinized or keratinized depending on the region of the mouth. The surface layer lining the inside of the mouth, composed of squamous cells, where squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) originates. The outer surface of the ovaries, where most ovarian cancers are found. The epithelium is a type of tissue that covers and protects the internal organs and structures of the body. In the context of ovarian cancer, epithelial ovarian cancer refers to cancer that originates in this outer layer of the ovary. A thin, moist layer of cells that forms the interior stomach lining. It produces a sticky, thick liquid called mucus that protects the stomach.

nodes.label: Physical Exam
nodes.description: A medical examination of a patient's body to assess their overall health, often conducted by a healthcare provider. It involves checking various aspects of a patient's health, such as temperature, blood pressure, pulse, and breathing rate, height and weight, lungs and heart, eyes, ears, nose, and throat, and skin. It is often conducted in conjunction with a medical history to gather information about a patient's health.

nodes.label: Tumor
nodes.description: An abnormal growth or mass of cells, which can be either benign or malignant and may lead to symptoms if they grow large enough to press on nearby organs. Tumors can be classified based on their depth of penetration into the rectal wall, with a T1 tumor indicating that the tumor has not grown beyond the second (muscle) layer of the rectal wall. They can also grow and spread to other parts of the body, and may be tested for specific DNA mutations, protein levels, or other molecular features to guide treatment decisions. In the context of adrenal cancer, tumors can be either benign or malignant. A medical condition characterized by the abnormal growth of cells, which can be cancerous and may be indicated by an irregular or hardened part of the prostate during a digital rectal exam. A growth associated with gliomas, whose growth can be slowed down for a period of time with treatment. A mass of abnormal cells that grows in the bladder wall, with different stages indicating the extent of its growth and spread.

nodes.label: CHEK2
nodes.description: CHEK2 is a gene that, when mutated, can increase the risk of different types of cancer, including prostate, breast, ovarian, pancreatic, and skin cancer (melanoma). Germline mutations in this gene are associated with an increased risk of cancer in general. A gene associated with germline mutations that can put an individual at risk for prostate cancer, breast cancer, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, and skin cancer (melanoma). CHEK2 is a gene that, when mutated, can increase the risk of different types of cancer. It is one of the genes typically looked at in hereditary gene testing for prostate cancer. A gene associated with inherited mutations that can increase the risk of developing certain cancers, including prostate cancer. A gene that may have mutations in the family history, associated with an increased risk of prostate, breast, ovarian, and certain other cancers.

nodes.label: Medical Records
nodes.description: Documents containing medical information, such as blood tests, imaging results, and pathology reports, which can be organized and stored in a medical binder. Documents containing detailed information about a patient's medical history, diagnoses, treatments, and test results. Patients are advised to create files for these records along with insurance forms and test results. Documents that contain detailed information about a patient's medical history, diagnoses, treatments, and test results, often maintained by healthcare providers. Documents containing detailed information about a person's health history, treatments, and medical conditions, including cancer, that need to be organized and kept in order. A type of medical document that patients should organize and keep with their medical documents.

nodes.label: Squamous Cell Skin Cancer
nodes.description: A type of skin cancer that often begins as scaly patches on the skin and can become solid and misshapen. It is also known as cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC). This type of cancer can be diagnosed through a skin biopsy, which involves removing a sample of the lesion and testing it for cancer. Skin biopsies are done using a local anesthetic and should remove as much of the suspected area as possible for an accurate diagnosis to be made. Squamous Cell Skin Cancer is the second most common type of skin cancer, highly treatable and can often be cured. Risk factors for CSCC include sunburns, excessive sun exposure, actinic keratoses, weakened immune system, and certain genetic syndromes. CSCC can form in old wounds, burns, or scars, which is known as Marjolin’s ulcer and may be harder to treat. Diagnosis involves a complete head-to-toe skin exam, lymph node exam, and possibly a skin biopsy to remove a sample and test it for cancer. Treatment options for Squamous Cell Skin Cancer include various types of surgery, topical therapies, and in some cases, systemic therapy. If metastatic and not treatable with surgery and/or radiation, systemic therapy is recommended.

nodes.label: Fertility
nodes.description: The ability to conceive and carry a pregnancy to term, which can be affected by certain types of cancer treatment, such as head and neck cancer, bone cancer, and cervical cancer. Patients should discuss their concerns with their care team, especially if planning a pregnancy, to consider fertility preservation options.

nodes.label: Treatment Process
nodes.description: The overall process of treating primary CNS lymphoma, which involves two distinct phases: induction and consolidation. This process is described in detail in the provided text.

nodes.label: Glioma
nodes.description: A glioma is a type of tumor that grows in the brain, developing from certain brain cells called glial cells, which support the function of nerve cells (neurons) in the central nervous system (the brain and the spinal cord). It is the most common type of malignant brain tumor in adults and can occur at any age, although it is more common in adults than in children. Gliomas can be challenging to treat due to their invasive nature and tendency to blend into normal brain parts, potentially causing harm to healthy brain cells during treatment. They can start in the brain or spinal cord but rarely spread to other parts of the body. Symptoms such as unusual headaches, seizures, and changes in personality may indicate the presence of a glioma. A type of brain tumor that may require a biopsy for diagnosis and treatment, and is often identified using MRI for its ability to show soft tissues and other details that help plan surgery.

nodes.label: Blood Cells
nodes.description: Cells present in blood that float in plasma, including red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. They have various functions such as carrying oxygen, fighting infections, and controlling bleeding. Cells that circulate in the bloodstream and perform various functions in the body. They include red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. These cells are formed from blood stem cells through a process called differentiation. Cells that circulate in the bloodstream and perform various functions in the body. The text discusses three types: red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets, each with specific roles.

nodes.label: Targeted therapy
nodes.description: A type of systemic therapy that targets specific molecules involved in cancer growth and survival, potentially causing side effects such as body aches, rash, high blood pressure, and abnormal bleeding. It can be used to treat various types of cancer, including thyroid, prostate, and squamous cell skin cancer, and may be used in combination with other treatments. Targeted therapies for thyroid cancer are typically kinase inhibitors taken as capsules and are used for cancers that cannot be treated with surgery or radioactive iodine therapy, have returned after treatment, have spread to areas far from the neck, and are continuing to grow. In the context of squamous cell skin cancer, targeted therapies are known as epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitors, such as cetuximab (Erbitux). Targeted therapy is also used in the treatment of AML and may be used as a standalone approach or in combination with chemotherapy, particularly for tumors with specific biomarkers like FRα. It is a form of systemic therapy that focuses on specific or unique features of cancer cells and seeks to stop the action of molecules that help cancer cells grow and/or survive.

nodes.label: Inflammatory Breast Cancer
nodes.description: A type of breast cancer that can be difficult to diagnose, often requiring a referral to a breast specialist and may involve the use of ultrasound or MRI to guide a biopsy. A type of breast cancer described as treatable with systemic therapy, followed by surgery and radiation therapy. The treatment plan is based on estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), and HER2 expression. A type of breast cancer often treated with a modified radical mastectomy. A type of breast cancer treated with chemotherapy, specifically mentioned in the context of using more than one chemotherapy drug or a single agent.

nodes.label: Primary liver cancer
nodes.description: Primary liver cancer is a type of liver cancer that originates in the liver, as opposed to spreading to the liver from another part of the body. The most common type is hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), with a subtype called fibrolamellar hepatocellular carcinoma (FLHC) affecting very few people and usually occurring at a younger age. The second most common type is intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, a cancer of the bile ducts. Primary liver cancer is a type of cancer that starts in the liver. An elevated or rising AFP might be a sign of primary liver cancer, and follow-up steps include more tests if necessary. A type of cancer that originates in the liver, characterized by the presence of nodules that may or may not be cancerous, and for which screening tests such as ultrasound and AFP (alpha-fetoprotein) levels are used to detect and monitor. The most common type in adults is hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).

nodes.label: Bone Scan
nodes.description: A medical imaging technique used to detect whether cancer has spread to the bones, involving the injection of a radioactive tracer into the bloodstream. The tracer is absorbed more by areas of bone damage than healthy bone, and a special camera takes pictures of the tracer in the bones, with areas of bone damage showing up as bright spots. The scan can take about 30 minutes, and patients are asked to hold still during the scan. It may be used if there is bone pain, a high risk for bone metastasis, or changes in certain test results. A bone scan can also be used to monitor treatment and detect metastasis or other abnormalities. It is not always necessary if FDG-PET/CT clearly shows cancer in the bone.

nodes.label: Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP)
nodes.description: A possible test for AML, often used in conjunction with other tests like CBC, differential, uric acid, LDH, B12, and folic acid to assess a patient's metabolic functions and organ health. A test that measures substances in the blood to provide information about organ function, such as the kidneys and liver. It includes creatinine as a component. A medical test that measures substances in the blood to provide information about organ function, specifically the kidneys and liver. It includes tests for creatinine, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), and electrolytes. A diagnostic test that measures substances in the blood to provide important information about various body functions, including kidney and liver health. It can detect higher than normal calcium levels in the blood, a condition known as hypercalcemia, which may indicate bone damage from cancer. A blood test that measures important chemicals, proteins, and other substances in the blood. It helps identify potential health problems in areas like the kidneys or liver by checking for levels that are too high or low.

nodes.label: Colorectal cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer that affects the colon or rectum, often associated with high levels of carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) in the blood. Colorectal cancer can be caused by inherited mutations in mismatch repair (MMR) genes, leading to Lynch syndrome. Monitoring CEA levels can help predict the risk of cancer recurrence. Screening for this cancer is recommended as part of overall health monitoring. Individuals with colorectal cancer tend to have higher levels of carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) in their blood than individuals without the disease. Most colon cancers occur for unknown reasons, but some people are born with inherited cancer syndromes that increase the risk. A term used to describe cancers that form in either the colon or rectum, with an increased risk associated with BRCA mutations in genes BRCA1 and BRCA2.

nodes.label: Targeted Therapy
nodes.description: A type of cancer treatment that uses drugs or other substances to identify and attack specific cancer cells with minimal harm to normal cells. It is a possible option for systemic therapy in clinical trials or as a standalone treatment for patients not eligible for immunotherapy. A type of systemic therapy that is mentioned as one of the approaches that might be used in combination with other therapies, along with chemotherapy and immunotherapy. A type of treatment most often used for recurrent and/or metastatic cervical cancer with specific biomarkers. A treatment option for thyroid cancers that don't respond to other treatments or that have metastasized and are continuing to grow. A type of cancer treatment that targets specific molecules involved in cancer growth and progression, with lenvatinib (Lenvima) and sorafenib (Nexavar) as recommended options for certain cancers. A type of treatment for adenocarcinomas that is more effective for the intestinal type due to its specific mutations.

nodes.label: Anal dysplasia
nodes.description: Pre-cancerous lesions known as low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL), high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL), or anal intraepithelial neoplasia (AIN) that can develop in or near the anus and may prevent anal cancer if identified and treated early. A pre-cancerous condition of the anus, also known as Low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL), High-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL), or Anal intraepithelial neoplasia (AIN). Identifying and treating anal dysplasia may prevent anal cancer. It is characterized by mild to severe dysplasia, and may present with symptoms such as bleeding from the anus, anal itching, or pain in the anal area. A condition characterized by the presence of fast-growing abnormal cells in the anal canal. Anal dysplasia is mentioned as a condition that can be identified or assessed through high-resolution anoscopy (HRA), alongside anal cancer. It is considered a precursor to anal cancer and may require further evaluation and treatment. A condition characterized by the presence of fast-growing abnormal cells in the anal region. It can be identified through medical procedures such as HRA and standard anoscopy. HRA may be more effective than standard anoscopy at identifying anal dysplasia.

nodes.label: Surgery
nodes.description: A medical procedure involving the removal of tissue, typically performed under general anesthesia and taking 3 or more hours to complete, with recovery times varying depending on the extent of the surgery. It can be used to treat various types of cancer, including ovarian, pancreatic, breast, and colorectal, and may involve the removal of organs or lymph nodes. Surgery may not always be an option due to the location of the tumor or other health problems.

nodes.label: Thyroid Cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer often diagnosed earlier in adulthood, particularly in adults aged 18 to 33 years. Those assigned female at birth are 3 times more likely to be diagnosed with thyroid cancer compared to those assigned male at birth. Risk factors include radiation exposure, such as from past head or neck radiation treatment for childhood cancers. A type of cancer involving the thyroid gland, diagnosed through techniques such as ultrasound and biopsy. A type of cancer affecting the thyroid gland, with various subtypes including papillary, follicular, and oncocytic carcinoma. Treatment options include active surveillance, RAI therapy, thyroid hormone replacement therapy, external beam radiation therapy, targeted therapy, and clinical trials. Differentiated thyroid cancers, such as papillary, follicular, and oncocytic carcinoma, usually grow slowly and have good treatment outcomes. A specific type of cancer that can spread to areas far from the neck, forming metastatic tumors. A type of cancer that affects the thyroid gland. It can be papillary, follicular, or oncocytic, and may spread to other parts of the body, forming metastatic tumors. Treatment options include RAI therapy, targeted therapy, or monitoring.

nodes.label: Breast Cancers
nodes.description: A group of diseases characterized by the uncontrolled growth of cells in the breast tissue, with variations in their characteristics and treatments.

nodes.label: Stage 4
nodes.description: A stage of ovarian cancer where cancer has spread to other parts of the body. There are two subcategories: Stage 4A – there are cancer cells in the fluid around the lungs (malignant pleural effusion). The final stage in the classification of cancer, where the cancer has spread to other parts of the body. It includes subtypes Stage 4A and Stage 4B. The fifth and most advanced stage in the TNM system for colon cancer, indicating that the cancer has spread to areas outside the colon and nearby lymph nodes, most often to the liver and/or lungs. The most advanced stage of bladder cancer, where the cancer has grown through the bladder wall and may have spread to lymph nodes or organs far from the bladder.

nodes.label: Nasopharyngeal cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer affecting the nasopharynx, a part of the throat connecting the back of the nose to the back of the mouth. It is the focus of the book and is characterized by the formation of a primary tumor in the nasopharynx area. Symptoms are similar to other less serious conditions and many people don't have symptoms until the cancer reaches an advanced stage. A type of cancer that originates in the nasopharynx, often associated with the Epstein-Barr virus. A type of cancer for which HPV testing might be done in some cases, as stated in the text.

nodes.label: Platelets
nodes.description: A type of blood cell that helps control bleeding. They are also known as thrombocytes. Cells in the blood that contribute to clotting, thereby preventing or stopping bleeding. They are responsible for making the clot that stops or prevents bleeding. Platelets (PLTs or thrombocytes) are responsible for controlling bleeding. They are formed from blood stem cells and undergo differentiation into mature cells. Small cell fragments that help control bleeding. They are also known as thrombocytes and are formed from blood stem cells. A type of blood cell that helps control bleeding. Also known as thrombocytes or PLTs.

nodes.label: Chemotherapy
nodes.description: A type of systemic therapy that uses drugs to kill cancer cells or stop them from growing, often administered in cycles involving treatment days followed by rest days. It can be used as a standalone treatment or in combination with other therapies, such as immunotherapy, radiation therapy, or stem cell transplant. Chemotherapy can have side effects including nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, hair loss, mouth sores, fatigue, and increased risk of lung problems, especially for smokers and vapers. It is a standard of care for treating acute myeloid leukemia (AML), ovarian cancer, and mediastinal gray zone lymphomas (MGZL), classical Hodgkin lymphoma (CHL), and non-Hodgkin large B-cell lymphoma (NHL). It can also be used for prostate cancer, colon cancer, and other types of cancer. Chemotherapy involves the use of powerful drugs that can have long-term side effects including other cancers, heart disease, and infertility.

nodes.label: Multidisciplinary Care
nodes.description: A type of care involving numerous doctors, specialists, and allied health providers during the diagnosis and treatment of a disease, such as primary CNS lymphoma. A type of care where multiple healthcare providers work together as a team to help manage and treat primary CNS lymphoma, involving coordination and communication between various specialists and allied health providers. A type of care where a team of doctors, specialists, and allied health providers work together to help cancer patients. It is mentioned as a key aspect of treating primary CNS lymphoma.

nodes.label: Staging System
nodes.description: A system created by the American Joint Committee On Cancer (AJCC) to determine how much cancer is in the body, where it is located, and what subtype it has, used in mouth cancer staging. A system created by the AJCC to determine the extent of cancer in the body, where it is located, and what subtype it is. The system includes information on tumor size, lymph node status, and distant metastasis, and is used to predict prognosis and make treatment decisions. A standard way of describing the extent of cancer in the body, used to guide treatment after surgery. There are two staging systems for ovarian cancer, developed by the AJCC and FIGO. A system created by the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) to determine the extent of NPC at the time of diagnosis, including tumor size, lymph node status, and distant metastasis. The staging system is used to predict prognosis and make treatment decisions.

nodes.label: Imaging Tests
nodes.description: A type of diagnostic test that involves the use of imaging technology to check for signs of cancer recurrence as part of surveillance care. A type of test used to stage the cancer, along with blood tests and a biopsy. The biopsy sample will be tested for hormone receptors (estrogen and progesterone) and HER2 receptors. A type of diagnostic test used to stage cancer, often performed alongside blood tests and biopsies. Medical tests that take pictures of the inside of the body to visualize internal structures and detect abnormalities, used in cancer diagnosis and monitoring. Diagnostic tests used to check for the extent of cancer, including CT, PET, and/or MRI scans. A type of test included in the testing process for stomach cancer, using imaging techniques to visualize internal structures. A type of diagnostic test used in surveillance for anal cancer, particularly for stage II and III anal cancers in complete remission after treatment. Recommended annually for 3 years, involving a CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis with contrast, or a CT of the chest without contrast and an MRI of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast.

nodes.label: Hospital
nodes.description: A healthcare institution that can be referred to for experience in treating a specific type of cancer. A large institution providing medical treatment and care, including specialized departments for certain types of cancer. Patients with bone cancer are encouraged to find a hospital with experience in diagnosing and treating this condition. A large medical facility where medical and surgical treatment is provided. Cystoscopy procedures can be done in a hospital, and if a tumor is found, it will need to be removed in an operating room at a hospital. A medical facility that may treat anal cancer. Patients may ask if there is a nearby hospital that specializes in anal cancer. A medical facility where patients receive treatment for various conditions, including anal cancer. It is mentioned as a potential resource for patients.

nodes.label: Abdominoperineal Resection (APR)
nodes.description: A type of transabdominal surgery used for tumors in the lower rectum that may have grown into the anus or nearby muscle, involving removing the rectum, anus, and creating a permanent colostomy. A surgical procedure involving the removal of the anus and the creation of a permanent colostomy for stool to leave the body. It is typically used for anal cancer that does not respond to initial treatment or returns after treatment.  A surgical procedure with questions about its necessity, the tissues or organs to be removed, and muscle flap reconstruction. A type of surgery for anal cancer that does not respond to initial treatment or returns after treatment, removing the anus, rectum, nearby cancerous lymph nodes, and other tissues.

nodes.label: Primary Central Nervous System Lymphoma
nodes.description: A type of lymphoma that primarily affects the central nervous system, typically developing in the brain tissue. It is treated with various medications, including methotrexate, and can cause side effects that vary depending on factors such as the drug, the amount taken, the length of treatment, and the individual patient. Treatment options may include high-dose methotrexate chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and stem cell rescue. Clinical trials are recommended for this condition, and a multidisciplinary team provides care, discussing options such as corticosteroids, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and stem cell rescue. It can also affect the central nervous system specifically in the eyes and may be treated with radiation therapy, targeted therapy, and chemotherapy.

nodes.label: Head And Neck Cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer that can affect the health of the jaw, teeth, and gums, requiring patients to inform their dentists and maintain regular dental care.

nodes.label: Placebo
nodes.description: A dummy or inactive substance used as a comparison in some clinical trials to determine the effectiveness of an investigational drug or treatment approach. An inactive version of a real medicine, almost never used alone in cancer clinical trials. It is common to receive either a placebo with a standard treatment or a new drug with a standard treatment. Participants are informed if a placebo is part of a clinical trial before they enroll. An inactive version of a real medicine that is almost never used alone in cancer clinical trials but is commonly given with a standard treatment or a new drug. An inactive version of a real medicine, almost never used alone in cancer clinical trials. It is common to receive either a placebo with a standard treatment or a new drug with a standard treatment. Participants are always informed if a placebo is part of a clinical trial before enrolling. An inactive version of a real medicine that is almost never used alone in cancer clinical trials, but is commonly given alongside a standard treatment or a new drug. An inactive version of a real medicine, almost never used alone in cancer clinical trials, but commonly used in combination with a standard treatment or a new drug. An inactive version of a real medicine that is almost never used alone in cancer clinical trials. It is commonly received in combination with a standard treatment or a new drug.

nodes.label: Mutation
nodes.description: A mutation is a change or error in the genetic code that can occur in genes or chromosomes. It can result from various factors and may lead to different outcomes, including microsatellite instability (MSI) or deficient mismatch repair (dMMR). A mutation is an abnormal change in a gene that can result in the production of a wrong or no protein. Mutations can be inherited from parents or occur spontaneously in some cells. They can increase the risk of different cancers and may be present in every cell in the body or only in some cells. A mutation is a change or alteration in the DNA sequence of a gene. Mutations can be inherited from parents or occur spontaneously in some cells, leading to the production of abnormal proteins and potentially causing diseases like cancer. Mutations can be passed down in families, affecting every cell in the body, or they can occur spontaneously in just some cells.

nodes.label: Stage 0
nodes.description: A numbered stage in the TNM system, indicating the least advanced stage of cancer. A numbered cancer stage used to classify tumors, indicating that the tumor is at an early stage and can potentially be completely removed with surgery. The first stage in the TNM system for colon cancer, indicating abnormal cells on the innermost layer of the colon wall that may become cancer and spread into deeper layers of the colon wall. Stage 0 colon cancer is also called carcinoma in situ of the colon. The earliest stage of bladder cancer, affecting only the inner lining of the bladder (urothelial layer). It has two subgroups: Stage 0a and Stage 0is (CIS). The earliest stage of bladder cancer, affecting only the inner lining of the bladder. It has two subgroups: Stage 0a and carcinoma in situ (CIS). Stage 0a describes cancer cells that grow from the inner lining toward the hollow center of the bladder, while CIS is a flat patch of cancer cells that haven't grown any farther than where they started.

nodes.label: MLH1
nodes.description: MLH1 is a gene that, when mutated, can increase the risk of different types of cancer, including prostate, breast, ovarian, pancreatic, and skin cancer (melanoma). Germline mutations in this gene are associated with an increased risk of cancer in general. A gene associated with germline mutations that can put an individual at risk for prostate cancer, colorectal and uterine cancers, and skin cancer (melanoma). MLH1 is a gene that, when mutated, can increase the risk of different types of cancer. It is one of the genes typically looked at in hereditary gene testing for prostate cancer. A gene associated with inherited mutations that can increase the risk of developing certain cancers, including prostate cancer and colorectal cancer.

nodes.label: Spinal Cord
nodes.description: A long, thin extension of the brain that transmits signals between the brain and the rest of the body, and is part of the central nervous system. It is protected by vertebrae and surrounded by cerebrospinal fluid. The spinal cord is a site where leukemia rarely spreads, and can be affected by primary CNS lymphoma, leading to various symptoms and challenges in patients. It is also a common relapse site and a common site for metastatic tumors from thyroid cancer, along with the liver, lungs, muscles, bones, and brain.

nodes.label: Colonoscopy
nodes.description: A diagnostic procedure used to examine the large bowel, including the rectum and colon. A scope is inserted into the anus and guided through the rectum and colon to visualize the interior surface of the large bowel and detect any abnormalities, such as polyps or tumors. It is a common method for detecting and removing polyps before they become cancer. Colonoscopy is often followed by a diagnostic colonoscopy to look for other possible areas of cancer. It is a minor surgical procedure used to remove polyps from the inner lining of the colon wall, often performed as a polypectomy. It is recommended for stage 1 colon cancers 1 year after surgery, and for stages 2 and 3 colon cancers as part of surveillance testing, involving visual examination of the colon for signs of cancer or abnormal growths.

nodes.label: Pharynx
nodes.description: A hollow, muscular tube inside the neck that starts behind the nose and opens into the larynx and esophagus, has three parts: nasopharynx, oropharynx, and hypopharynx. A hollow, muscular tube inside the neck that starts behind the nose and opens into the larynx and esophagus. It has three parts: the nasopharynx, oropharynx, and hypopharynx. A hollow, muscular tube inside the neck that starts behind the nose and opens into the larynx and esophagus, with three parts: the nasopharynx, oropharynx, and hypopharynx.

nodes.label: Primary CNS lymphoma
nodes.description: A type of lymphoma that affects the central nervous system, often diagnosed based on symptoms that develop over several weeks, with common symptoms including neurological changes, vision problems, and pressure-related symptoms from tumor growth. A type of lymphoma that affects the central nervous system, for which NCCN experts recommend considering joining a clinical trial for treatment. A type of lymphoma that primarily affects the central nervous system (CNS), including the brain and spinal cord. Chemotherapy drugs used to treat this condition are usually given intravenously or by mouth, and treatment is often administered in cycles. A specific type of lymphoma that affects the central nervous system. Stem cell rescue is not recommended for everyone with this condition.

nodes.label: Cytarabine
nodes.description: Cytarabine, also known as Ara-C, is an antimetabolite and anthracycline used in the treatment of certain medical conditions. It can be used alone or in combination with other drugs and has different doses, such as Standard, High (HiDAC), and Intermediate Low (LDAC). It might be given as a single dose to reduce a very high white blood cell count. Cytarabine can also be used to treat AML in the fluid that surrounds the spine or brain through intrathecal chemotherapy. A type of chemotherapy used to treat AML, often combined with other chemotherapies in a multi-agent regimen. Cytarabine, also known as Ara-C, is an anthracycline chemotherapy drug used in many treatment regimens. It can be used alone or in combination with other drugs like daunorubicin. It has different doses, such as Standard High (HiDAC) and Intermediate Low (LDAC). It may be used to reduce a very high white blood cell count. It is also used in intrathecal chemotherapy for AML in the fluid surrounding the spine or brain.

nodes.label: Colon cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer that affects the colon. It is associated with Lynch syndrome, which is the most common cause of hereditary colon and uterine cancers. A type of cancer that develops in the colon, often associated with Lynch syndrome and familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP). It can be diagnosed through various tests, including blood tests like CEA and genetic testing for inherited syndromes. A type of cancer that develops in the colon, often associated with high levels of carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) in the blood. Monitoring CEA levels can help predict the risk of cancer recurrence, but it is not always helpful for everyone, especially for pregnant women and smokers. A type of cancer that originates in the colon, often forming in polyps on the lining of the colon but can also form as lesions. This disease is the focus of the chapter, with an emphasis on treatment for non-metastatic cancer. It is important to note that colon cancer can have inherited syndromes related to it, such as Lynch syndrome and familial adenomatous polyposis.

nodes.label: Treatment team
nodes.description: A group of medical professionals responsible for providing instructions on how to prepare for surgery. They may advise stopping the intake of certain medicines for a short time before the procedure. A group of healthcare professionals responsible for providing treatment options and information about clinical trials to patients. A group of medical professionals who provide treatment and information about common and rare side effects of systemic therapies. A group of health care professionals involved in the treatment and care of cancer patients, who can provide guidance on dietary changes and pelvic floor physical therapy for anal cancer survivors.

nodes.label: Contrast Material
nodes.description: Substances used to enhance and improve the images of several organs and structures in the body during imaging tests, not dyes but temporary substances that leave the body in urine after the test. A substance used to improve the quality of the pictures of the inside of the body, making the images clearer. It can be administered orally or through a vein (IV) and is used in various imaging tests such as CT and MRI.
