A substance used to improve the clarity of images in both CT and MRI scans, not a dye but a substance that enhances and improves the images of several organs and structures in the body. It is not permanent and leaves the body through urine immediately after the test. A substance used to improve the quality of the pictures of the inside of the body by making the pictures clearer. Can be taken by mouth or given through a vein and has different types for CT and MRI scans. Substances used to improve the pictures of the inside of the body during imaging tests. They are not dyes but help enhance and improve the images of several organs and structures. The contrast is not permanent and leaves the body in the urine immediately after the test. The types of contrast vary for CT and MRI, and individuals with a history of allergic reactions to contrast may be given medicines to avoid the effects of those allergies. A substance used to improve the quality of the pictures of the inside of the body. It helps enhance and improve the images of several organs and structures in the body, making the pictures clearer. The contrast is not permanent and leaves the body in the urine immediately after the test. The types of contrast vary and are different for CT and MRI. Tell your care team if you have had allergic reactions to contrast in the past. This is important. You might be given medicines to avoid the effects of those allergies. Contrast might not be used if you have a serious allergy or if your kidneys aren’t working well.

nodes.label: ICC Classification System
nodes.description: A classification system for follicular lymphoma that groups grades 1 and 2 as classic FL (cFL). This system is followed by the book.

nodes.label: Bevacizumab
nodes.description: A chemotherapy drug used in the treatment of ovarian cancer, often in combination with other drugs like paclitaxel and carboplatin. A drug, also known as Avastin, that may be added to chemotherapy to stop the growth of new blood vessels that feed the tumor. Bevacizumab is a drug used in chemotherapy, particularly for HRD-deficient and BRCA-mutated cancers. It can be used in combination with PARP inhibitors for maintenance therapy. A medication that can be continued as maintenance therapy if included in recurrence chemotherapy regimen and if there is a BRCA mutation. A biologic targeted therapy called bevacizumab, designed to work with chemotherapy, often given in combination with other medicines. A biologic drug used in the treatment of metastatic cervical cancer, often in combination with other chemotherapy drugs. It is a type of targeted therapy designed to work with chemotherapy.

nodes.label: Maintenance Therapy
nodes.description: A follow-up treatment that may be recommended after chemotherapy if it is effective, providing additional support for the patient's recovery. A type of therapy that can be continued until the cancer grows or spreads, or until the side effects make it intolerable or unsafe to continue. It can involve a PARP inhibitor or bevacizumab, depending on the treatment history and biomarkers. A type of intravesical BCG therapy involving three treatments given in one week at 3 months and again at 6 months after TURBT to prevent recurrence of bladder cancer.

nodes.label: Glioblastomas
nodes.description: The most destructive and dangerous type of glioma tumor, coming from precursor cells that develop into cells like astrocytes and oligodendrocytes. They are categorized by grade, with high-grade glioblastomas growing rapidly. One of the most common types of glioma tumors, developing from glial cells in the brain and spinal cord. Like other gliomas, they can disrupt brain function and be difficult to treat due to their invasive nature. Glioblastomas are one of the three most common types of glioma tumors, characterized by an abnormality or mutation in glial cells that causes them to grow out of control. They are a type of brain tumor that can be difficult to treat due to their invasive and aggressive nature. The most common grade 4 gliomas, characterized by very abnormal tumor cells that grow and spread very quickly.

nodes.label: Hysterectomy
nodes.description: Hysterectomy is a surgical procedure to remove the uterus. When the cervix is also removed, it is called a total or complete hysterectomy. Hysterectomy is a common surgery for ovarian cancer and is often the first treatment option if the patient is willing and able. A surgery to remove the uterus (including the cervix). There are different types of hysterectomy that may be used to treat cervical cancer, such as extrafascial (simple) hysterectomy, which removes only the uterus (including the cervix) and can be performed through the vagina, through the abdomen, or using a minimally invasive approach. This type is most commonly used for stage IA1 cancer. A surgical procedure involving the removal of the uterus, which may or may not include the ovaries depending on the patient's health and the doctor's recommendation. A surgical procedure that removes the uterus, including the cervix, and may also involve the removal of some of the vagina and cervical connective tissue. The ovaries may be removed or left in place, causing surgical menopause if removed. A surgical procedure that involves removing the uterus, which can cause surgical menopause. A surgical procedure involving the removal of the uterus, which makes carrying a pregnancy impossible afterward. It is often the surgical treatment for early-stage cervical cancer.

nodes.label: Radiation therapy
nodes.description: A type of cancer treatment that uses beams of intense energy, such as electrons, photons, or protons, to kill cancer cells. It usually involves 5 daily brief treatments per week over 3 to 7 weeks and should be given by a practicing radiation oncologist. It is an option for people after resection of their cancer or for those who cannot or choose not to have surgery. It can be very effective for small tumors or tumors in areas such as the head and neck. It should not be used in people with certain genetic conditions or connective tissue diseases. It is not recommended for the same area more than once, as it can weaken tissues and affect healing, especially for CSCC on the scalp. A treatment option for squamous cell skin cancer that is used after surgery to kill remaining cancer cells. It is not often used for CSCC unless it has spread elsewhere in the body or surgery and radiation therapy are not possible or were not successful. A recommended treatment option for CSCC if surgery is not an option. It involves using high-energy radiation to kill cancer cells or prevent them from growing. Further treatment may be needed if testing after surgery finds cancer cells in the surrounding tissue removed with the tumor. A type of treatment used for high-risk or very high-risk squamous cell skin cancer in non-surgical candidates, along with systemic therapy.

nodes.label: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL)
nodes.description: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is a type of blood cancer that grows slowly and may not require treatment for years. It is characterized by the presence of cancerous lymphocytes in the blood, which are a type of white blood cell. A type of cancer characterized by the presence of abnormal white blood cells in the blood and bone marrow. It can transform into a more aggressive form known as Richter transformation. Treatment aims to prevent the disease from causing problems and becoming life-threatening.

nodes.label: Blood tests
nodes.description: A type of testing used to analyze the patient's blood for signs of various health issues, including adrenal tumors, hormone secretion, and liver cancer. Blood tests are part of the broader testing process used to diagnose and plan treatment for medical conditions. They involve drawing a sample of a patient's blood to analyze various aspects of their health, such as blood cells, blood sugar levels, or other substances. Results from these tests are used to determine the most appropriate treatment plan for the patient. Patients are encouraged to get copies of their blood test results as part of their medical records.

nodes.label: Metastatic prostate cancer
nodes.description: Metastatic prostate cancer is a type of advanced-stage prostate cancer where cancer cells have spread to distant organs in the body, such as the bones, liver, lungs, or other organs. This type of prostate cancer is characterized by the presence of cancer cells outside the prostate gland, affecting multiple areas of the body. A stage of prostate cancer where the disease has spread to other areas of the body, typically involving bones, liver, lungs, or other organs, and is usually a life-long disease. Metastatic prostate cancer is a stage of prostate cancer where the disease has spread from the prostate gland to other parts of the body, such as the lymph nodes, bones, liver, lungs, and other organs.

nodes.label: Radiation Therapy
nodes.description: A type of cancer treatment that uses high-energy rays or particles to kill cancer cells or stop them from growing. It can be used alone or in combination with surgery or systemic therapy to treat various types of cancer, including squamous cell skin cancer, primary CNS lymphoma, and perianal cancers. Radiation therapy involves the use of beams of intense energy from electrons, photons, or protons and is typically administered in 5 daily brief treatments per week over 3 to 7 weeks. It can have short-term side effects such as skin redness, itching, mild discomfort, and feeling tired, and long-term side effects such as hardening of the skin and soft tissue, change in skin color, spider veins, non-healing ulcers, and cataracts. It can also increase the risk of developing a second cancer in the treated area, especially in young patients many years later.

nodes.label: Esophageal cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer that originates in the esophagus, characterized by the uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells in the layers of the esophagus inner lining. Esophageal cancer is a type of cancer that starts when cells in the epithelium of the esophagus begin to grow out of control. It has two main types: esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) and esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC). Esophageal cancer is a type of cancer that affects the esophagus, typically starting in the innermost layer (mucosa) and growing outward through and along the layers of the esophagus wall. It can spread to nearby lymph nodes, veins, arteries, and organs such as the liver, pancreas, lung, and spleen. The development of esophageal cancer can be slow, with precancerous changes often occurring in the inner lining (mucosa) of the esophagus before symptoms appear. The staging of esophageal cancer is based on the extent of the tumor's spread, with three main categories: early-stage, locally advanced, and metastatic. Esophageal cancer is a type of cancer that affects the esophagus, a muscular tube connecting the throat to the stomach. There are three stages of esophageal cancer: stage 0, stage I, and stage II, with stage II being the most common. Stage II esophageal cancer is contained in the esophagus, often small, and not in any lymph nodes. Locoregional or locally advanced esophageal cancer has invaded other layers of the esophagus wall and/or spread to the lymph nodes or organs near or in direct contact with the esophagus. Cancer can spread to distant parts of the body through the blood or lymphatic system, a process known as metastasis, with distant metastases potentially occurring in the liver, distant lymph nodes, and lung. Esophageal cancer is a type of cancer that can be caused by HPV and is associated with the presence of the p16 protein. A type of cancer that affects the esophagus, a part of the throat. It is mentioned as a type of cancer that can affect the throat, but is not the focus of the book.

nodes.label: Cancer Cells
nodes.description: Abnormal cells that grow and divide uncontrollably, forming a mass of tissue called a tumor. Cancer cells do not behave like normal cells and can invade surrounding tissues. Abnormal cells that grow and divide uncontrollably, forming tumors. They do not follow normal cell growth rules and can invade other body parts. Cells that differ from normal cells in various ways, such as forming a primary tumor, invading surrounding tissues, and spreading to other parts of the body to form metastases. They can arise from epithelial cells in the terminal duct lobular units (TDLUs) of the breast and can grow into surrounding tissues, leading to invasive breast cancer. Cells that may be tested for in the vitreous or cerebrospinal fluid as part of the diagnosis of primary CNS lymphoma. Abnormal cells that grow out of control, leading to the development of bladder cancer. They are characterized by genetic errors (mutations) and the ability to avoid normal cell death.

nodes.label: Esophageal Cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer that develops in the esophagus, with stages categorized based on how far the cancer has spread, including early-stage, locoregional or locally advanced, and metastatic.

nodes.label: Diagnostic Mammogram
nodes.description: A type of mammogram used for diagnosing cancer, which may use either the standard 2-dimensional (2D) digital mammogram or 3-dimensional (3D) mammogram known as tomosynthesis. It is used for those who have symptoms or whose breasts have changed shape or size, as well as to take a closer look at an abnormal area found in a screening mammogram. A radiologist evaluates the diagnostic mammogram while the patient waits so if additional testing is needed, it can be done right away. An imaging test used in the diagnostic process for breast health, potentially supplemented by ultrasound and breast MRI as needed. A medical imaging technique that uses x-rays to take detailed pictures of the inside of the breast, often used to look at specific areas of the breast that may not be clearly seen on screening mammograms. A type of mammogram that includes detailed pictures of both breasts, used for diagnosis rather than screening.

nodes.label: Anus
nodes.description: The opening at the end of the digestive tract through which stool exits the body, connected to the anal canal by muscles (anal sphincters) that relax to allow stool to leave the body. Removal of the anus during surgery always requires a permanent colostomy.

nodes.label: Thyroid cancer
nodes.description: Thyroid cancer is a type of cancer that affects the thyroid gland, a butterfly-shaped gland in the front of the neck. It is characterized by the uncontrolled growth of cells in the thyroid gland. There are different types of thyroid cancer, including papillary thyroid cancer, follicular thyroid cancer, medullary thyroid cancer, and anaplastic thyroid cancer. Most types of thyroid cancer are curable with the right treatment, which typically involves surgery, radiation therapy, and hormone therapy. A type of cancer that originates in the thyroid gland, which is a butterfly-shaped gland in the neck. It produces hormones that help regulate metabolism and other body functions. The most common cancer in adults aged 18 to 33 years. Risk factors include radiation exposure and a family history of thyroid cancer. Thyroid cancer is a type of cancer that starts as small, often round areas of abnormal growth called nodules in the thyroid gland. It is the most common cancer in adults aged 18 to 33 years. A group of diseases characterized by the uncontrolled growth of cells in the thyroid gland. There are several types of thyroid cancer, including papillary, follicular, oncocytic, medullary, and anaplastic carcinomas, each with its own characteristics and treatment approaches. A type of cancer that affects the thyroid gland, for which surgery is the main treatment and where active surveillance may be an option for very-low-risk cancers.

nodes.label: Squamous cell carcinoma
nodes.description: A type of cancer that originates in squamous cells, often found in the skin but also in other organs like the lungs, thyroid, and esophagus. It is characterized by the uncontrolled growth of squamous cells and can form a tumor. It is treated differently than cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. A type of skin cancer that can spread to nearby lymph nodes, known as regional CSCC, and can be treated with surgery, radiation therapy, or systemic therapy. Biopsies and imaging tests are used to determine the extent of the disease and plan treatment. A subtype of non-small cell lung cancer that starts in the flat cells that line the inside of the airways (bronchi) in the lungs. It accounts for about 3 out of 10 lung cancers. The most common type of nasopharyngeal cancer, forming in the thin, flat cells of the mucus membranes of the nasopharynx. It is the focus of the book and can spread to lymph nodes in the neck and less frequently to the lungs. The most common type of cervical cancer, characterized by areas of abnormal, microscopic cells on the surface of the cervix. It is one of the types of cervical cancer mentioned in the text. The most common type of cervical cancer mentioned as a condition for considering ovarian transposition before starting EBRT. A type of cancer formed in squamous cells, which are found in the tissues that form the surface of the skin and in other areas of the body. It is the most common type of cancer associated with anal cancer and is distinguished from other types of colorectal cancers such as adenocarcinomas.

nodes.label: Blood Tests
nodes.description: A type of test to be organized and stored in folders, focusing on blood samples. A series of medical tests performed during AML treatment and recovery to monitor treatment results, blood counts, and the health of organs like the liver and kidneys. These tests include complete blood count (CBC), differential, and comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP). A type of medical test involving the analysis of a patient's blood, often part of surveillance and follow-up procedures for thyroid cancer. Includes TSH, Tg, and Tg ab tests. Medical tests that involve taking a sample of a patient's blood to check for various conditions or abnormalities.

nodes.label: FIGO system
nodes.description: A medical staging system used by the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) to determine the stage of cervical cancer, including four main stages: I (1), II (2), III (3), and IV (4).

nodes.label: Multidisciplinary team (MDT)
nodes.description: An MDT is a team of health care and psychosocial care professionals from different professional backgrounds who have knowledge and experience in treating acute myeloid leukemia. They are involved in the planning and implementing of treatment, and their expertise is used to guide treatment decisions. A team of health care and psychosocial care professionals from different professional backgrounds who have knowledge and experience in a patient's type of cancer. The MDT is responsible for planning and implementing treatment for breast cancer, and it may include diagnostic radiologists, interventional radiologists, pathologists, surgical oncologists, reconstructive surgeons, medical oncologists, radiation oncologists, anesthesiologists, residents, fellows, nurse practitioners, and physician assistants.

nodes.label: Gliomas
nodes.description: A specific type of brain tumor discussed in the text, occurring in both children and adults. The most common types are astrocytomas, oligodendrogliomas, and glioblastomas, each made of different kinds of glial cells and having unique molecular characteristics and behaviors. A type of brain tumor that develops from glial cells, which support the function of nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord. Gliomas can disrupt brain function, be difficult to treat due to their tendency to invade normal brain tissue, and often start with an abnormality that causes glial cells to grow out of control. The most common types are astrocytomas, oligodendrogliomas, and glioblastomas. Gliomas are a type of brain tumor that can be difficult to treat due to their tendency to invade and blend into normal brain tissue. The exact cause of gliomas is unknown, but they often originate from an abnormality or mutation in glial cells leading to uncontrolled growth. Common types include astrocytomas, oligodendrogliomas, and glioblastomas. Gliomas can be challenging to diagnose and treat, and they tend to recur. Gliomas are a type of brain tumor, specifically identified by the biomarkers present in each type. Treatment options for gliomas are discussed in the next chapter.

nodes.label: Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML)
nodes.description: A serious health condition and type of blood cancer that can cause fatal outcomes if left untreated. It is characterized by the presence or absence of certain gene mutations or abnormal chromosomes and is treated accordingly. AML is a type of blood cancer, and its cells are present in the blood, which is a tissue made up of plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. A type of cancer that affects the blood and bone marrow, characterized by the overproduction of abnormal white blood cells. Flow cytometry and immunophenotyping are used to identify markers on cells, particularly in the immune system, for AML treatment. Additional biopsies like lymph node or skin lesion biopsies may be required for the BPDCN subtype of AML. A specific type of leukemia that involves abnormal changes in very immature white blood cells called myeloid blasts or myeloblasts, preventing them from becoming mature blood cells. A type of cancer affecting the blood and bone marrow, characterized by the presence of abnormal myeloblasts. These blasts crowd out other blood cells, leading to impaired function of the bone marrow or blood. AML is discussed in various chapters of the book, including testing methods, treatment options, and specific subtypes such as APL and BPDCN. A type of leukemia characterized by abnormal changes that prevent very immature white blood cells from becoming mature blood cells, leading to a buildup of blasts in the bone marrow and blood and making it hard for blood to do its work. A diagnosis is confirmed using a bone marrow aspirate and biopsy.

nodes.label: Side Effects of Stem Cell Rescue
nodes.description: Unwanted reactions or symptoms that can occur as a result of the stem cell rescue procedure, particularly from the high-dose chemotherapy used in the process.

nodes.label: Primary care physician (PCP)
nodes.description: A medical professional who provides ongoing primary health care to patients. The patient is advised to keep their PCP informed of changes to their care team list and to maintain open communication with them. PCPs are described as great partners in patient care. A medical professional who provides primary healthcare services and is typically the first point of contact for patients. The PCP is updated regarding any changes in the patient's care, including details about the specific type of cancer, treatment, and dates. A primary care physician (PCP) is a healthcare professional who provides ongoing healthcare services and manages a patient's overall health. Patients are advised to keep their PCP informed of any changes to their contact information and to include relevant details about their cancer, treatment, and symptoms in their contact list. A healthcare professional, typically a general practitioner, that patients should update regarding any changes in their CML treatment. A healthcare professional who provides primary health care services to patients, often serving as the first point of contact for medical concerns. PCPs are encouraged to be kept informed of changes to a patient's contact information and are valued as partners in care. A healthcare professional who provides ongoing medical care for patients and serves as the first point of contact for medical concerns. PCPs are encouraged to be kept informed of changes to the patient's contact information and are considered great partners in the patient's care. They provide ongoing medical care and are involved in the patient's cancer care. A healthcare professional who is a key partner in a patient's care, encouraged to be kept informed of changes to the patient's care team contact list. They provide general healthcare and are involved in the management of chronic conditions.

nodes.label: Testing and Staging
nodes.description: The process of determining the type, stage, and grade of anal cancer, as well as the risks involved, and preparing for a biopsy. It also involves considering treatment options and the impact of various factors on these options.

nodes.label: Testing for ovarian cancer
nodes.description: A series of tests used to learn more about suspected ovarian cancer, including whether surgery is possible. The testing includes abdominal and pelvic exams, imaging tests, biopsies, family history and genetic testing, nutritional and digestive tract health assessments, blood tests, and biomarker testing. These tests can help identify potential symptoms, confirm a diagnosis, and guide treatment decisions.

nodes.label: TURBT
nodes.description: A medical procedure for examining and removing tumors on the bladder wall, typically performed in an operating room under anesthesia. It involves guiding an instrument with a small cutting device through the urethra and into the bladder to remove the tumor. The procedure aims to confirm the initial bladder cancer diagnosis, take a sample of the bladder wall, and remove all visible tumor. Recovery time includes a few days of rest and potential pain or burning when urinating. A second TURBT may be needed to ensure complete tumor removal or for a deeper biopsy sample. A procedure that examines and removes tumors on the bladder wall. It is a transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT). A surgical procedure mentioned in the text, typically performed to remove bladder cancer that hasn’t invaded the muscle layer. It’s followed by intravesical BCG therapy and a full re-evaluation at 12 weeks. A one-time dose of intravesical chemotherapy can be given within 24 hours of TURBT surgery.

nodes.label: Platinum-Based Chemotherapy
nodes.description: A type of chemotherapy that uses platinum-based drugs like cisplatin and carboplatin to stop the growth of cancer cells by killing the cells or stopping them from dividing. It is the most commonly used systemic therapy for cervical cancer and is commonly used to treat metastatic cervical cancer, often involving the use of platinum-based medicines like cisplatin or carboplatin. It is a recommended option for use with radiation therapy, especially when an immune checkpoint inhibitor is not an option or when a patient is not eligible for a clinical trial. It can work well or very well during recurrence treatment, potentially leading to the option of maintenance therapy.

nodes.label: Adrenal tumor
nodes.description: A medical condition referring to a tumor that develops in the adrenal glands, which are located above the kidneys. Adrenal tumors can vary in size and may cause symptoms if they grow large enough to press on nearby organs. The causes of most adrenal tumors are unknown, but hereditary conditions can increase the risk of their development. Diagnosis and treatment planning for adrenal tumors are based on a series of test results, which can include blood tests, imaging tests, genetic tests, and biopsies. A tumor located in the adrenal gland, which can cause hormonal imbalances and related symptoms. Biochemical tests are used to detect and monitor the presence or progression of adrenal tumors.

nodes.label: Screening
nodes.description: A medical examination or test used to detect diseases, such as lung cancer, at an early stage, often before symptoms appear. A process of assessing an individual's level of distress, which is part of their cancer care and can help identify any mental, physical, social, or spiritual issues that may need addressing. Screening is a process of detecting diseases early before symptoms occur, when it is more likely to be cured with treatment. In the context of liver cancer, it involves two recommended tests every 6 months for those at risk: an ultrasound (US) and an alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) test. Follow-up steps include repeating the tests if the AFP is elevated or if nodules are found on the ultrasound.

nodes.label: Mitomycin
nodes.description: An anti-cancer medicine used in chemotherapy regimens for anal cancer, often administered in combination with other drugs like capecitabine, 5-FU, or cisplatin. It is given as a single intravenous dose on the day treatment with capecitabine begins. A chemotherapy drug used in combination with capecitabine, typically administered as a single intravenous dose on the day treatment begins and possibly again when the second 5-FU infusion starts. A chemotherapy drug used in the treatment of perianal cancer, typically administered in conjunction with 5-FU. A single dose is given on the first day of the first 5-FU infusion and may be given again when the second 5-FU infusion begins. A chemotherapy drug component of a recommended regimen for treating cancer that returns to lymph nodes in the groin, often used in combination with capecitabine or 5-FU.

nodes.label: Bladder Wall
nodes.description: The wall of the bladder, a part of the human body involved in the storage and elimination of urine. The text explains that the stage of bladder cancer is measured by how far the cancer has grown into the bladder wall, with numbers ranging from 0 to 4. The wall of the bladder, which is invaded by cancer in different stages. It has a muscle layer and a fatty layer covering the outside. The outer layer of the bladder mentioned in the text. Stage 4 cancer has grown through this layer and may have spread to lymph nodes or organs far from the bladder.

nodes.label: Anatomic Stage
nodes.description: A component of cancer staging based on the extent of cancer as defined by tumor size (T), lymph node status (N), and distant metastasis (M). It provides a general idea of the cancer's spread before specific details are known.

nodes.label: Breast
nodes.description: An organ and a gland found on the chest, composed of milk ducts, fat, nerves, lymph and blood vessels, ligaments, and other connective tissue. It contains glands that can make milk, called lobules, which are connected to the nipple by small tubes called ducts. The breast skin is darker around the areola, and the nipple is the raised tip within the areola. Lymph drains from breast tissue into lymph vessels and travels to lymph nodes near the armpit. The breast is a glandular organ made up of milk ducts, fat, nerves, blood and lymph vessels, ligaments, and other connective tissue. It contains lobules, which are glands that can make milk, and these are connected to the nipple by small tubes called ducts. The breast also includes the areola, a ring of darker skin around the nipple, and the nipple itself, which is the raised tip within the areola. Collectively, the nipple and areola are known as the nipple-areola complex (NAC). Breast tissue drains lymph into lymph vessels, which travel to lymph nodes near the armpit, known as axillary lymph nodes (ALNs). The breast can develop cancer, with different types arising from cells in the lining of the terminal duct lobular units (TDLUs). Anyone, regardless of assigned sex at birth, can develop breast cancer, and treatment is similar across genders. Breast cancer can spread from the primary tumor to other parts of the body through a process called metastasis. An anatomical structure in the human body containing lobules, ducts, fat, blood and lymph vessels, ligaments, and connective tissue. It is the site where breast cancer can develop, particularly in the terminal duct lobular units (TDLUs). The breast is an organ and a gland found on the chest, responsible for producing and secreting milk in mammals, including humans. It is composed of milk ducts and lobules, fat, nerves, lymph and blood vessels, ligaments, and other connective tissue. A glandular organ in humans, composed of milk ducts, fat, nerves, blood and lymph vessels, ligaments, and other connective tissue. It contains glands that can make milk, called lobules, which are connected to the nipple by small tubes called ducts. The darker skin surrounding the nipple is called the areola, and the raised tip within the areola is called the nipple. The nipple-areola complex (NAC) refers to both parts. Breast tissue drains into lymph vessels and travels to lymph nodes near the armpit, known as axillary lymph nodes (ALNs). Breast cancer can start in the cells of the breast and can spread to other parts of the body. The breast is a glandular organ made up of milk ducts, fat, nerves, blood and lymph vessels, ligaments, and other connective tissue. It is also the site of milk production in females and the location of structures like lobules and ducts. Breast is the body part where ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is found and where breast milk is carried to the nipple through ducts. An organ and a gland found on the chest, composed of milk ducts, fat, nerves, lymph and blood vessels, ligaments, and other connective tissue. Behind the breast is the pectoral muscle and ribs, with muscle and ligaments helping hold the breast in place. The breast is a glandular organ located on the chest, composed of milk ducts, fat, nerves, blood and lymph vessels, ligaments, and other connective tissue. It contains glands that can make milk, called lobules, which are connected to the nipple by small tubes called ducts. The darker breast skin is called the areola. Behind the breast is the pectoral (chest) muscle and ribs. Breast tissue contains glands that can make milk, called lobules, which are connected to the nipple by small tubes called ducts. The breast is an organ and a gland found on the chest, composed of milk ducts, fat, nerves, lymph and blood vessels, ligaments, and other connective tissue. It contains glands that can make milk, called lobules, which are connected to the nipple by small tubes called ducts. The breast is also supported by muscle and ligaments. The areola, a ring of darker skin, surrounds the nipple, and the entire complex is known as the nipple-areola complex (NAC). Breast tissue drains into lymph vessels and travels to lymph nodes near the armpit, called axillary lymph nodes (ALNs). A body part in humans, particularly in those assigned female at birth, containing lobules, ducts, fat, blood and lymph vessels, ligaments, and connective tissue. Lobules make breast milk, and ducts carry breast milk from the lobules to the nipple. An anatomical structure in the human body containing lobules, ducts, fat, blood and lymph vessels, ligaments, and connective tissue. Lobules make breast milk and ducts carry breast milk from the lobules to the nipple. A part of the body, specifically the breast, where invasive lobular carcinoma (IBC) can occur and may present symptoms similar to an infection, making diagnosis challenging. The body part from which skin and breast biopsies are taken, and where lymph nodes drain lymph fluid. The body part that is removed in a mastectomy or reconstructed after a mastectomy.

nodes.label: Biomarker testing
nodes.description: A type of diagnostic test used to detect specific molecules or genetic markers associated with cancer, often used in conjunction with other tests to determine a treatment plan. Biomarker testing can involve analyzing a piece of tumor tissue in a lab, testing a sample of blood, or examining features of the cancer, such as mutations. It can provide information about the presence and severity of certain biomarkers, guide treatment decisions, and determine eligibility for certain clinical trials or maintenance therapies. Biomarker testing is recommended for specific types of cancer, such as ovarian cancer and throat cancer, and can be used to identify the presence of HPV in throat cancer. It is also used in the diagnosis and treatment planning of other types of cancer, such as breast cancer, esophageal cancer, and mouth cancer.

nodes.label: Lobules
nodes.description: A component of the breast, glands that can make milk. They are connected to the nipple by small tubes called ducts. Structures within the breast that make breast milk. They are part of the breast anatomy and can be affected by breast cancer, leading to the formation of tumors. Lobules are small clusters of gland cells within the breast that produce milk. They are connected to the milk ducts by small tubes, forming the milk-producing units of the breast. Lobules are structures in the breast that make breast milk and are involved in lobular carcinoma.

nodes.label: Abdomen
nodes.description: A body part, typically the area below the chest and above the pelvis, that may be imaged using MRI, CT scan, or other imaging techniques. It is the region where cancer can invade structures or organs outside of the colon if left untreated, growing through the layers of the colon wall from the inside out. The abdomen is also the part of the body where a colostomy is connected to the outside, a stoma is made in continent urinary diversion procedures, and where stool exits the body through a stoma in colostomy procedures. Surgical interventions through the abdomen can be traditional (big) or minimally invasive (laparoscopic), and it is a major region examined for cancer spread, often along with the pelvis, using CT scans or other imaging methods. Stage 4A cancer has invaded the wall of the pelvis or abdomen, and a radical cystectomy involves cutting into this region, which requires a hospital stay for at least several days and can take 2 to 3 months or longer to recover from.

nodes.label: Weakened Immune System
nodes.description: A condition where the immune system is not functioning properly, making it difficult for the body to fight off viruses, bacteria, and fungi, and increasing the risk of squamous cell skin cancer. This can occur after organ transplantation or due to other health conditions such as lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, HIV or AIDS. A condition that can increase the risk of developing squamous cell skin cancer.

nodes.label: Skin
nodes.description: The largest organ of the body, serving as a protective barrier and playing a role in temperature regulation and sensory perception. It is composed of three layers: epidermis, dermis, and hypodermis. The outer layer of the body that forms the surface lining of the mouth and is similar to the top layer of skin. Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is the most common type of mouth cancer and forms in the thin, flat cells of the mucous membranes of the mouth. A site where leukemia can spread outside the bloodstream. The outer layer of the body, which can be affected by inflammatory breast cancer, causing symptoms such as peau d'orange, skin thickening, edema, and erythema.

nodes.label: RAI Therapy
nodes.description: Radioactive iodine therapy used after total thyroidectomy to kill any remaining cancer cells in thyroid cancer treatment. Radioactive iodine therapy used to kill cancer cells left in the body after surgery. May be used for follicular or oncocytic thyroid cancer. Radioactive iodine therapy, a treatment option for thyroid cancer after total thyroidectomy, particularly if the cancer had spread significantly beyond the thyroid, invaded blood vessels, had a high Tg level, or involved large lymph nodes with cancer. A treatment involving radioactive iodine (RAI) that may be administered after total thyroidectomy. Whole-body RAI imaging may be used to look for cancer after this treatment. A treatment for cancer that involves the use of radioactive iodine (RAI), often considered for cancers that take up iodine, but not always necessary.

nodes.label: Carboplatin
nodes.description: A platinum-based chemotherapy drug used in the treatment of ovarian and cervical cancer, often in combination with other drugs like paclitaxel and bevacizumab. It is also a type of systemic therapy and can be used as an alternative to cisplatin when it is too harsh or cannot be given for other reasons. Repeated use increases the risk of a hypersensitivity reaction.

nodes.label: Bladder cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer affecting the urinary system, specifically the bladder, characterized by the growth of abnormal cells in the inner lining or muscle layer of the bladder wall. It can be muscle-invasive, indicating the cancer has spread through the inner lining and invaded the muscle layer of the bladder wall. Bladder cancer can be diagnosed through various tests including urine cytology, biomarker tests, and cystoscopy with biopsy. It can be classified by stage, with stages 0, 1 being non-muscle-invasive and stages 2, 3, 4 being muscle-invasive. Bladder cancer can also be classified by grade, with low grade being slow-growing and high grade growing more quickly. People who smoke are at a higher risk of developing bladder cancer, with a 3 times greater likelihood of dying from the disease compared to non-smokers. Quitting smoking can reduce the risk of getting cancer and help treatments for bladder cancer work better. Treatments for bladder cancer can cause side effects, which may vary in severity and duration based on the type and length of treatment.

nodes.label: LHRH agonists
nodes.description: Luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone (LHRH) agonists are a class of drugs used in hormone therapies for prostate cancer. They cause the testicles to stop making testosterone. Common examples include goserelin, leuprolide, or triptorelin, which are typically given as injections on a monthly or seasonal basis. LHRH agonists are drugs that stop LHRH from being made, which stops the ovaries from making hormones. They include goserelin (Zoladex) and leuprolide (Lupron Depot).

nodes.label: Early-stage prostate cancer
nodes.description: A stage of prostate cancer characterized by the absence of spread beyond the prostate gland, typically growing slowly and remaining confined to the prostate. Early-stage prostate cancer, also known as localized prostate cancer, is a form of prostate cancer that has not spread beyond the prostate gland. It usually grows slowly and is often curable. This type of prostate cancer is characterized by cancer cells that are contained entirely within the prostate. An early form of prostate cancer that is contained within the prostate gland, typically grows slowly, and is highly treatable and often curable. A stage of prostate cancer characterized by its location within the prostate gland, not visibly spreading beyond it, and typically growing slowly, also known as localized prostate cancer. Early-stage prostate cancer is a type of prostate cancer that has not spread beyond the prostate. It usually grows slowly and stays in the prostate. This stage is also called localized prostate cancer.

nodes.label: Myeloblasts
nodes.description: Very immature or most immature cells formed from myeloid progenitor cells. They are often referred to simply as blasts in CML. Abnormal immature white blood cells found in the bone marrow or blood in AML. They mature into granulocytes, specifically neutrophils, which are types of immune cells that help prevent and control infection. Myeloblasts are a type of myeloid blast, very immature white blood cells that are abnormal in acute myeloid leukemia (AML). They cannot become mature blood cells, leading to a buildup in the bone marrow and blood. Immature cells that develop from myeloid progenitor cells and are involved in the development of myeloid blood cells. They are not directly associated with ALL but are mentioned as part of the broader progenitor cell system.

nodes.label: Neurological Exam
nodes.description: A medical examination involving simple tests to check alertness, thinking, balance, coordination, reflexes, strength, hearing, and senses of touch and smell, and may also include an eye exam to check the health of the nerves in the back of the eyes.

nodes.label: Subtypes
nodes.description: Different types of urothelial cell cancer that have features resembling other types of cells. Some of them include glandular subtype, squamous cell subtype, micropapillary subtype, plasmacytoid subtype, sarcomatoid subtype, nested subtype, lymphoepithelioma-like subtype, microcystic and tubular subtype. It is important to investigate whether a patient has one of these subtypes.

nodes.label: Treatment Plan
nodes.description: A personalized plan made by doctors for cancer treatment, which requires gathering information about the cancer and the patient's general health through various tests and examinations.

nodes.label: Blood
nodes.description: A biological sample obtained from a vein in the arm or other site, used for diagnostic testing. Blood tests, such as a CEA blood test, a complete blood count (CBC), or a chemistry profile, are used to detect the presence of certain substances or abnormalities that can indicate the presence of a disease or condition. Blood is the liquid connective tissue that circulates in the body, carrying oxygen, nutrients, and waste products. In the context of AML, blood tests can be used to detect the presence of myeloid blasts, which are abnormal white blood cells. These blasts must constitute at least 20 percent of all cells in the bone marrow to diagnose AML. Blood is a tissue composed of different cells and plasma that performs essential functions in the body, such as moving oxygen and nutrients, carrying away waste, supporting the immune system, and preventing bleeding. It contains four main components: plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. The biological sample used in the PSA test to measure the amount of prostate-specific antigen (PSA) in the bloodstream. A biological fluid used in genetic cancer risk testing. It is collected by spitting into a cup or using a cheek swab to gather saliva, which is then analyzed for gene mutations.

nodes.label: Metastasis
nodes.description: The process by which cancer cells spread through the blood and lymph to form tumors in other areas of the body. It is mentioned in the context of metastatic squamous cell skin cancer, where it is noted that squamous cell skin cancer does not metastasize often. The spread of cancer to an area of the body such as lymph nodes or lung, potentially requiring a biopsy to confirm the presence of cancer. The spread of cancer to an area of the body such as lymph nodes or lung, which may require a biopsy to confirm the presence of cancer. If there is more than one metastasis, each site may be biopsied. Metastasis refers to the spread of prostate cancer from the prostate gland to other areas in the body. This term is used to describe advanced-stage prostate cancer that has spread beyond the prostate. The process by which cancer cells spread from the primary tumor to other parts of the body, forming secondary tumors. This can occur through the blood or lymph vessels, and is possible even when the axillary lymph nodes are negative for cancer. The spread of cancer to an area of the body such as lymph nodes or lung. A biopsy of the metastasis may be needed to confirm the presence of cancer. If there is more than one metastasis, each site may be biopsied.

nodes.label: Genetic testing
nodes.description: A type of testing used to learn more about a patient's subtype of AML, target treatment, and determine the prognosis. It involves analyzing a person's DNA to identify genetic mutations or other abnormalities that may be contributing to the development or progression of the cancer. It is different from family history or cancer risk testing and focuses on changes in leukemia cells. Genetic testing may be more appropriate for people who have a family history of cancer, have had cancer, have a close relative with bladder cancer, are under the age of 50, have cancer of the upper urinary tract, have a high-grade cancer, or have Lynch syndrome or a family member with Lynch syndrome. It can also be used to identify individuals at risk of developing certain types of cancer, such as Lynch syndrome or familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), and to detect inherited gene mutations in blood or saliva tests. A diagnostic test used to identify inherited (germline) mutations in the BRCA genes and other important genes involved in DNA repair, and is recommended for everyone diagnosed with ovarian cancer to guide treatment decisions. It is sometimes called molecular testing, tumor profiling, gene expression profiling, or genomic testing.

nodes.label: Actinic keratosis
nodes.description: A condition characterized by abnormal skin growths, which can be treated with various topical therapies including calcipotriene, imiquimod, and tirbanibulin.

nodes.label: Stomach cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer that develops in the stomach, often starting in cells that line the inside of the stomach wall and secrete mucus, known as adenocarcinomas. It can grow inwards, forming ulcers or masses, and may spread to nearby lymph nodes, other parts of the stomach, or other parts of the body, including the liver, abdominal lining, lungs, or bone.

nodes.label: Catheter
nodes.description: A thin, long tube often placed in the upper arm that goes into a large vein and stays there until treatment is complete. It is used to deliver systemic therapy, fluids, and blood products into the body. A thin tube used in intraperitoneal (IP) chemotherapy to deliver the medicine directly to the cancer cells in the belly area. The catheter is usually connected to a port placed inside the abdomen during surgery. A device inserted into the reservoir of a continent urinary diversion several times a day to drain urine. A flexible tube used to drain urine from the body. In the context of a neobladder or an Indiana pouch, a catheter may be inserted through the urethra or the stoma to help empty the bladder or pouch, respectively. A flexible tube used to insert medicine directly into the bladder during intravesical therapy. It's also used to drain urine from the stoma into the pouch several times a day.

nodes.label: Primary Care Physician (PCP)
nodes.description: A medical professional who provides ongoing care and coordination for a patient's health, serves as the patient's main point of contact for medical care, and is encouraged to be informed of changes to the patient's care team contact list, including details about the type of cancer, treatments, and their start dates. They play an important role in the care of cancer survivors after finishing cancer treatment.

nodes.label: Checkpoint Inhibitors
nodes.description: A class of immunotherapy drugs that work by blocking certain proteins, improving the body's ability to recognize and attack cancer cells. Recommended for use before colectomy in dMMR/MSI-H cancers, including Pembrolizumab (Keytruda), Nivolumab (Opdivo), and sometimes with ipilimumab (Yervoy). A type of immunotherapy that blocks the natural braking mechanisms in the body to allow the immune system to better identify and fight cancer. They are used to treat bladder cancer and other cancers. A type of cancer treatment that blocks the natural braking mechanisms in the body to allow the immune system to better identify and fight cancer. Includes Keytruda (pembrolizumab), Opdivo (nivolumab), Bavencio (avelumab), and Tecentriq (atezolizumab) as examples for bladder cancer.

nodes.label: Stem Cell Rescue
nodes.description: A type of treatment used for primary central nervous system lymphoma, often combined with chemotherapy. It is an essential part of having a stem cell rescue. A medical procedure used to jumpstart the bone marrow to make more healthy blood cells. It is a way to address damage to hematopoietic stem cells caused by cancer or its treatment. A medical procedure involving high-dose chemotherapy and stem cell transplantation, which can have side effects such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, hair loss, mouth sores, and fatigue. Medicines are available to help reduce these side effects. A type of treatment used for primary CNS lymphoma, often combined with other therapies.

nodes.label: Red Blood Cells
nodes.description: A type of blood cell that carries oxygen throughout the body. They are also known as erythrocytes. Red blood cells (RBCs or erythrocytes) are responsible for carrying oxygen throughout the body. They are formed from blood stem cells and undergo differentiation into mature cells. A type of blood cell that carries oxygen throughout the body. They are formed from blood stem cells and are released into the bloodstream as needed. A type of blood cell that carries oxygen throughout the body. Also known as erythrocytes or RBCs.

nodes.label: ovarian cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer that affects the ovaries. It can be hereditary, with an increased risk associated with BRCA mutations or Lynch syndrome. Ovarian cancer usually starts at an older age than ovarian cancer associated with a BRCA mutation or Lynch syndrome. Genetic testing is recommended for everyone diagnosed with ovarian cancer. A type of cancer that affects the ovaries, a pair of female reproductive organs located in the lower abdomen. Ovarian cancer has two main staging systems: the AJCC system and the FIGO system, both of which are used to describe the extent of cancer in the body and guide treatment decisions.

nodes.label: Barrier Methods
nodes.description: A class of birth control methods that include condoms, diaphragms, cervical caps, and the contraceptive sponge, used to prevent pregnancy. A class of non-hormonal birth control methods that include physical barriers to prevent pregnancy. Examples include condoms, diaphragms, cervical caps, and the contraceptive sponge.

nodes.label: Actinic Keratoses
nodes.description: A precancerous skin condition caused by exposure to the sun over time. It can vary in appearance and may be red, white, tan, or pink in color. Some may even look like warts. Having actinic keratoses increases the risk of developing squamous cell skin cancer. A skin condition associated with an increased risk of developing squamous cell skin cancer. Pre-cancerous lesions that are in the same general area as the Bowen’s lesion and can be treated with superficial treatments like photodynamic therapy. They are characterized by abnormal cell growth in the skin's outer layer. Pre-cancerous lesions that can be treated with superficial treatments, often in the same general area as Bowen’s lesions. A skin condition that may be treated with various therapies, including topical diclofenac, chemical peels, and resurfacing techniques such as laser or dermabrasion. Pre-cancerous lesions that can be treated with photodynamic therapy, cryotherapy, or topical therapy.

nodes.label: MyChart
nodes.description: A personal health record system or account that allows patients to track their appointments, communicate with their care team, and access medical documents. Messages may not be immediately seen by healthcare providers, so urgent concerns should be addressed through the triage phone number.

nodes.label: Vaping
nodes.description: A behavior involving the inhalation and exhalation of vapor from electronic cigarettes or similar devices, which increases the risk of developing various types of cancer and may limit the effectiveness of cancer treatment. The act of inhaling and exhaling the vapor produced by electronic cigarettes or similar devices. It is advised to quit due to its negative impact on cancer treatment and increased risk of lung problems during and after chemotherapy. The act of inhaling and exhaling the vapor produced by an electronic cigarette, a behavior that is also associated with an increased risk of developing bladder cancer and can limit the effectiveness of cancer treatments.

nodes.label: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC)
nodes.description: A specific subtype of kidney cancer, discussed in the text as a key point related to kidney cancer. The most common type of kidney cancer that originates in the cells lining the renal tubules, accounting for almost all kidney cancers and the focus of the book. A type of kidney cancer characterized by tumors that can grow in any part of the kidney and potentially spread to the renal vein and vena cava. Treatment for RCC is based on histology, tumor size and location, and metastasis to other areas in the body.

nodes.label: Cancer
nodes.description: A group of diseases characterized by the uncontrolled growth and spread of abnormal cells, which can affect various parts of the body and may run in families. It can cause symptoms like paraneoplastic syndromes and may impact fertility. Cancer can be diagnosed through various tests and may require treatment decisions based on staging. It can spread to other organs, and early detection is important for effective treatment.

nodes.label: Bone marrow tests
nodes.description: A type of medical test involving the examination of a patient's bone marrow, used to detect abnormalities or diseases, including AML. Bone marrow tests are procedures used to examine the bone marrow for the presence of myeloid blasts and other abnormalities. These tests are part of the possible tests and procedures used to diagnose and treat AML. Bone marrow tests are medical procedures used to diagnose leukemia, a type of cancer that affects the bone marrow. These tests involve taking a sample of bone marrow from the hip bone and examining it under a microscope to look for signs of cancer. Leukemia starts in the bone marrow, so these tests are an important tool for diagnosing and monitoring the disease. A type of test included in the testing process for CML, along with general health tests, blood tests, fertility tests, performance status tests, and heart tests. A medical procedure used to diagnose ALL by examining the bone marrow for the presence of lymphoblasts. Results from these tests, along with blood and imaging studies, are used to determine a patient's treatment plan. Bone marrow tests are medical procedures that involve analyzing samples of a patient's bone marrow to diagnose or investigate certain conditions, including CLL. They are not often needed to diagnose CLL but may be done to find out what's causing low blood cell counts.

nodes.label: Primary CNS Lymphoma
nodes.description: A rare and aggressive cancer that affects the central nervous system (CNS), starting in the brain and spinal cord, involving lymphocytes that grow out of control. It can spread to other areas within the nervous system, such as from the brain to the eyes. Risk factors include an impaired immune system. A type of lymphoma that affects the central nervous system (CNS), including the brain, spinal cord, and eyes. It can be diagnosed through several tests, such as a neurological exam, imaging, biopsies, blood tests, and an eye exam. Treatment options include chemotherapy, radiation therapy, stem cell transplant, and clinical trials. Remission may occur, but the disease often relapses in the brain, spinal cord, or eye, and can be fatal for some patients. A rare and aggressive cancer that most often affects the brain, but can also occur in the spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and/or the eyes. It can't be cured in most people, but it can be treated, which can slow down the lymphoma's growth, reduce its symptoms, and prolong life. It often relapses in the brain, spinal cord, or the eye, even with the best treatment. A type of cancer that affects the central nervous system, specifically the brain and spinal cord, characterized by the development of lymphoma cells. It can present with various symptoms such as slower thinking, memory loss, difficulty moving or walking, trouble speaking, inability to do everyday activities, changes in behavior, losing one’s sense of self, and other problems. A type of cancer that affects the central nervous system, which may present with one or multiple tumors on an MRI scan. A type of cancer that affects the central nervous system, specifically the brain and spinal cord. It can cause distress and psychological symptoms such as depression and anxiety in patients and their caregivers. A type of cancer affecting the central nervous system, specifically the brain and spinal cord. It is treated with chemotherapy and, in some cases, radiation therapy. A type of cancer that affects the central nervous system, specifically the brain and spinal cord. It can cause distress and psychological symptoms such as depression and anxiety in patients and their caregivers. A type of cancer affecting the central nervous system, specifically the brain and spinal cord. It is treated with chemotherapy and, in some cases, radiation therapy.

nodes.label: genetic testing
nodes.description: A diagnostic procedure that examines an individual's DNA to identify mutations in genes associated with hereditary diseases, such as BRCA and Lynch syndrome. It can determine if an individual has a BRCA mutation or other mutations that play a role in hereditary cancer. It is recommended for everyone diagnosed with ovarian cancer and can be done through a gynecology or oncology care team, or by a genetic counselor. The testing is done on normal tissue, such as blood, saliva, or a cheek swab. Those with a positive genetic test or a strong cancer family history should see a health expert, typically a genetic counselor, who has special training to help patients understand changes in genes related to disease.

nodes.label: Book
nodes.description: A book that contains information about lung cancer, clinical trials, and recommendations for patients to discuss with their care team, as mentioned in the text. A book organized into chapters that provides information about AML, including testing, treatment, and a general overview of AML treatment. The book is not further described in the text. A book published by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network® (NCCN®) that contains information about blood cell formation and related topics. The specific contents of the book are not detailed in the text. A resource intended for caregivers and loved ones of people with primary CNS lymphoma. It aims to help them understand the disease, its challenges, and how to provide support to the affected person. A book intended to help caregivers and loved ones understand brain tumors and the challenges they present. The book provides information on gliomas, their symptoms, and the support needed for people with brain tumors.

nodes.label: Astrocytomas
nodes.description: One of the three most common types of glioma tumors, astrocytomas are made of star-shaped glial cells called astrocytes, whose main job is to maintain the chemical environment for nerve cell communication. One of the most common types of glioma tumors, developing from glial cells in the brain and spinal cord. Like other gliomas, they can disrupt brain function and be difficult to treat due to their invasive nature. Astrocytomas are one of the three most common types of glioma tumors, characterized by an abnormality or mutation in glial cells that causes them to grow out of control. They are a type of brain tumor that can be difficult to treat due to their invasive nature.

nodes.label: PARP inhibitors (PARPi)
nodes.description: A newer option for maintenance therapy after initial treatment of ovarian cancer, which work best in homologous recombination deficiency (HRD)-positive cancers, including those caused by a BRCA mutation. They include Olaparib (Lynparza), Niraparib (Zejula), and Rucaparib (Rubraca). The most common side effects of PARP inhibitors are similar to those caused by chemotherapy.

nodes.label: Bone marrow aspirate
nodes.description: A bedside procedure used to obtain a sample of liquid bone marrow from the bone marrow for diagnostic testing. It involves inserting a hollow needle through the skin and into the bone to aspirate a small amount of the liquid marrow, which is then analyzed by a pathologist to identify cellular abnormalities. Bone marrow aspirate is a procedure where a sample of liquid bone marrow is removed for testing. It is used in conjunction with a biopsy to study cells for the immunophenotype of AML. A bedside procedure used to obtain a sample of liquid bone marrow by inserting a hollow needle through the skin and into the bone. It is one of the two types of bone marrow tests often done at the same time for diagnosing leukemia. A medical procedure where a sample of bone and liquid bone marrow is removed from the body, often used in the diagnosis and monitoring of blood cancers such as AML. The sample is then analyzed using laboratory methods like flow cytometry. A bone marrow aspirate is a medical procedure where a sample of bone marrow is removed for testing, often used in the diagnosis of AML alongside a bone marrow biopsy. It helps determine the presence and percentage of myeloblasts in the bone marrow. A medical procedure where a hollow needle is used to extract liquid and cells from the bone marrow, typically performed at the cancer center where treatment will be received. It is recommended that this procedure be done by an experienced surgeon and is usually taken from the back of the hip bone (pelvis).

nodes.label: Bile Ducts
nodes.description: Anatomical structures in the body that transport bile from the liver to the small intestine. They are covered by the lamina propria, muscularis, perimuscular fibrous tissue, and serosa. Structures through which bile flows from the liver. Blockage of these ducts can be indicated by abnormal levels of chemicals in liver function tests. Small channels and thin tubes that drain bile from the liver and gallbladder into the small intestine. They include the left and right hepatic ducts, the common hepatic duct, the cystic duct, and the pancreatic duct.

nodes.label: Mouth
nodes.description: The mouth, also known as the oral cavity or buccal cavity, is the starting point of the digestive tract where food enters the body. It is an anatomical structure that includes the lips, cheeks, palate, teeth, and tongue, responsible for various functions such as eating, speaking, breathing, chewing, tasting, swallowing, and holding food. Cancer can develop in any of these parts, with squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) being the most common type of mouth cancer. The mouth is the opening of the digestive and respiratory systems and can be examined using a rochoscopy or an endoscope.

nodes.label: Clinical Trial
nodes.description: A research study involving human participants that tests new medical treatments, interventions, or tests of outcomes, providing access to investigational treatments for various types of cancer, including metastatic Squamous Cell Skin Cancer, lung cancer, cervical cancer, anal cancer, and glioma. Clinical trials are designed to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of new treatments or interventions, and may involve the use of placebos, standard treatments, or new drugs. They are managed by a research team and are conducted in a controlled setting, with informed consent forms provided to participants outlining the study's purpose, risks, and benefits. Patients can leave the trial and seek treatment outside at any time, and there is no fee to enroll in a clinical trial as the study sponsor covers research-related costs, including the study drug.

nodes.label: Contraceptive Sponge
nodes.description: A type of barrier method used to prevent pregnancy during cancer treatment, which involves a soft, flexible sponge inserted into the vagina to block sperm from entering the uterus. A type of barrier method used for birth control, mentioned as a component of the barrier methods category. A type of barrier method used for contraception to prevent pregnancy during and immediately after cancer treatment, particularly for individuals with testicles. A type of barrier method used for contraception, classified under the category of barrier methods. A type of barrier method for preventing pregnancy during cancer treatment, which involves a small, soft, dome-shaped sponge that is inserted into the vagina to prevent sperm from reaching the cervix. A type of barrier method used for preventing pregnancy during cancer treatment. It is a soft, sponge-like device that is inserted into the vagina to prevent sperm from reaching the cervix.

nodes.label: Staging and Treatment
nodes.description: The process of categorizing anal cancer based on the size of the tumor, the presence of cancer in nearby lymph nodes, and the invasion of nearby organs, and the recommended treatment for each stage. Nonmetastatic anal cancers are potentially curable and typically treated with chemotherapy and radiation, while metastatic anal cancer is usually treated with chemotherapy or immunotherapy to help with symptoms and prolong life.

nodes.label: Active surveillance
nodes.description: A management strategy for early-stage prostate cancer where patients undergo regular tests to monitor their cancer without immediate treatment, with the option for treatment if the cancer grows or changes in a way that requires it. A monitoring strategy for certain very-low-risk cancers, involving closely observing the cancer instead of performing surgery immediately. It is an option for some thyroid cancers, particularly those that are slow-growing and unlikely to cause harm. A monitoring approach where the cancer is closely watched instead of being treated immediately. It may be an option for some very-low-risk cancers, involving regular checkups and monitoring rather than surgery. A monitoring approach for small papillary tumors without surgery, where the size of the cancer is monitored using ultrasound. This approach is an option if there are no nearby suspicious lymph nodes and the tumor is not in a high-risk location.

nodes.label: Pembrolizumab
nodes.description: A checkpoint inhibitor drug, also known as Keytruda, used in immunotherapy for dMMR/MSI-H cancers. An immune checkpoint inhibitor (a type of immunotherapy) used in the treatment of metastatic cervical cancer, often given in combination with other medicines. An immune checkpoint inhibitor, a type of immunotherapy used in the treatment of metastatic cervical cancer. It is preferred for cancers with specific biomarkers such as TMB-H, PD-L1-positive, MSI-H/dMMR. A medication, often used to treat MSI-H/dMMR tumors, with the brand name Keytruda. The active ingredient in Keytruda, a checkpoint inhibitor used in immunotherapy for treating bladder cancer and other cancers. A type of immune checkpoint inhibitor used to treat metastatic anal cancer.

nodes.label: Prostate Cancer
nodes.description: A medical condition characterized by the abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, potentially detected through high PSA levels and further testing. It can be associated with germline mutations in genes such as BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, CHEK2, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PALB2, PMS2, and others, and can be at high-risk, very-high-risk, regional, or metastatic. Prostate Cancer can be detected using common tests like the PSA test and digital rectal exam, and monitored in patients who have been diagnosed. Imaging methods include MRI, CT, PET, ultrasound, bone scan, or a combination of these. Genetic germline testing is performed to look for inherited mutations in genes such as BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, CHEK2, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PALB2, PMS2, and others. Prostate Cancer can be screened for as part of regular health checkups and cancer screenings recommended by healthcare providers.

nodes.label: Granulocytes
nodes.description: Granulocytes are a type of white blood cell that helps fight infections. They are a component of white blood cells (WBCs or leukocytes). A type of white blood cell that includes neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils. These cells are involved in the immune response and help fight infections.

nodes.label: Levothyroxine
nodes.description: The most commonly used thyroid hormone replacement therapy, taken as a pill once a day. It is used to maintain the level of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) in the low normal range or suppressed for higher risk thyroid cancers or recurrence. A synthetic thyroid hormone used for thyroid hormone replacement therapy after total thyroidectomy, requiring lifelong administration. A thyroid hormone replacement therapy mentioned as a potential recommendation by the doctor to keep the TSH level low or normal after surgery. A medication used to manage thyroid hormone levels in people with thyroid cancer. It is taken continuously to keep the TSH level down and prevent symptoms of hypothyroidism.

nodes.label: Head and Neck Cancers
nodes.description: A type of cancer that is not typically inherited from biological parents, but may run in families. Care teams ask about the health history of blood relatives to determine if there is a family history of these cancers. A type of cancer that may be affected by smoking or vaping, potentially leading to side effects during and after surgery. A group of cancers that affect the head and neck area, including throat cancer. A type of cancer that affects the head and neck region, where stopping smoking or vaping is essential to maximize the chance for cure and minimize side effects. A type of cancer associated with a history of smoking or vaping nicotine. They are one of several types of cancer increased by smoking or vaping, along with lung and other cancers. A type of cancer affecting the head and neck region. The text emphasizes the importance of quitting smoking or vaping to maximize the chance for cure and minimize side effects in this type of cancer.

nodes.label: Prognosis
nodes.description: An estimate of the likely course and outcome of a disease, including the likelihood of recovery or recurrence, which is used to guide treatment decisions. A prediction of the likely course and outcome of a disease, guiding treatment options for patients with prostate cancer. Risk groups are the basis for a patient's prognosis. A prediction of the likely course and outcome of a disease, including the chances of recovery and the likelihood of the disease returning. Discussing prognosis with a doctor can help with treatment planning. The likely course and outcome of a disease, predicting how a glioma will turn out for an individual patient. A prediction of the likely course and outcome of a disease, including the likelihood of recovery and the chance of recurrence. It's mentioned as a topic that patients may want to discuss with their care team. The likely course and outcome of a disease based on tests, used to predict how cancer will turn out, especially in the context of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL).

nodes.label: Invasive breast cancer
nodes.description: A type of breast cancer that has spread from the milk ducts or milk glands into the breast tissue or nearby lymph nodes. It is a key point in understanding how breast cancer spreads. Invasive breast cancer is a type of breast cancer that has spread from the milk ducts or milk glands (lobules) into the surrounding breast tissue or nearby lymph nodes. It is characterized by cancer cells that can grow into surrounding tissues. A form of breast cancer that has grown outside the ducts or lobules into surrounding tissue. Once outside the ducts or lobules, it can spread through lymph or blood to lymph nodes or other parts of the body. A type of breast cancer where the cancer has grown outside the ducts or lobules into surrounding tissue, and can spread through lymph or blood to lymph nodes or other parts of the body. Invasive breast cancer is breast cancer that has spread from the milk ducts or milk glands (lobules) into the surrounding breast tissue or nearby lymph nodes. Once outside the ducts or lobules, breast cancer can spread through lymph or blood to lymph nodes or other parts of the body. It is a more advanced form of cancer than DCIS.

nodes.label: Prostate gland
nodes.description: The prostate gland is an anatomical structure located in the pelvis just below the bladder, an important part of the male reproductive system. It is about the size of a ping-pong ball and can develop prostate cancer, a disease where cells grow out of control. A gland in the male reproductive system located deep inside the lower body, responsible for producing semen and containing muscles that help propel semen during ejaculation. It is surrounded by the urethra just beneath the bladder. The prostate gland is a male reproductive organ where cancer can develop and be detected through biopsy samples. The presence and amount of cancer in the prostate gland are estimated based on the results of the biopsy and examination by a pathologist. An important part of the male reproductive system, located in the pelvis just below the bladder and typically about the size of a ping-pong ball. The prostate gland is a male reproductive organ located below the bladder and in front of the rectum, responsible for producing a fluid that forms part of the semen. A small, walnut-shaped gland in men that produces fluid for semen. Prostate cancer develops when cells in this gland grow out of control.

nodes.label: Cystoscopy
nodes.description: A medical procedure used to visualize the inside of the urethra and bladder for any signs of cancer. It involves inserting a cystoscope, a tube with a camera and light at the end, into the urethra and through to the bladder. This procedure can be done in a urologist’s office, a hospital, or a clinic and typically does not require general anesthesia. A medical procedure for examining the bladder, commonly using a white light but now sometimes using a blue light, especially when combined with a special dye. A medical procedure during which a pyelogram is usually done, often involving the use of anesthesia and the administration of contrast solution into the ureters or a vein. A medical procedure done in the operating room where anesthesia is given, and contrast is administered intravenously or directly into the ureters during the procedure.

nodes.label: Lymphoblasts
nodes.description: A type of blast cell that is often referred to simply as blasts in CML. They are a type of lymphoid progenitor cell. Abnormal white blood cells that are produced in excessive amounts in patients with ALL. The presence of at least 20 percent lymphoblasts in the bone marrow is required for a diagnosis of ALL. In certain cases, a diagnosis of ALL is possible with less than 20 percent lymphoblasts. Immature lymphocytes produced in excess in the bone marrow of patients with ALL. They can crowd out other blood cells, causing blood to not work as it should. The presence of lymphoblasts in the bone marrow is a key diagnostic criterion for ALL, with a minimum of 20% required for a diagnosis. Abnormal white blood cells that are overproduced in individuals with ALL, constituting at least 1 out of every 5 marrow cells. Immature white blood cells that are characteristic of ALL. In ALL, the presence of 20 percent or more lymphoblasts in the bone marrow is necessary for a diagnosis, and the overproduction of these cells leads to the formation of tumors and the spread of cancer to nearby tissues and organs.

nodes.label: Radiologist
nodes.description: A medical professional who specializes in interpreting imaging tests and communicating the results to an oncologist or the patient's care team for further evaluation and discussion. They analyze the results and send a report to the healthcare provider, which can include evaluating diagnostic mammograms, studying images of the nervous system from MRI or CT scans, or reviewing CT scans for cancer deposits.

nodes.label: High-dose Methotrexate Chemotherapy
nodes.description: A type of chemotherapy used as the most effective induction treatment for primary CNS lymphoma.
