A type of imaging that combines PET and CT techniques to take images of the whole body to find cancer, often done with one or two machines depending on the cancer center. A medical imaging technique that combines positron emission tomography (PET) and computed tomography (CT) scans to visualize the whole body for cancer detection. A combined medical imaging technique that uses PET and CT to provide detailed images of the body's internal structures, often used when other imaging results are unclear. A combination of PET and CT scans, using a radioactive drug injected into a vein to detect cancer cells and providing detailed images of the body.

nodes.label: Stage 2
nodes.description: The third stage in the TNM system for colon cancer, indicating that the cancer has grown into, or beyond, the fourth layer of the colon wall, with no cancer in nearby lymph nodes or in areas outside the colon. A stage of cervical cancer, for which imaging is recommended 3 to 6 months after treatment and may include an FDG-PET/CT scan or a CT with contrast. A stage of bladder cancer where the cancer has grown into the muscle layer of the bladder wall (muscle-invasive), but not reached the fatty layer covering the outside of the bladder nor spread anywhere else.

nodes.label: Cancer staging
nodes.description: The process of determining the extent and characteristics of a cancer, including the size and location of the tumor and the presence or absence of cancer spread to lymph nodes or other parts of the body. Cancer staging is the process of determining the extent of a cancer, including the size of the tumor, the spread to nearby lymph nodes, and the presence of metastasis to distant sites. This process is used to predict prognosis and guide treatment decisions. It is not the same for all cancer types and locations and is based on a combination of information, including tumor size, lymph node status, distant metastasis, and grade of the cancer. Biomarker testing may also be used to identify genes, proteins, or mutations that might suggest treatment.

nodes.label: Stage 1A1 Cancers
nodes.description: A specific stage of cancer characterized by the size and location of the tumor, often diagnosed through cone biopsy. Treatment decisions depend on the presence of LVSI and the margins of the removed tissue.

nodes.label: Bone marrow biopsy
nodes.description: A bedside procedure used to obtain a small piece of bone and surrounding marrow tissue for diagnostic testing. It involves inserting a wider needle through the skin and into the bone to extract a core sample, which is then analyzed by a pathologist to identify cellular abnormalities. A bedside procedure used to remove a small piece of bone and its marrow by inserting a wider needle. It is one of the two types of bone marrow tests often done at the same time for diagnosing leukemia. A bone marrow biopsy is a medical procedure where a sample of bone marrow tissue is removed for testing, often used in the diagnosis of AML alongside a bone marrow aspirate. It helps determine the presence and percentage of myeloblasts in the bone marrow. A medical procedure where a wider needle is used to remove a core sample from the bone marrow. This procedure is typically performed at the cancer center where treatment will be received and is recommended to be done by an experienced surgeon. It is usually taken from the back of the hip bone (pelvis).

nodes.label: Chemotherapy
nodes.description: Chemotherapy is a medical procedure used to treat ovarian cancer, often administered before or after surgery. It involves the use of drugs to kill cancer cells and can be an effective treatment for ovarian cancer. A type of cancer treatment involving the use of drugs to kill cancer cells, which can cause side effects such as nausea, vomiting, extreme tiredness, fever, tingling or numbness, rash, diarrhea, and increased risk of infection. A specific treatment option that may be considered in treatment decision-making, potentially causing feelings of discomfort or concern among patients due to side effects like nausea and vomiting.

nodes.label: Breast cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer that affects the breast tissue, typically starting in the milk ducts or lobules and spreading into surrounding tissue. It can be invasive, meaning it has grown outside the ducts or lobules, or noninvasive, meaning it is found only in the ducts or lobules. Breast cancer can spread to other parts of the body through a process called metastasis, forming metastatic breast cancer (MBC). It can affect anyone, including those assigned male at birth. Breast cancer is a significant health concern for both women and men. Early detection and screening are important for successful treatment and reducing the risk of dying from breast cancer. Breast cancer can be classified based on the presence or absence of hormone receptors, such as estrogen and progesterone receptors, and HER2 status. Treatment for breast cancer involves a team approach and a multidisciplinary team (MDT) of health care and psychosocial care professionals, often including endocrine therapy, which uses hormones or hormone-related drugs to slow tumor growth or shrink the tumor.

nodes.label: Diagnostic CT
nodes.description: A type of CT scan used for diagnostic purposes, involving more radiation than regular CT and the use of a contrast agent, often referred to as a CAT scan.

nodes.label: Bladder Cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer affecting the bladder, characterized by the uncontrolled growth of cells in the inner lining of the organ. It can be non-muscle-invasive, muscle-invasive, or metastatic, depending on how far it has grown or spread. Risk factors include smoking, age, family history, and chemical exposure. Bladder cancer can be treated with various therapies including surgery, chemotherapy, immunotherapy, radiation therapy, and targeted therapy. It can come back even after treatment, and there are various symptoms, risk factors, and treatments associated with it. Bladder cancer is typically diagnosed through a TURBT procedure and may require multiple treatments over months or years.

nodes.label: Uterus
nodes.description: A muscular organ in the female reproductive system where a baby grows and develops before being born. It is part of the cervical system and is distinct from the cervix, ovaries, fallopian tubes, and vagina. The uterus can be removed during a hysterectomy and may be removed during a radical cystectomy if the disease has spread. Its tissues can be visualized using an MRI. A reproductive organ that can be invaded by bladder cancer in Stage 3A and is a potential target for Stage 3A cancer invasion.

nodes.label: Anesthesia
nodes.description: A medication or procedure used to induce unconsciousness or numbness during medical procedures, such as surgical operations, cystoscopy, or examinations under anesthesia. It can also refer to a substance or treatment given to relieve pain and induce unconsciousness before or during medical procedures.

nodes.label: Adrenal Glands
nodes.description: Small, triangle-shaped glands found on the top of the kidneys. They produce hormones that help regulate the immune system, response to stress, metabolism, and other functions.

nodes.label: Recurrence
nodes.description: The return of cancer after initial treatment, often requiring testing for biomarkers to guide treatment decisions. It can occur in various locations, including the anus, lymph nodes, liver, or lungs, and may involve symptoms such as pain, bloating, weight loss, or frequent urination. MRI can be used to check for recurrence, and biomarker testing may be recommended for certain types of cancer. Treatment for recurrence depends on the location of the returned cancer.

nodes.label: Testing
nodes.description: A process that starts with accurate testing to diagnose and treat CML, involving various types of tests such as blood tests, bone marrow tests, and tests for CML biomarker and genetic changes. The process of conducting various tests to determine a patient's treatment plan, including medical history, physical examination, imaging studies, biopsy, and biomarker testing.

nodes.label: Bone marrow
nodes.description: A soft, spongy tissue found inside bones, particularly in the pelvis, that serves as the primary site for the production of blood cells, including red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. It is the source of bone marrow aspirate and biopsy samples for diagnostic testing. In conditions such as acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), bone marrow can make too many immature lymphocytes, leading to less blood being produced. Changes or mutations in the bone marrow can also lead to the development of certain blood cancers, such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL).

nodes.label: Biopsy of the prostate
nodes.description: A medical procedure where a sample of prostate tissue is removed and tested for cancer, specifically described as a transperineal biopsy involving a needle inserted through the perineum and guided by an ultrasound probe. MRI scans may be combined with the ultrasound image for accuracy.

nodes.label: Ovaries
nodes.description: Female reproductive organs that primarily produce hormones estrogen and progesterone, and in men, testosterone. They are part of the female reproductive system and are involved in the process of sexual reproduction. Ovaries can be affected by cancer and its treatment, potentially leading to damage, impact on fertility, and the need for hormone replacement therapy. They may be removed during certain surgical procedures, such as a radical cystectomy or hysterectomy, to manage risks associated with surgical menopause or disease spread. Ovaries can also be left intact during a trachelectomy, allowing for the possibility of natural pregnancy in the future.

nodes.label: Biomarker Testing
nodes.description: A test that examines the molecular components of a tumor sample to identify abnormal changes (mutations) in genes. A type of test used to stage the cancer, along with blood tests, imaging tests, and a biopsy. The biopsy sample will be tested for hormone receptors (estrogen and progesterone) and HER2 receptors. A type of testing used to identify features of a cancer that can help guide treatment, often involving mutations in particular genes or proteins made in response to the cancer. A testing procedure used to determine eligibility for certain targeted therapies or immunotherapies by identifying specific biomarkers in the tumor. A type of test included in the testing process for stomach cancer, targeting specific biomarkers to aid in diagnosis and treatment planning.

nodes.label: Bones
nodes.description: A hard, calcified structure forming the skeleton of the human body, often a site for metastatic prostate cancer and other types of cancer to spread, potentially requiring radiation therapy to stop the cancer from growing.

nodes.label: Topical Therapies
nodes.description: A group of superficial treatments applied directly to the skin, including 5-fluorouracil, imiquimod, and tirbanibulin, used to treat early squamous cell skin cancer and actinic keratoses.

nodes.label: Immunotherapy
nodes.description: A type of cancer treatment that uses the body's immune system to fight cancer, often preferred over systemic therapy for CSCC when surgery and radiation therapy are not possible or were not successful. It can involve the use of immune checkpoint inhibitors and is a recommended treatment option if eligible. Immunotherapy can treat cancer cells throughout the body and is a newer type of systemic therapy used in combination with other therapies like chemotherapy or targeted therapy. It may be an option for biomarker-based treatment of cancer, especially if involving immune checkpoint inhibitors. Potential side effects include hepatitis B virus reactivation and infertility. Immunotherapy is also used in the treatment of various types of cancer, including bladder cancer, primary central nervous system lymphoma, and anal cancer.

nodes.label: Pelvis
nodes.description: A basin-shaped structure in the lower part of the human body that supports the spinal column and protects the abdominal organs, containing the pelvic cavity where various organs and glands, including the prostate and bladder, are located. The pelvis can be imaged using MRI, CT, or PET/CT scans to check for cancer spread, and is a common site for taking bone marrow samples. The lower abdomen area between the hip bones, containing reproductive organs, the bladder, and the rectum, often examined using a CT scan for cancer spread.

nodes.label: Methotrexate
nodes.description: An antimetabolite used in the treatment of certain medical conditions, particularly primary CNS lymphoma, and as an induction therapy for primary CNS lymphoma in combination with other chemotherapy medicines. It works by blocking the body's use of folate, a form of vitamin B, which prevents lymphoma cells from multiplying and spreading as quickly. High doses of methotrexate are needed to overcome the blood-brain barrier and still have enough strength to kill lymphoma cells. It is a chemotherapy drug that is often administered in high-dose forms and requires monitoring of kidney function and other organs. It can cause toxicity and is typically administered in a hospital setting with fluid and medication support to manage side effects.

nodes.label: Medical Binder
nodes.description: A binder or notebook designed for organizing medical records, including blood tests, imaging results, and reports about specific types of cancer, to help in getting a second opinion and managing health information. A binder or notebook used to organize medical records, including blood tests, imaging results, and reports about specific types of cancer, for easy access and second opinions. A physical binder used to organize and store medical records, forms, and other important documents. A physical or digital organizer used to store and manage medical records, test results, and other important documents, mentioned as a helpful tool for patients managing their cancer care. A physical or digital organizer used to store and manage medical records, including blood tests, imaging results, and reports about specific types of cancer. It can be helpful when seeking a second opinion and can include sections for questions and notes. It can also be used to store insurance cards and other important documents. A binder or notebook used to organize medical records, including copies of blood tests, imaging results, and reports about specific types of cancer, to facilitate second opinions and communication with healthcare providers. A physical binder used to organize and store important medical records, including blood tests, imaging results, reports, insurance forms, treatment information, and personal notes. It is recommended to use a binder with a zipper pocket for convenience and to include items like a pen, small calendar, and insurance cards. The binder should be organized by date and brought to appointments for easy access to information.

nodes.label: Standard Surgical Excision
nodes.description: A surgical procedure for treating CSCC, where the tissue is sent for testing after the surgery. A type of surgery for squamous cell skin cancer that involves removing the entire tumor and a margin of healthy tissue around it. A standard surgical procedure for removing cancerous tissue, used as an option for treating high-risk or very high-risk CSCC when Mohs surgery or PDEMA is not preferred or applicable. A recommended treatment option for high-risk or very high-risk local CSCC, involving the removal of a wider margin (area of normal tissue around the lesion). If successful but other concerning features are noted during surgery, a discussion with different cancer doctors is recommended to determine next steps, which may include radiation therapy. If cancer still remains and more surgery is not possible, a discussion between different cancer doctors to consider next steps is recommended, which may include radiation therapy with or without systemic therapy. A recommended type of surgery for local, low-risk Squamous Cell Skin Cancer, involving the removal of the tumor and a margin of healthy tissue.

nodes.label: Digital Rectal Exam
nodes.description: A medical examination involving the insertion of a finger into the rectum to feel the prostate for signs of cancer, typically used in conjunction with PSA testing and other factors to determine the need for further testing. A medical examination of the rectum, used to detect possible prostate cancer along with a high PSA level. A simple procedure used to check the size and texture of the prostate, typically performed by a healthcare professional.

nodes.label: Clinical Trial
nodes.description: A research study involving human volunteers to test new medical treatments, interventions, or devices. Enrolling in a clinical trial for systemic therapy may be an option for patients who are not candidates for surgery or who have cancer that remains after surgery. Clinical trials could involve treatment with chemotherapy, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy. They are a recommended treatment option for primary CNS lymphoma and an experimental treatment option for bladder cancer. Patients with various types of cancer, including metastatic thyroid cancer, anal cancer, and bladder cancer, are encouraged to consider enrolling in a clinical trial if standard treatments are not available or appropriate. Clinical trials are a method for testing experimental treatments and may involve participation in a research study to test new treatments or approaches. Participants in clinical trials may receive treatment while also contributing to medical research.

nodes.label: BCR::ABL1
nodes.description: A fused gene that occurs when a piece of chromosome 9 and a piece of chromosome 22 break off and switch places, creating the Philadelphia chromosome (Ph). It is the cause of CML and makes a new protein that leads to uncontrolled blood cell growth. A fused gene resulting from the abnormal gene created when a piece of chromosome 9 and a piece of chromosome 22 break off and trade places. This gene is associated with chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). BCR::ABL1 is a fused gene that occurs when a piece of chromosome 9 and a piece of chromosome 22 break off and switch places, leading to the formation of the Philadelphia chromosome. It is the hallmark of CML and is not found in normal blood cells. A gene that makes a new protein leading to uncontrolled blood cell growth, ultimately causing CML. It is not passed down from birth parents to children and is not found in normal blood cells.

nodes.label: Non-small cell lung cancer
nodes.description: A type of lung carcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer, which can be broken down into subtypes by looking at the cancer cells under a microscope. Adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and large cell carcinoma are mentioned as subtypes. It accounts for about 6 out of 10 lung cancers.

nodes.label: Care Team
nodes.description: A group of healthcare professionals involved in a patient's care, including doctors, nurses, and other specialists, who work together to provide comprehensive care and support for patients, including lung cancer screening and risk assessment, diagnosis, treatment, and management of various aspects of the patient's condition. The composition of the care team can vary depending on the diagnosis and may include medical oncologists, surgical oncologists, radiation oncologists, dermatologists, Mohs surgeons, pathologists, plastic surgeons, head and neck surgeons, social workers, researchers, mind and body therapists, and other designated professionals. Effective communication with the care team is essential, especially in emergency situations, and patients are encouraged to choose a friend, family member, or peer to provide emotional support and help with logistics during diagnosis and treatment.

nodes.label: Numbered Stages
nodes.description: Stages of throat cancer based on TNM scores, ranging from stage 0 to stage 4, with 4 being the most advanced. A system for staging breast cancer based on TNM scores and receptor (hormone and HER2) status, ranging from stage 0 to stage 4, with stage 4 being the most advanced.

nodes.label: Cancer Treatment
nodes.description: A general term for medical treatments aimed at addressing cancer, which may be affected by smoking or vaping. A medical procedure for which imaging can be used after to evaluate its effectiveness and check for recurrence. Medical interventions aimed at treating cancer. Smoking and vaping can limit how well these treatments work and prevent wound healing, as well as increase the risk of side effects during and after surgery. The medical treatment for cancer, which should not be affected by the presence of HIV.

nodes.label: Spleen
nodes.description: A part of the lymphatic system, involved in the filtering and storage of blood cells and lymphocytes. A part of the body where tumors can be found in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), a more aggressive type of lymphoma that can be transformed from follicular lymphoma (FL). A large, dark red, soft organ located in the upper left part of the abdomen that is part of the lymphatic system. It can become enlarged in certain conditions, such as follicular lymphoma, and may be tested for as part of the diagnostic process. An organ where leukemia can spread outside the bloodstream. A part of the body where abnormal cells associated with CLL or SLL can be found. The spleen may be swollen due to a buildup of cancer cells from these conditions. A part of the body’s immune system and a component of the lymphatic or lymph system. It is involved in the filtering of blood and the removal of old or damaged red blood cells.

nodes.label: National Cancer Institute (NCI)
nodes.description: A U.S. government agency under the National Institutes of Health responsible for cancer research, treatment, and prevention. NCI provides resources for finding clinical trials and has a Cancer Information Service (CIS) available at (6237) CANCER. They offer information about clinical trials at cancer.gov/about-cancer/treatment/clinical-trials/search and have a website at cancer.gov/types/anal, providing information about anal cancer.

nodes.label: Throat
nodes.description: A muscular tube located in the back of the mouth and neck, serving as a passageway for air to enter the lungs and food and liquid to enter the esophagus. It includes the oropharynx, which consists of the soft palate, tonsils, side and back walls of the throat, and the base of the tongue. The throat is examined during a physical exam to assess throat health and potential issues with airway or swallowing function. It is also a part of the respiratory and digestive systems, which can be affected by cancer and its treatment.

nodes.label: Systemic therapy
nodes.description: A type of cancer treatment that involves the use of medicines that travel through the bloodstream, reaching and affecting cells throughout the body. It includes chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy. Systemic therapy can affect both cancer cells and normal cells, potentially causing side effects. It is often used in the treatment of AML and is one of the key components of the multidisciplinary team's approach to treating the condition. Regular discussions with the care team about goals and treatment plans are essential, as treatment responses can vary among individuals.

nodes.label: Stomach
nodes.description: A muscular, sac-like organ in the digestive system that receives and holds food, secretes gastric juices to aid in digestion, and is located below the diaphragm. It meets the esophagus at the esophagogastric junction (EGJ) and is part of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. The stomach stores and initially breaks down food, preparing it for passage into the small intestine. It has different parts including the cardia, fundus, body, antrum, and pylorus, and is active during digestion. The stomach is examined as part of an upper endoscopy, which involves guiding a scope down the throat into the esophagus, stomach, and small bowel.

nodes.label: Vagina
nodes.description: The muscular passage through which babies are born, connecting the cervix and the external genitalia. A muscular canal that serves as the passageway for menstrual flow, childbirth, and sexual intercourse. It is part of the female reproductive system and connects the external genitalia to the cervix. A body part whose tissues can be visualized using an MRI. A body part through which surgery can be performed, either by entering through the vagina or making an incision. A female reproductive organ that can be invaded by bladder cancer in Stage 3A. A nearby reproductive organ mentioned in the text as a potential target for Stage 3A cancer invasion. An anatomical structure in the human body, part of the female reproductive system. It is mentioned alongside the uterus and vagina.

nodes.label: Maintenance therapy
nodes.description: A type of treatment used to manage advanced ovarian cancer, often involving the continuation of chemotherapy or other medications to prevent recurrence or progression of the disease. It may be an option if initial treatment is successful. The use of systemic therapy after successful initial treatment for ovarian cancer, which can reduce the risk of cancer returning or extend the time until it returns or gets worse. It is an option for stage 2, 3, and 4 cancers that respond well to surgery and platinum-based chemotherapy, and includes PARP inhibitors (PARPi) like Olaparib (Lynparza), Niraparib (Zejula), and Rucaparib (Rubraca). A type of therapy provided after initial treatment to help prevent recurrence, particularly if bevacizumab was included in the recurrence chemotherapy regimen or if a PARP inhibitor is an option due to a BRCA mutation.

nodes.label: Antimetabolites
nodes.description: Antimetabolites are a class of drugs that prevent the building blocks of DNA from being used, including examples such as Cladribine (Mavenclad), Clofarabine (Clolar), Cytarabine (Ara-C), Fludarabine, and Methotrexate. A type of chemotherapy that prevents the building blocks of DNA from being used, with examples including cladribine (Mavenclad), clofarabine (Clolar), cytarabine (Ara-C), fludarabine, and methotrexate. A class of chemotherapy drugs that include capecitabine, fluorouracil, gemcitabine, and methotrexate, and are known to reduce the cells that fight infection.

nodes.label: Rectal cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer that affects the rectum, the last several inches of the large intestine (bowel). Rectal cancer is common and treatable, and many cancers that start in the rectum can be cured, especially when found and treated early. This guide describes treatment for adenocarcinoma, the most common type of rectal tumor. A type of colorectal cancer that forms in the rectum. It can invade structures or organs outside of the rectum, and its treatment is different from that of colon cancer. The most common type of rectal cancer is adenocarcinoma, which forms in an adenoma, a common type of polyp. Removing polyps can prevent rectal cancer before it starts. A specific type of cancer that affects the rectum, characterized by the uncontrolled growth and spread of abnormal cells. Rectal cancer can be caused by inherited mutations in mismatch repair (MMR) genes, leading to Lynch syndrome and familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP). Individuals with rectal cancer should have their tumor tested for mutations in the MMR genes. Rectal cancer is a type of cancer that affects the rectum, often forming in polyps on the lining of the rectum or as lesions. It can be non-metastatic, early, locally advanced, or recur.

nodes.label: Risk Assessment
nodes.description: The process of evaluating an individual's risk of developing lung cancer based on various factors, such as age, sex, smoking history, and family health history. A process for identifying potential problems and considering the consequences of their occurrence, particularly in the context of early-stage prostate cancer, including the likelihood of remaining within the prostate, spreading outside, recurrence, and controllability with different treatments.

nodes.label: Rectum
nodes.description: The final segment of the large bowel, located between the colon and the anus, where stool is held until it leaves the body through the anus. The rectum is examined as part of a colonoscopy and is involved in the formation of rectal cancer, which can develop from non-cancerous growths called polyps, with the most common type being adenomas. These adenomas can potentially become invasive rectal cancer over time, and removing polyps can prevent cancer before it starts. The rectum is also the site where most rectal cancers start in polyps called adenomas. It is a part of the large intestine that connects the colon to the anus and can be connected to the remaining colon in a colostomy procedure. The rectum is a part of the digestive or gastrointestinal (GI) tract and can be examined using various medical procedures, such as a digital rectal exam, CT scan, or MRI.

nodes.label: Stage 4 Breast Cancer
nodes.description: A stage of breast cancer where the cancer has spread to other parts of the body (metastasized). A stage of breast cancer where cancer has spread to distant sites. It can develop from earlier stages and might be diagnosed as stage 4 metastatic breast cancer at first. Breast cancer is often staged twice, before and after surgery, using the TNM system. Clinical stage (c) is the rating given before any treatment, while pathologic stage (p) or surgical stage is determined by examining tissue removed during surgery. Grade describes how abnormal the tumor cells look under a microscope.

nodes.label: Primary Care Doctor
nodes.description: A medical professional who handles medical care not related to cancer. They can help patients express their thoughts about treatments to their cancer care team and provide general medical advice. A healthcare professional, also known as a general practitioner (GP) or primary care physician (PCP), who plays an important role in the care of cancer survivors after finishing cancer treatment. A healthcare professional who provides general medical care and can advise on cancer screening tests based on a patient's sex, age, and risk level.

nodes.label: Biomarkers
nodes.description: Biomarkers are proteins found on the surface or inside white blood cells that are targeted in AML treatment. They are also detected through immunohistochemistry and genetic testing of leukemia cells. Specific features of cancers that make them more or less susceptible to targeted therapy and immunotherapy. These treatments are most effective at treating cancers with biomarkers. Specific genetic markers tested for in recurrent, advanced, or metastatic cancers that can't be treated with RAI therapy, including ALK gene fusion, NTRK gene fusion, BRAF gene mutations, RET gene fusion, mismatch repair deficiency (dMMR), microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H), and tumor mutational burden-high (TMB-H). Biomarkers are specific markers or characteristics used to identify different types of gliomas, indicating the presence or absence of certain biomarkers.

nodes.label: Cystoscope
nodes.description: A medical device used in cystoscopy, it is a tube with a camera and a light at the end. It is inserted into the urethra and through to the bladder to view the inside of the bladder. It can also be used to remove small tissue samples for biopsy and, in some cases, very small cancer growths.

nodes.label: Lymphocytes
nodes.description: A type of white blood cell that is an important part of the immune system and helps fight infections and diseases. They are further classified into B lymphocytes, T lymphocytes, and natural killer (NK) cells. In acute lymphoblastic leukemia, lymphocytes become cancerous and start growing out of control, leading to the production of too many immature lymphocytes called lymphoblasts or blasts. An abnormal overgrowth of lymphocytes is called a lymphoma, which is a type of cancer. Certain cells in the immune system that can develop a genetic abnormality, leading to the growth of cancerous cells and the development of lymphoma.

nodes.label: AML Cancer Cells
nodes.description: Cells specifically affected by AML, used in mutation testing to look for specific mutations that may determine the type of treatment given.

nodes.label: Cystoscopy
nodes.description: A medical procedure used to look inside the bladder, often performed as part of diagnostic tests for bladder cancer. A medical procedure used to examine the urethra and bladder for signs of cancer. It involves inserting a cystoscope, a tube with a camera and a light at the end, into the urethra and through to the bladder. The procedure can be done in a urologist’s office, a hospital, or a clinic and takes only a few minutes. It does not require general anesthesia and patients can go home afterward. During the procedure, the urologist views real-time images of the inside of the bladder on a monitor. If any areas appear suspicious, the urologist may use a small tool on the cystoscope to remove tiny tissue samples for testing (biopsy). In some cases, very small cancer growths can be completely removed during the cystoscopy, but if a tumor is found, it will need to be removed in an operating room at a clinic or hospital.

nodes.label: Metastatic Cancer
nodes.description: Cancer that has spread to other organs in the body. Stage 4 cancer is considered metastatic cancer at the time of diagnosis. A stage of cancer where the disease has spread to the tissue lining around the lung or to other organs after diagnosis, often referred to as stage 4 cancer. Information about metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) can be found at NCCN.org/patientguidelines and on the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app. Cancer that has spread far from the pancreas, which can be caused by Stage 4 pancreatic cancer but may also occur in other stages over time. A stage of thyroid cancer where the cancer has spread to other parts of the body, often requiring more aggressive treatments like external beam radiation therapy or targeted therapy. Cancer that has spread to areas far from the neck, most commonly to the lungs, liver, muscles, bones, brain, and spinal cord. A type of cancer that has spread to areas far from the original tumor, such as the lungs, liver, muscles, bones, brain, and spinal cord. It can be treated with therapies like RAI therapy, radiation therapy, or monitoring. A stage of cancer where the disease has spread to other parts of the body, as mentioned in the context of radiation therapy options and side effects.

nodes.label: Renal Cell Carcinoma
nodes.description: A type of kidney cancer that arises in cells lining the small tubes in the kidney called renal tubules. It is the most common type of kidney cancer and can have various subtypes, including clear cell papillary, fumarate hydratase-deficient, and ELOC-mutated forms.

nodes.label: Myeloid blasts
nodes.description: Very immature white blood cells that are abnormal in acute myeloid leukemia (AML), preventing them from becoming mature blood cells. Very immature white blood cells that are abnormal in AML, preventing them from becoming mature blood cells and leading to a buildup in the bone marrow and blood. Myeloid blasts are abnormal white blood cells that are present in the bone marrow and blood in individuals with AML. They must constitute at least 20 percent of all cells in the bone marrow to diagnose AML. The presence of these blasts is a key indicator of AML. Myeloid blasts are very immature white blood cells that, in AML, fail to develop into mature blood cells. They are a key indicator in the diagnosis of AML, with a presence of 20 percent or more in the bone marrow or blood confirming the diagnosis.

nodes.label: External Beam Radiation Therapy (EBRT)
nodes.description: A type of radiation therapy that uses a machine outside of the body called a linear accelerator (linac) to aim high-energy x-rays or particles at cancer from outside the body. It is often used in conjunction with surgery to treat or slow the growth of cancer, and can cause side effects such as fatigue, skin redness and irritation, diarrhea, nausea, and frequent or painful urination. EBRT can also cause premature menopause if the ovaries are included in the radiation field. It is recommended for cancers with risk factors, and used in combination with platinum chemotherapy as chemoradiation. It can also be given alone or in combination with other treatments after surgery for early-stage cancers. A specific type of radiation therapy used for bladder cancer, involving a large machine aiming radiation at the tumor area.

nodes.label: Care team
nodes.description: A group of healthcare professionals involved in a patient's diagnosis and treatment, including a primary care physician (PCP). Patients are encouraged to get to know their care team and help them get to know them.

nodes.label: General health tests
nodes.description: A category of tests used to evaluate an individual's overall health, which may include asking about health problems, treatments, illnesses, injuries, symptoms, and medications. Family history and symptoms are also considered as part of general health tests. They can be part of the diagnostic process for various conditions such as breast cancer, prostate cancer, adrenal tumors, mouth cancer, AML, kidney cancer, CML, and NPC. These tests may involve medical history and physical examination, checking temperature, blood pressure, pulse, and breathing rate, height and weight, lung and heart function, and examination of the eyes, ears, nose, and throat. They may also include blood tests, urine tests, imaging tests, biopsy, biomarker testing, genetic risk testing, and performance status assessment.

nodes.label: Epidermis Lesions
nodes.description: Skin lesions that can appear in the epidermis, such as flat, pale or yellow areas, red patches, small, pink or red, shiny bumps, or open sores that don't heal and might bleed or go away and come back.

nodes.label: Stage 1 Chemotherapy
nodes.description: A specific chemotherapy regimen recommended for most newly diagnosed stage 1 cancers, typically involving paclitaxel with carboplatin given every 3 weeks. It may be followed by maintenance therapy if effective. A type of chemotherapy not recommended after colectomy for stage 1 cancers.

nodes.label: Radical Cystectomy
nodes.description: A type of cystectomy that involves removing the entire bladder as well as nearby lymph nodes, and sometimes other nearby organs if the disease has spread. It is the most widely used surgery for muscle-invasive bladder cancer. The most common surgery for muscle-invasive bladder cancer. It involves removing the entire bladder, nearby lymph nodes, and other organs. Common side effects include constipation, diarrhea, bleeding, bowel problems, infections, and changes in sexual function. It requires a hospital stay for at least several days and can take 2 to 3 months or longer to recover from.

nodes.label: Contrast Agent
nodes.description: A substance used with a CT scan to improve image clarity, but not used with MRI due to potential patient discomfort. A substance used in MRI scans to make blood vessels, organs, and other tissues stand out more clearly in the images. It is injected into the bloodstream and flushed out in urine. A substance used in MRI to highlight areas in organs, blood vessels, or other tissues, making them easier to see. The contrast agent used for primary CNS lymphoma is called gadolinium. It is injected into the bloodstream through an intravenous (IV) line before or during the imaging test and later flushed out in urine. A substance used in medical imaging to make pictures clearer, similar to a CT scan. A substance used in medical imaging to make pictures clearer, used in both CT scans and MRI scans.

nodes.label: Testing
nodes.description: A series of procedures and analyses used to diagnose, stage, and monitor various types of cancer, including prostate cancer, breast cancer, and primary bone cancer. Testing may involve medical and family history review, physical and skin exams, biopsy, imaging studies, blood tests, genetic tests, tumor profiling, genomic testing, tumor gene testing, next-generation sequencing (NGS), mutation testing, liquid biopsy, and precision oncology. The results of these tests are used to diagnose cancer, determine the appropriate treatment plan, and monitor the individual's health.

nodes.label: Transabdominal Surgery
nodes.description: A surgical procedure recommended for tumors that have invaded the muscle layer of the rectal wall (T2 tumors), or smaller (T1) tumors, and some larger (T3) cancers that haven't spread to lymph nodes. It involves cutting into the abdomen to reach and remove the rectal tumor, some surrounding healthy tissue, and nearby lymph nodes. At least 12 lymph nodes should be removed during all types of transabdominal surgery. A pathologist examines the removed tissue and determines the cancer stage. The type of transabdominal surgery performed depends on the location of the tumor and the extent of the cancer. This method is also a recommended option for: smaller (T1) tumors, and some larger (T3) cancers that haven't spread to lymph nodes. In staging terms, these are T2 tumors.

nodes.label: AYA
nodes.description: Adolescents and young adults, defined as individuals aged 15 to 39 years at the time of initial cancer diagnosis, who can be treated by pediatric or adult oncologists depending on the type of cancer. Adolescents and young adults who are 15 to 39 years of age at the time of initial cancer diagnosis and are included in the pediatric ALL category. They can be treated in pediatric or adult centers depending on the type of cancer.

nodes.label: Health Care Provider (HCP)
nodes.description: A medical professional or facility where individuals can receive regular checkups and cancer screenings, including for skin, breast, prostate, and other types of cancer. HCPs may request more frequent visits based on risk factors for lung cancer.

nodes.label: PDEMA
nodes.description: A surgical procedure recommended as a treatment option for low-risk CSCC that has not spread to lymph nodes. It is a combination of partial dermatome electrosurgery and Mohs surgery, often used in conjunction with Mohs surgery for further treatment options. It involves using an electric current to destroy cancer cells and a precision surgical technique to remove them layer by layer, preserving as much healthy tissue as possible. A form of surgery, likely related to Mohs surgery, used for the treatment of high-risk or very high-risk CSCC, involving the removal of cancerous tissue and examination of each layer for cancer cells. A surgical procedure used for removing cancer, but may not always completely remove the cancer. If not, a discussion with different cancer doctors is recommended to consider next treatment options, which may include another surgery or radiation therapy. A form of surgery used to treat cancer, specifically mentioned as a possible first treatment option if testing after surgery finds cancer in the margin. A form of surgery used in combination with Mohs surgery for local, high-risk or very high-risk Squamous Cell Skin Cancer, involving the removal of the tumor and a margin of healthy tissue with microscopic examination of each layer.

nodes.label: Blood
nodes.description: A route through which cancer can spread to distant parts of the body, mentioned in the context of metastatic esophageal cancer. A fluid that circulates in the body, carrying oxygen, nutrients, and waste products to and from cells. In the context of ALL, blood tests are used to diagnose the condition, often in conjunction with bone marrow tests and imaging studies. The results from blood tests, along with bone marrow tests and imaging studies, are used to determine a patient's treatment plan. A body fluid that is checked for signs of cancer after a diagnosis of primary CNS lymphoma. A body fluid where abnormal cells associated with CLL or SLL can be found. CLL is mostly found in the blood, while SLL is mostly found in lymph nodes and the spleen. A body fluid where lymphocytes are found.

nodes.label: Gallbladder
nodes.description: An anatomical structure in the body, specifically an organ involved in bile storage and secretion. It is covered by the lamina propria, muscularis, perimuscular fibrous tissue, and serosa. The gallbladder is a small organ located near the right side of the liver and close to the first part of the small intestines (duodenum). It stores and secretes bile. The gallbladder is a part of the hepatobiliary system, along with the liver and bile ducts, and is involved in the storage and concentration of bile. An organ in the digestive system that is involved in breaking down food and absorbing nutrients. It is one of the organs included in the digestive system, along with the liver, stomach, pancreas, and intestines.

nodes.label: Urothelial cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer that originates in the urothelial cells, characterized by features that can resemble other types of cells, leading to subtypes such as glandular, squamous cell, micropapillary, plasmacytoid, sarcomatoid, nested, lymphoepithelioma-like, and microcystic and tubular. Treatment for these uncommon subtypes is generally similar to typical urothelial cancer in the early stages but may require more aggressive treatment due to faster growth rates.

nodes.label: Pathology report
nodes.description: A pathology report is a document created by a pathologist that details the results of a biopsy examination, including the presence and percentage of cancer in each core sample. It is reviewed by a doctor with the patient. A document recording the type and other features of biopsied lesions, used by care teams to plan the next steps of care. Patients are encouraged to request a copy of the report for their records. A report containing lab results used for diagnosis, sent to a hematologist-oncologist and often accessible to patients through an online patient portal. It is used to plan treatment and is reviewed by the oncologist with the patient. A medical document containing results of a medical examination, used to plan treatment for CLL.

nodes.label: MRI Scan
nodes.description: An imaging test that uses radio waves and powerful magnets to take pictures of the inside of the body without x-rays or radiation. It can detect metal in the body and requires patients to hold their breath during the test. MRI scans can be either closed or open, with closed MRIs being more common and potentially causing discomfort for patients with claustrophobia. They can take longer to perform than CT scans and may involve the use of contrast. MRI scans are often used to detect cancer spread, confirm diagnoses, and visualize the brain for tumors. They are also sometimes combined with PET scans to provide a more detailed image, called a PET/MRI scan.

nodes.label: Inflammatory Breast Cancer (IBC)
nodes.description: A specific type of breast cancer where cancer cells block lymph vessels in the skin of the breast, causing redness, swelling, and warmth. It can be difficult to diagnose as it can look like an infection and there may be no lump that can be felt during a breast exam or seen on a mammogram. A type of breast cancer that is often invasive ductal carcinoma, characterized by the presence of tumors and the potential spread to lymph nodes, organs, or other parts of the body, typically diagnosed as stage 3 or 4 disease. A type of breast cancer that is most often an invasive ductal carcinoma, meaning cancer started in the cells that line the milk ducts and has spread into surrounding tissue. At diagnosis, it is typically stage 3 or 4 disease, with a tumor of any size and involvement in lymph nodes, the skin, or chest wall. It can sometimes be called advanced disease.

nodes.label: blood
nodes.description: A tissue in the body that moves oxygen and nutrients throughout the body, carries away waste, plays an important role for the immune system, and helps prevent bleeding. It is composed of plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.

nodes.label: Prostate cancer tests
nodes.description: A variety of tests used by healthcare providers to detect prostate cancer, determine its advancement, plan treatment, check treatment effectiveness, and monitor health after treatment ends.

nodes.label: Cisplatin
nodes.description: Cisplatin is a platinum-containing chemotherapy drug used to treat squamous cell skin cancer and other cancers. It is often administered in combination with other chemotherapy drugs. Cisplatin, sold under the brand name Platinol, is a chemotherapy drug used in the treatment of cancer. It is one of the examples of chemotherapy drugs mentioned in the text. A chemotherapy drug used in combination with other medicines as dose-dense methotrexate, vinblastine, doxorubicin, and cisplatin (or ddMVAC) for treating bladder cancer. A chemotherapy drug that may be used with radiation in chemotherapy regimens for perianal cancer. It is used in combination with mitomycin, capecitabine, and 5-FU. A platinum-based chemotherapy medicine used in various regimens, including the DCF regimen. It can cause kidney damage and, when used over an extended period, may lead to hearing problems or hearing loss. Individuals receiving platinum-based chemotherapy may receive routine IV hydration to reduce its effect on the kidneys. A recommended chemotherapy drug for use with radiation to treat anal cancer, often used in combination with mitomycin or 5-FU.

nodes.label: Mouth cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer that affects the oral cavity, including the lips, the front two-thirds of the tongue, the gums, the lining inside the cheeks and lips, the floor (bottom) of the mouth under the tongue, the hard palate (bony top of the mouth), the bony ridges that hold the sockets of the teeth, and the small area of the gum behind the wisdom teeth. It is a serious condition that requires medical attention and treatment. Mouth cancer, also known as oral cancer or oral cavity cancer, is a type of cancer that occurs on the inside of the mouth and is one of several types of cancers grouped into a category called head and neck cancers. It is often treated similarly to other head and neck cancers. A type of cancer that develops in any of the parts that make up the mouth, such as the lips, gums, lining inside the cheeks and lips, front two-thirds of the tongue, roof of the mouth, bony raised areas that hold the teeth sockets, floor of the mouth, and small area of the gum behind the wisdom teeth. It is a type of head and neck cancer and the most common type of mouth cancer, with squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) being the focus of this book. A type of cancer that develops in any of the parts that make up the mouth, such as the lips, cheeks, tongue, gums, floor of the mouth, and bony roof of the mouth. It is a subset of head and neck cancers and the most common type is squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), which forms in the thin, flat cells of the mucous membranes of the mouth. A type of head and neck cancer that arises in the oral cavity.

nodes.label: Cancer survivorship
nodes.description: A concept that addresses various topics relevant to survivors of cancer, including mental health, side effects, and lifestyle changes. Available resources include Survivorship Care for Healthy Living and Survivorship Care for Cancer-Related Late and Long-Term Effects on NCCN.org/patientguidelines.

nodes.label: TNM System
nodes.description: A staging system used for mouth cancer, assigning scores or numbers to the letters T, N, and M based on imaging and pathology results, indicating tumor depth and size, lymph node status, and metastasis. A staging system developed by the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) used to determine the cancer stage, involving three key pieces of information: T (tumor size and extent of invasion), N (lymph node involvement), and M (metastasis or spread of cancer to areas far from the anus).

nodes.label: NSCLC
nodes.description: Non-small cell lung cancer, the most common type of lung cancer, according to the text. Non-small cell lung cancer, a type of lung cancer that is the most common form of the disease. It is covered in detail in the text and is described as forming from cells that line the airways of the lungs. Non-small cell lung cancer, a type of lung cancer often categorized by the size and location of the cancer cells. Adenocarcinoma, large cell carcinoma, and squamous cell carcinoma are common types of NSCLC. An acronym for non-small cell lung cancer, a group of cancers that are the most common type of lung cancer. It can be broken down into subtypes by looking at the cancer cells under a microscope.

nodes.label: Side Effects
nodes.description: Adverse reactions that may occur as a result of systemic therapy, with varying severity and duration. Adverse reactions that may occur as a result of immunotherapy, including rituximab. These can include drowsiness, fatigue, constipation, joint pain, loss of appetite, low blood cell counts, serious blood clots, and rashes. Adverse reactions that may occur during or after surgery. Smoking and vaping can greatly increase the chances of experiencing these side effects. Adverse reactions or discomforts experienced by patients undergoing medical treatments, such as chemotherapy and radiation therapy, which may require management or prevention strategies.

nodes.label: Biomarker testing
nodes.description: A type of testing that examines a sample from a biopsy of a tumor to look for specific DNA mutations/alterations, protein levels, or other molecular features. This information is used to choose the best treatment for the patient. It is sometimes called molecular testing or tumor profiling, tumor sequencing, gene expression profiling, or genomic testing. It includes tests of genes or their products (proteins) and identifies the presence or absence of mutations and certain proteins that might suggest treatment. Examples of biomarkers include BRCA genes and HER2 and hormone receptor status. Biomarker testing is a case-by-case procedure that assesses the presence or absence of mutations and certain proteins in genes or their products (proteins), to identify potential treatments for diseases like Ewing sarcoma. It may increase the time it takes for biopsy results and is sometimes called molecular testing, tumor profiling, tumor sequencing, gene expression profiling, or genomic testing.

nodes.label: Complete Remission
nodes.description: A state or condition where anal cancer is no longer detectable or present after treatment, requiring surveillance including imaging every year for 3 years.

nodes.label: Vaccine
nodes.description: A vaccine is available that protects against 9 different strains of HPV, including the highest-risk strains. It is recommended for routine use in adolescents and young adults, but vaccination is now an option for adults aged 45 and under in the United States. There are two other HPV vaccines available in other parts of the world, one of which protects against HPV-16 and HPV-18 only, and the other targets these and two additional types. The vaccine works best in younger people (ideally under age 13) because they are less likely to have been exposed to HPV. However, the vaccine does not treat existing HPV infections or HPV-related cancer. A vaccine that can prevent new HPV infections but not treat existing HPV infections or HPV-related cancer. It is most effective in younger people under age 13 because they are less likely to have been exposed to HPV.

nodes.label: Total Thyroidectomy
nodes.description: A surgical procedure where the entire thyroid gland is removed. It is followed by the use of thyroid hormone replacement therapy for life. A surgical procedure involving the removal of the entire thyroid gland, often used in the treatment of thyroid cancer. It may be the standard treatment for all thyroid cancers, but newer research suggests lobectomy may be effective for small, low-risk cancers that haven't grown or spread beyond the thyroid. A surgical procedure involving the removal of the entire thyroid gland, often used in the treatment of thyroid cancer. It may be the standard treatment for all thyroid cancers, but newer research suggests lobectomy may be effective for small, low-risk cancers that haven't grown or spread beyond the thyroid. A surgical procedure where the entire thyroid gland is removed. It may be recommended if cancer is larger or more invasive than expected during a lobectomy, or if the cancer has spread beyond the thyroid. A surgical procedure involving the removal of the entire thyroid gland, leading to short-term follow-up that includes a physical exam, blood tests, and a neck ultrasound 6 to 12 months after surgery. RAI therapy may be an option if cancer cells are left in the body, and whole-body RAI imaging may be recommended for high-risk patients or those with abnormal results. A surgical procedure involving the complete removal of the thyroid gland. Short-term follow-up includes a physical exam, blood tests, and a neck ultrasound 6 to 12 months after surgery. A surgical procedure involving the complete removal of the thyroid gland, often used in the treatment of thyroid cancer. Unlike after lobectomy, Tg testing isn’t helpful after total thyroidectomy.

nodes.label: Indiana Pouch
nodes.description: A type of urinary diversion that uses a portion of the large intestine to create a pouch to hold urine. It is also known as a continent cutaneous pouch and was developed by surgeons at Indiana University. A small bandage can cover the stoma, and a catheter must be inserted into the stoma several times a day to drain the urine.

nodes.label: Pathologist
nodes.description: A medical professional who examines tissue samples and cells under a microscope to diagnose diseases, particularly cancers. Pathologists determine the presence and percentage of cancer in biopsy samples, identify the type and grade of cancer, and assess the overall appearance and characteristics of cells. They also play a key role in diagnosing diseases based on laboratory tests and histological examination of cells, tissues, and bodily fluids. In the context of leukemia diagnosis, pathologists review bone marrow samples. Pathologists may also determine the stage of cancer based on their findings.

nodes.label: Small Cell Lung Cancer
nodes.description: A different type of lung cancer, not covered in the same book as NSCLC, mentioned in the text. A different type of lung cancer, not covered in the same book as NSCLC, as mentioned in the text. A type of lung cancer that is mentioned in contrast to NSCLC. It is described as a different cancer covered in another book. A type of lung cancer, which is less common than non-small cell lung cancer. A type of lung cancer that forms from cells lining the inner airways of the lungs, is often aggressive, and grows quickly. This chapter provides basic information about small cell lung cancer. A type of lung cancer characterized by small and blue cancer cells when viewed under a microscope. It is less common than non-small cell lung cancer and is the focus of the book. Often treated like small cell lung cancer when found in lung tumors.

nodes.label: Tumor
nodes.description: An abnormal growth of cells that could be detected in the prostate during a digital rectal exam as an irregular or hardened part of the gland. A growth that can occur in various parts of the body, including the nasopharynx, oropharynx, parapharyngeal space, and other structures. It can be measured in centimeters (cm) and can grow into nearby structures. The main (primary) cancerous growth in the body. The size and depth of the tumor are described by the letter T in the TNM system. A higher number indicates a larger tumor.

nodes.label: Uterine Cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer that can be associated with germline mutations in genes such as MSH2, MSH6, MLH1, and PMS2. A type of cancer that can be associated with inherited mutations in genes like MSH2, MSH6, MLH1, and PMS2.

nodes.label: Blood Tests
nodes.description: A component of short-term follow-up after total thyroidectomy, involving laboratory tests to assess the patient's blood. Laboratory tests involving the analysis of blood samples, conducted as part of short-term follow-up after total thyroidectomy to measure TSH, Thyroglobulin, and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies.

nodes.label: Breast Cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer that can affect anyone, regardless of assigned gender at birth, and is characterized by the formation of a primary tumor, invasive cancer cells, and potential metastasis to other parts of the body such as the bone, lungs, liver, brain, or lymph nodes. It can develop in lobules or milk ducts and is more common in individuals assigned female at birth. Breast cancer can be associated with germline mutations in genes such as BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, CHEK2, and others, and can increase the risk of developing pancreatic cancer. It can be screened for as part of regular health checkups and cancer screenings recommended by healthcare providers. Clinical stage (c) is the rating given before any treatment, while pathologic stage (p) or surgical stage is determined by examining tissue removed during surgery. Grade describes how abnormal the tumor cells look under a microscope.

nodes.label: Leukemia
nodes.description: A type of cancer involving the blood and bone marrow, characterized by the uncontrolled growth of abnormal white blood cells. It can spread outside the bloodstream to various organs and tissues, including lymph nodes, liver, spleen, skin, and rarely the lining of the brain and spinal cord. Leukemia can lead to an impaired clotting process, which is called coagulopathy, and is associated with an increased risk of bleeding, bruising, or blood clots. Seeded intravascular coagulation (DIC) is common in leukemia. A type of cancer that originates in the bone marrow, specifically affecting the production and function of blood cells. It includes acute myeloid leukemia (AML), which can have genetic abnormalities such as CBF or FLT3 mutations. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is a specific type of leukemia that affects the lymphoid progenitor cells of the immune system. Leukemia can cause leukemic meningitis, which may require a lumbar puncture to check for leukemia cells in the spinal fluid.

nodes.label: Hereditary gene testing
nodes.description: Hereditary gene testing is a type of genetic test used for prostate cancer care that looks for inherited (germline) mutations in specific genes, such as BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, CHEK2, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PALB2, PMS2, and others. This type of testing is done using a sample of blood, urine, or saliva and is used to identify inherited cancer risks.

nodes.label: Surveillance
nodes.description: Recommended follow-up procedures for checking for recurrence after Endoscopic Submucosal Dissection (ESD) or Transanal Local Excision. They include Proctoscopies and imaging, performed every 3 to 6 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months the next 3 years after Transanal Local Excision. A process involving physical exams and follow-up visits for monitoring common types of cervical cancer and small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of the cervix (NECC), especially in the first 5 years after treatment. The recommended time frames for follow-up visits vary from every 3 to 6 months in the first year to once a year or as agreed upon with the doctor after year 5, depending on individual risk of recurrence and patient and provider preference. A series of tests and examinations conducted after finishing treatment for anal cancer to detect early signs of the cancer's return. It includes follow-up physical exams with digital rectal examination (DRE) and anoscopy, imaging tests, and other care measures.

nodes.label: TNM system
nodes.description: A staging system developed by the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) to determine the stage of colon cancer. The TNM system uses three key pieces of information: T (tumor size and depth), N (lymph node involvement), and M (metastasis) to assign a stage to the cancer (0, I, II, III, or IV).

nodes.label: Appendicular Skeleton
nodes.description: The bones of the upper limbs, lower limbs, shoulder girdle, and pelvic girdle, which include 126 bones. A skeletal system that includes the bones connecting the arm to the body and the bones connecting the leg to the body, as described in the text.

nodes.label: Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML)
nodes.description: A type of blood cancer caused by a specific abnormal gene and a shortened chromosome 22 called the Philadelphia (Ph) chromosome. It is characterized by the presence of the BCR::ABL1 gene and the absence of the Ph chromosome indicates the absence of CML. A type of leukemia caused by a specific abnormal gene, the Philadelphia chromosome, which is created when a piece of chromosome 9 and a piece of chromosome 22 break off and trade places. It is thought to arise from blood stem cells that make an increased amount of myeloid progenitor cells. A type of cancer that affects white blood cells and worsens slowly over time. It is caused by a single, specific abnormal gene that leads to the formation of the Philadelphia chromosome.

nodes.label: Head and neck cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer that affects the head and neck region, often involving the mouth, throat, or other structures in these areas. It can occur in various parts such as the mouth (oral cavity), middle part of the throat near the mouth (oropharynx), space behind the nose (nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses), upper part of the throat near the nasal cavity (nasopharynx), voice box (larynx), or lower part of the throat near the voice box (hypopharynx). Head and neck cancer requires special consideration when it comes to dental care and fertility, and treatment teams may include mind and body therapists to support patients. It can be diagnosed and monitored through various examinations such as a physical exam, dental exam, and distress screening. One type of head and neck cancer is associated with HPV.

nodes.label: High-resolution anoscopy (HRA)
nodes.description: A specialized diagnostic procedure used to evaluate anal cancer, typically performed after a digital rectal exam (DRE). It involves the use of a magnifying lens to examine the anal canal for abnormalities. It is an important tool for the diagnosis and evaluation of anal cancer. A medical procedure that allows for the detailed examination of the anal canal using magnification. HRA is typically performed after a digital rectal exam (DRE) and involves the insertion of a hollow tool called an anoscope into the anus, followed by the application of acetic acid to the anal canal tissue. A colposcope is then used to closely examine the tissues for any abnormal cells. If abnormal areas are detected, a biopsy may be taken for further testing. HRA is more effective than standard anoscopy at identifying anal cancer and anal dysplasia and is generally a brief, painless procedure with minimal recovery time.

nodes.label: Imaging
nodes.description: Imaging is a diagnostic test used to visualize the body and detect potential abnormalities or diseases, including computed tomography (CT) with contrast. It is used in various contexts such as colon cancer diagnosis, rectal cancer testing and treatment planning, pancreatic cancer staging, prostate cancer diagnosis, primary CNS lymphoma confirmation, and glioma diagnosis. Imaging tests can reveal the location, size, and other features of a lymphoma, tumors, or potential abnormalities in the brain and spinal cord.

nodes.label: Differential
nodes.description: A possible test for AML, often used in conjunction with other tests like CBC, CMP, uric acid, LDH, B12, and folic acid to assess a patient's blood cell types and counts. A test that counts the number of each type of white blood cell and checks if the counts are in balance with each other, which may show a high number of blasts in the blood in AML patients. A laboratory test that determines the types and percentages of different blood cells in the body, used as part of the medical history and physical exam for acute myeloid leukemia. A test that counts the number of each type of white blood cell and checks if the counts are in balance with each other. It can detect high numbers of blasts in the blood, which may indicate AML. A differential is a part of a complete blood count (CBC) that specifically counts the most common types of white blood cells in the blood and checks if their counts are in balance with each other.

nodes.label: MRI
nodes.description: An imaging scan used to calculate the depth of invasion (DOI) of a tumor. A type of imaging test that uses radio waves and powerful magnets to take pictures of the inside of the body. It can provide a detailed view of the cancer within the prostate and check for cancer spread to nearby lymph nodes or bones in the pelvis. Magnetic Resonance Imaging, an important diagnostic test used to confirm primary CNS lymphoma, along with other imaging techniques like CT scans and biopsies. A type of imaging test used to confirm primary CNS lymphoma, often performed alongside a CT scan. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a diagnostic imaging technique that uses radio waves and powerful magnets to take detailed pictures of the inside of the body, particularly useful for identifying primary CNS lymphoma. It is good at showing the spine, soft tissues, including the brain, and other details that are helpful for planning surgery. A medical test that uses radio waves and powerful magnets to take pictures of the inside of the body, providing a more detailed view of cancer within the bladder or urinary tract, and checking for cancer spread to the liver, nearby lymph nodes, or the bones in your pelvis.

nodes.label: Ovarian Cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer affecting the ovaries, often diagnosed using biopsy and guided by biomarker testing for treatment decisions. It may require surgery for treatment, which can involve removing one or both ovaries and fallopian tubes, the uterus, and lymph nodes. Chemotherapy, particularly paclitaxel with carboplatin given every 3 weeks, is a common treatment after surgery. Ovarian cancer can increase the risk of developing pancreatic cancer and can be associated with germline mutations in genes such as BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, CHEK2, and others, as well as inherited mutations in genes like BRCA1 and BRCA2. It may spread to the lungs and potentially show up in the chest through a PET scan, for which a chest x-ray may be used to check treatment results.

nodes.label: Pelvis
nodes.description: The bony structure located in the lower part of the human body, forming the ring that supports the weight of the upper body and containing the hip bones. Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy samples are usually taken from the back of the hip bone, which is part of the pelvis. The area of the body between the hip bones, below the abdomen, where organs such as the bladder, uterus, ovaries, vagina, and prostate gland are located, along with the rectum and anus.

nodes.label: White Blood Cells
nodes.description: Cells that help fight infection and other diseases, found in lymph tissue and every organ in the body. They are part of the immune system and include lymphocytes. Also known as leukocytes, these cells fight infections. They include granulocytes (neutrophils), monocytes, and lymphocytes. They are formed from blood stem cells in the bone marrow and are released into the bloodstream as needed. A type of blood cell that includes granulocytes, monocytes, and lymphocytes, and fights infections. They are formed from blood stem cells in the bone marrow and released into the bloodstream as needed.

nodes.label: B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma
nodes.description: A type of cancer mentioned in the text, characterized by the growth of B-cell lymphoblasts in the thymus rather than the bone marrow. A type of lymphoma where cancer cells grow primarily in the lymph nodes rather than the bone marrow, often associated with B-cell lymphoblastic leukemia (B-LL) or B-LBL. A type of cancer that occurs when B-cell lymphoblasts grow mostly in the lymph nodes rather than in the bone marrow.

nodes.label: Assessment team
nodes.description: A group of board-certified experts that may include thoracic radiologist, interventional radiologist, pulmonologist, thoracic surgeon, medical oncologist, and radiation oncologist, who work together to evaluate a patient for cancer.

nodes.label: Allergic Reactions
nodes.description: Adverse reactions to contrast material in the past, which may require the administration of medicines to avoid the effects of those allergies. Adverse reactions that can occur if a patient has had a previous allergic response to contrast. Medicines might be given to avoid these effects, and contrast might not be used if the patient has a serious allergy or kidney problems. Adverse reactions to contrast, requiring communication with care teams and potential medical intervention to avoid effects. Adverse reactions to contrast, especially to iodine or shellfish such as shrimp, that could require medical intervention. Adverse reactions to contrast materials that can occur in patients who have had previous allergic reactions. Patients are advised to inform their care team about any past allergic reactions to contrast in order to avoid the effects of those allergies. Contrast might not be used if a patient has a serious allergy or if their kidneys aren’t working well.

nodes.label: Gene
nodes.description: A gene is a segment of DNA that contains instructions for the development and function of an organism. The p16 protein is produced by a gene located on chromosome 9, which is involved in regulating cell division. Genes are coded instructions for the proteins that cells make. They are identified in italics and are part of chromosomes, containing thousands of genes each. Mutations in genes can lead to changes in protein production. Gene is a small segment of DNA inside every cell that provides the instructions to tell the cell how to make proteins, which carry out a lot of important functions in the body. Mutations in genes can lead to disease, such as cancer.

nodes.label: Fertility
nodes.description: Fertility refers to the ability to have children, which can be affected by cancer and cancer treatment, including targeted therapy and other forms of systemic therapy. It is a concern for all genders and can be preserved through various methods, with specialists available to assist in decision-making. The ability to have children, which can be affected by cancer and cancer treatment, especially chemotherapy. Preservation measures should be considered before starting treatment, and specialists can help discuss options. The ability to conceive a child, which may be temporarily or permanently impaired or interrupted due to changes in fertility treatment. Fertility refers to the ability to have children. Cancer and cancer treatment can affect fertility, or the ability to have children, in all genders. It is important to consider fertility preservation options before starting therapy, as these can help to keep open the option of having children in the future. Fertility preservation is a concern for both men and women, and can involve a variety of techniques, such as sperm or egg freezing. Fertility and reproductive specialists can help individuals sort through the best options for their specific situation. A person's ability to conceive and carry a pregnancy to term, which can be temporarily or permanently impaired or interrupted by cancer treatment. Treatment for head and neck cancer can affect a patient's fertility, as mentioned in the text. The ability to have a baby. The text mentions that many people with cancer and its treatment can still have healthy babies, indicating a high likelihood of fertility preservation success.

nodes.label: Lung Cancer
nodes.description: A broad term for cancer that affects the lungs, with NSCLC being the most common type, as mentioned in the text. A type of cancer that originates in the cells of the lungs. It is a significant health concern, and regular screening is recommended for those at risk to detect it at its earliest, most treatable stages. Risk factors for lung cancer include smoking tobacco, exposure to second-hand smoke, and various environmental toxins. A type of cancer, almost always a subtype called carcinomas, that originates in the cells lining the airways of the lungs. It includes non-small cell lung cancer and small cell lung cancer as main types, and can also refer to other types of cancer that have spread to the lungs, such as breast cancer. A type of cancer that starts in the cells lining the lungs, with two main subtypes: carcinomas and small cell lung cancer (SCLC). Early detection can help prevent death and increase the chances of successful treatment. A type of cancer that can be screened for and for which risk factors may require more frequent health care provider visits based on family health history and genetic factors.

nodes.label: Diabetes
nodes.description: A metabolic disorder affecting the body's ability to produce or respond to the hormone insulin, characterized by high levels of sugar in the blood. It is a chronic condition that can run in families and increase the risk of developing pancreatic and liver cancer. Diabetes is managed by regulating blood sugar levels and can be inherited or develop over time.

nodes.label: Treatment Planning
nodes.description: A process in cancer care that starts with testing and involves organizing medical documents, including insurance forms, medical records, and test results, and communicating with the care team, especially in an emergency. The process of determining the most appropriate course of action for managing breast cancer, which begins with testing and gathering information about the specific type of cancer. The process of determining the best course of action for treating cancer, which starts with testing and involves considering the results of various tests such as biopsy, imaging studies, and estrogen receptor status. A process starting with testing, involving the use of test results to determine a treatment plan for stomach cancer.

nodes.label: Cancer care team
nodes.description: A team of medical professionals who work together to provide treatment and supportive care for pancreatic cancer patients. They make a treatment plan specific to the patient and discuss options for treatment and supportive care.

nodes.label: Digestive System
nodes.description: A biological system responsible for breaking down food into nutrients that can be absorbed and used by the body. It includes the esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, and other organs. A system in the body responsible for taking in food, breaking it down, absorbing nutrients, and removing waste. The hepatobiliary system is a part of this system, along with the stomach, small intestine, and other organs. A complex system of organs and structures that takes in and breaks down food, absorbs nutrients, and removes waste from the body.
