It includes organs like the liver, gallbladder, stomach, pancreas, and intestines. The digestive system is responsible for processing food and maintaining overall health.

nodes.label: Bone Marrow Aspirate
nodes.description: A procedure where a hollow needle is pushed through the skin and into the bone to remove liquid bone marrow. It is mentioned as a source of cells for flow cytometry analysis. A procedure used to confirm a diagnosis of acute myeloid leukemia by removing a sample of tissue or group of cells from the bone marrow for testing. A type of bone marrow test that involves taking some of the liquid and cells out of the bone marrow, which is like a sponge holding liquid and cells. It is often performed at the same time as a bone marrow biopsy.

nodes.label: Tumor
nodes.description: A mass or growth of tissue, which can be cancerous or benign, and is often the subject of medical examination and testing to determine its size, spread, and potential for cancerous growth. In the context of cancer, a tumor refers to an abnormal growth of cells, which can be tested for specific mutations, protein levels, or other molecular features. Tumors can form in various parts of the body, including the brain, esophagus, rectum, and bladder, and can grow through the airway, lung tissue, and lung wall, potentially invading other body parts.

nodes.label: Bone marrow
nodes.description: A soft, spongy tissue found inside bones, particularly in the pelvis, sternum, and skull, responsible for producing blood cells, including red blood cells, platelets, and white blood cells. It is the site of hematopoietic stem cell production and where high-dose chemotherapy can damage and destroy cells. There are two types of bone marrow: red and yellow. Bone marrow is a key component of the body's immune system and a part of the lymphatic or lymph system, involved in the production of blood cells, including lymphocytes. It is also a common site for the formation of tumors associated with certain types of leukemia, such as acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL).

nodes.label: Alcohol use
nodes.description: The use of alcohol, which is a known risk factor for developing head and neck cancer and can limit how well treatment works. It is considered in the context of treatment planning for NPC and other medical conditions. A known risk factor for developing head and neck cancer, which can limit the effectiveness of treatment and affect survival rates. Patients are advised to limit alcohol use during treatment. Alcohol use is a risk factor for developing liver disease, including cirrhosis, chronic hepatitis, and liver cancer. High alcohol use can cause damage to the liver.

nodes.label: Radiologist
nodes.description: A medical professional specializing in the interpretation of medical images, such as those obtained from imaging tests, to assist in cancer staging and treatment planning. They are responsible for evaluating diagnostic mammograms while the patient waits, and sending the results to the patient's doctor or care team for further discussion and planning of care. Radiologists are medical experts in interpreting imaging tests and often part of the treatment team for thyroid cancer patients and other medical conditions.

nodes.label: Chemotherapy
nodes.description: A type of cancer treatment that uses drugs to stop the growth of cancer cells, often administered in cycles followed by days of rest to allow the body to recover. It can be given intravenously or intraperitoneally and may cause side effects such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, mouth sores, loss of appetite, hair loss, low blood cell counts, and fatigue. Chemotherapy can be given before or after surgery, or alone for metastatic bladder cancer. It can also be used in combination with other therapies like immunotherapy, radiation therapy, or steroids. Maintenance therapy may follow if the treatment is effective. Chemotherapy can affect a patient's fertility by potentially causing temporary or permanent impairment or interruption of fertility, depending on various factors such as age, treatment type, dose, and length.

nodes.label: Health Care Provider
nodes.description: A medical professional who provides advice and guidance on lung cancer screening, risk assessment, and overall health care. A medical professional who can provide guidance and support during diagnosis and treatment of cancer. A healthcare professional who asks patients about their medications and complementary medicines at the beginning of testing, and who needs to be informed about potential interactions with cancer tests or treatment. A medical professional who provides care and guidance based on a patient's medical history and physical examination results.

nodes.label: Oropharynx
nodes.description: A part of the throat, the oropharynx is located at the back of the roof of the mouth (soft palate), including the tonsils, side and back walls of the throat, and the base of the tongue. Cancer can form in this area. The oropharynx is the area of the throat where throat cancer starts, including the back of the roof of the mouth (soft palate), the tonsils, the side and back walls of the throat, and the base of the tongue. An anatomical structure that can be examined using a rochoscopy. It is located at the back of the mouth and is part of the upper respiratory tract. A part of the throat located in the head and neck area, where cancer can develop and be difficult to see without specialized tools like a special mirror or fiberoptic scope. A location in the head and neck that can be affected by tumors, along with the nasopharynx, and is measured in centimeters (cm), with a baseball being 7 cm, a golf ball being 4 cm, and a pea being 1 cm. A location in the neck where tumors can grow, along with the base of the skull, larynx, bones and muscles behind the nasal cavity, jaw, and roof of the mouth.

nodes.label: Esophagus
nodes.description: A long, muscular tube located behind the trachea and in front of the spine, through which food passes from the throat to the stomach as part of the digestive system. It contains 4 layers: mucosa, lamina propria, muscularis mucosa, submucosa, and muscularis propria. The upper part is made of striated muscle, the middle part is a mixture of striated and smooth muscle, and the lower part consists only of smooth muscle. The esophagogastric junction (EGJ) is found just beneath the diaphragm where the esophagus meets the stomach. It is a part of the digestive or gastrointestinal (GI) tract, located between the mouth and the stomach. The esophagus is examined as part of an upper endoscopy, which involves guiding a scope down the throat into the esophagus, stomach, and small bowel. It is a muscular tube that connects the mouth to the stomach, allowing food and liquids to pass from the mouth into the stomach and is part of the digestive system that works in conjunction with the stomach and small intestine to transport food and liquids into the stomach. It is also a tube-like structure that connects the mouth to the stomach, through which food and liquids pass during swallowing.

nodes.label: Longer-Term Surveillance
nodes.description: A period of medical monitoring after thyroid cancer treatment, involving physical exams, blood tests (TSH, Tg, and Tg ab), and neck ultrasound. May also involve additional lab work, neck ultrasounds, TSH-stimulated testing, or imaging procedures if there is reason to suspect the cancer has returned.

nodes.label: Blood Tests
nodes.description: Medical tests involving the collection and analysis of blood samples, used to diagnose conditions such as CML, assess health conditions, and monitor treatment. They may include general health tests, thyroid endocrine levels, and tests ordered during chemotherapy monitoring or to check for cancer recurrence. Results are recommended to be included in a medical binder for organization and future reference.

nodes.label: Imaging Scans
nodes.description: A type of imaging test that uses radio waves and powerful magnets to produce detailed images of the body's internal structures, often used to examine the prostate in prostate cancer.

nodes.label: Dose-dense Chemotherapy
nodes.description: A method of speeding up chemotherapy by shortening the amount of time between treatments. The most common systemic chemotherapy used to treat bladder cancer is a combination of medicines known as dose-dense methotrexate, vinblastine, doxorubicin, and cisplatin (ddMVAC).

nodes.label: Treatment
nodes.description: The process of managing or curing a medical condition, such as CML or lung cancer, as mentioned in the text. A general term for medical procedures or therapies used to manage or cure cancer, mentioned as a category of records to be organized in a medical binder. The process or methods used to manage or cure bladder cancer. It can improve the quality of life for most people with the disease, though it may not always be a permanent solution as the cancer can recur. A medical procedure or therapy related to cancer management, including questions about frequency, duration, side effects, cost, and impact on daily life. A medical procedure or therapy involving chemotherapy and radiation that may cause side effects and may require adjustments based on patient responses.

nodes.label: PSA Level
nodes.description: A measurement of prostate-specific antigen (PSA) in nanograms of PSA per milliliter (ng/mL) of blood, used to detect prostate cancer. A measurement of prostate-specific antigen (PSA) in the blood, which may indicate the need for additional blood or urine testing. A measurement used to detect possible prostate cancer, along with an abnormal digital rectal exam as a sign of possible prostate cancer. A measurement of prostate-specific antigen (PSA) in the blood, which can vary based on prostate size but doesn't necessarily indicate a greater risk for prostate cancer on its own.

nodes.label: Cisplatin
nodes.description: A platinum-based chemotherapy drug used in the treatment of various types of cancer, including ovarian, cervical, bladder, anal, and perianal cancer. It is typically given on a 7-day cycle for 5 to 6 weeks as part of chemoradiation and can cause kidney damage, ringing in the ears, hearing problems, or hearing loss, and other side effects. It may not be suitable for patients with poor kidney function and can cause a hypersensitivity reaction when repeated. It is often used in combination with other drugs such as paclitaxel, topotecan, 5-FU, or carboplatin.

nodes.label: Physical exam
nodes.description: A medical examination conducted by a healthcare provider to assess a patient's overall health and detect potential issues. It involves checking various vital signs such as temperature, blood pressure, pulse, and breathing rate, assessing height and weight, listening to the lungs and heart, examining the eyes, ears, nose, throat, and lymph nodes, and feeling and applying pressure to different parts of the body to evaluate organ size, texture, and response to touch. A physical exam may also involve checking for enlarged lymph nodes in specific areas of the body and assessing a patient's ability to manage daily tasks and activities.

nodes.label: Family history
nodes.description: Information about the health history of family members who are blood relatives, used by healthcare providers to determine the best treatment for a patient's medical condition. Family history refers to the health history of blood relatives, including information about heart disease, cancer, and diabetes, and at what age they were diagnosed. This information is important for determining the risk of certain cancers and other diseases running in families.

nodes.label: Liver
nodes.description: A large, flat organ located in the upper right part of the abdomen. Cancer cells can travel through the blood to distant organs like the liver, where they can grow and form new tumors. An essential organ responsible for various functions in the human body, including detoxification, protein synthesis, and storage of nutrients. The liver is one of the organs monitored for health during AML treatment and recovery through blood tests to assess its function and overall health. An organ whose health can be assessed through liver function tests (LFTs) and whose chemicals, such as bile, are measured to evaluate its function and the condition of bile ducts. The liver is an organ responsible for various functions in the body, including processing nutrients, detoxification, and producing bile. Its proper functioning is essential for overall health, and abnormalities can indicate issues like blocked bile ducts. A vital organ in the human body responsible for processing sugar for energy and producing lymph. It has two lobes, receives blood from the hepatic artery and portal vein, and sends blood out through the hepatic veins into the inferior vena cava. The liver is located near the gallbladder, stomach, pancreas, spleen, and small intestine. An organ in the body that filters blood, helps with blood clotting, makes bile, breaks down fats, and helps process sugar for energy. It also produces lymph. The liver, gallbladder, and bile ducts are part of the hepatobiliary system. An organ in the body that can be affected by health problems indicated by protein levels in the blood. Issues with the liver can be signaled by abnormal protein levels.

nodes.label: Brain
nodes.description: A vital organ of the central nervous system, responsible for controlling and coordinating bodily functions, and a common site for metastatic cancer to spread, including breast, thyroid, and kidney cancer, as well as primary CNS lymphoma. It is protected by the skull and shielded by meninges and cerebrospinal fluid. Symptoms of glioma-related brain dysfunction include slower thinking, memory loss, difficulty moving or walking, trouble speaking, inability to do everyday activities, changes in behavior, losing one’s sense of self, and other issues.

nodes.label: chemotherapy
nodes.description: A type of cancer treatment that uses drugs to kill cancer cells or prevent them from growing and dividing. Chemotherapy regimens used to treat rectal cancer are listed in Guide. Any regimen that has “OX” in the name includes oxaliplatin, which can cause nerve damage, and any regimen that has “IRI” in the name contains irinotecan, which tends to cause abdominal cramping, nausea, diarrhea, and hair loss.

nodes.label: Prostate cancer
nodes.description: Prostate cancer is a disease where cells in the prostate gland grow out of control, often affecting men aged 65 years and above. It can be categorized into early-stage cancer, which has not spread beyond the prostate, and advanced-stage cancer, where cancer cells have spread outside the prostate to other areas in the body. Early-stage prostate cancer is often curable and can be localized to the prostate, while advanced-stage prostate cancer can be regional, affecting nearby lymph nodes, or metastatic, spreading to distant organs like the bones, liver, or lungs. Prostate cancer is a common cancer among men, with symptoms typically not present until the disease is more advanced. Risk factors include age, family history, and certain medical conditions, with Black males being more likely to develop it earlier and with greater severity. Prostate cancer can be diagnosed through various tests, including prostate-specific antigen (PSA) test and digital rectal exam, and treated with methods such as hormone therapy, chemotherapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, radiation therapy, and surgery.

nodes.label: Care team
nodes.description: A group of healthcare professionals involved in a patient's care, including doctors, nurses, and other specialists. They are responsible for gathering a patient's health information, discussing symptoms, and making treatment recommendations based on diagnostic test results. Patients are encouraged to make shared decisions with their care team, ask questions, and advocate for themselves. The care team may prescribe medications and need to be informed about a patient's supplement use and symptoms in order to determine the most appropriate treatment approach.

nodes.label: Total thyroidectomy
nodes.description: A surgical procedure where the entire thyroid gland is removed, along with nearby lymph nodes if they are known or suspected to have cancer. This is called a neck dissection and is performed under general anesthesia with a small incision in the front of the neck.

nodes.label: Ultrasound
nodes.description: A non-invasive medical imaging technique that uses high-energy sound waves to form pictures of the inside of the body, similar to the sonogram used for pregnancy. It is painless, does not use x-rays, and can be repeated as needed. Ultrasound is effective at detecting small areas of cancer in various parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, and can guide biopsies, including fine-needle biopsies. It is commonly used in the diagnostic process for breast health, prostate cancer, and thyroid and neck imaging.

nodes.label: NCCN Guidelines for Patients
nodes.description: A trusted resource for patients and providers, developed by respected experts in the field of cancer care, that provides clear explanations of current care recommendations based on the latest research and practices at leading cancer centers. These guidelines help patients understand cancer care, enabling them to discuss their care more effectively with their team and share their concerns. They are not to be reproduced without express written permission from NCCN and may not be used for commercial purposes. NCCN Guidelines for Patients are designed to assist patients in making informed decisions about their treatment and are organized into chapters, each ending with a section called 'Questions to ask' to encourage patient engagement and shared decision-making with the care team.

nodes.label: Multidisciplinary Care Team
nodes.description: A team of specialists and care providers working together to treat cancer. The team includes various medical professionals such as primary care doctors, urologists, urologic oncologists, medical oncologists, radiation oncologists, oncology nurses, pharmacists, diagnostic radiologists, anesthesiologists, and advanced practice providers. The team communicates and coordinates to bring the best knowledge from each specialty to the patient's care.

nodes.label: Distress Screening
nodes.description: A process to assess the level of distress experienced by individuals diagnosed with cancer, which can affect mental, physical, social, or spiritual well-being. A process where a care team assesses the level of distress experienced by a patient, which is an unpleasant experience of a mental, physical, social, or spiritual nature, that can affect how a patient feels, thinks, and acts. A process to assess the level of distress experienced by individuals diagnosed with cancer, which can affect their mental, physical, social, or spiritual well-being.

nodes.label: National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN)
nodes.description: A leading cancer care and research organization that provides guidelines for the treatment of various types of cancer, including NSCLC, and offers patient guidelines and information about metastatic NSCLC through their website and app. The NCCN also funds and distributes NCCN Guidelines for Patients, and supports cancer treatment by advancing the work of promising doctors in cancer research. Additionally, they provide resources for managing chemotherapy side effects, specifically for nausea and vomiting.

nodes.label: Stem Cell Rescue
nodes.description: A medical procedure involving the removal, concentration, freezing, and later transfusion of stem cells to restore blood cell production and bone marrow function. It's used after other treatments or in case of relapse in primary CNS lymphoma.

nodes.label: Radiation Therapy
nodes.description: A type of cancer treatment that uses high-energy rays to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors, often administered externally using a large machine. It can be used alone or in combination with other therapies such as systemic therapy, chemotherapy, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy. Commonly used for anal cancer, primary CNS lymphoma, and bladder cancer, among other types. May cause side effects such as headaches, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, fatigue, and nervous system damage, especially in older adults. Can cause vision problems, cataracts, and other eye-related issues. May be more likely to damage the nervous system than chemotherapy. Palliative radiation therapy may be an option if the cancer is causing symptoms, with care taken to avoid treating areas initially treated with radiation a second time.

nodes.label: Kidneys
nodes.description: A pair of organs found in the abdomen, responsible for filtering blood, removing waste, and controlling fluid and chemical levels. Each kidney is about the size of an adult's fist, functions independently, and can support the body with less than one complete kidney. They are also responsible for producing urine, which flows down to the bladder through the ureters. Most people can live full, healthy lives with only one kidney. Cancer can start in the kidneys, although bladder is the most common site for urothelial carcinoma. The anatomical structures examined during a ureteroscopy, which goes a little farther than a cystoscopy to look at the upper parts of the urinary tract, are also examined. In an ileal conduit procedure, urine drains from the kidneys and passes through the ureters into the ileal conduit tube.

nodes.label: Chemoradiation
nodes.description: A combination treatment involving both platinum chemotherapy and EBRT, recommended for cancers with risk factors or if cancer is found in pelvic or paraaortic lymph nodes or tissues outside the cervix. A combination of chemotherapy and radiation therapy given during the same time period. It is recommended for cervical cancers with risk factors and for cancers found in any pelvic or paraaortic lymph nodes, or in any tissues outside the cervix. A treatment approach for locally advanced cervical cancers that combines external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) and platinum chemotherapy. A combination treatment for bladder cancer that involves the use of chemotherapy and radiation therapy together, which is more effective than when given alone. It is also known as chemoradiotherapy. A primary treatment for most non-metastatic anal cancers, involving the combination of chemotherapy and radiation, recommended to cure the cancer. A treatment approach for perianal cancer involving the combined use of chemotherapy and radiation therapy, typically used for stages I through III perianal cancer, which are nonmetastatic. A type of cancer treatment combining chemotherapy and radiation therapy, which may be given after certain chemotherapy regimens to treat metastatic anal cancer.

nodes.label: Biopsy
nodes.description: A medical procedure where a sample of tissue or fluid is removed from the body for examination under a microscope, often used to confirm the presence of cancer, identify specific DNA mutations, protein levels, or other molecular features, and determine the type and stage of the disease. It may involve various types such as fine-needle aspiration (FNA), core needle biopsy (CNB), vacuum-assisted core biopsy (VACB), incisional biopsy, excisional biopsy, skin biopsy, and may be guided by imaging techniques like mammogram, ultrasound, or MRI. A biopsy does not cause cancer to spread or worsen and is typically followed by a pathology report written by a pathologist.

nodes.label: Biomarker Testing
nodes.description: A type of testing used in cancer staging to determine if the cancer has any genes or mutations that might suggest treatment. The results of biomarker testing can help guide treatment decisions. A process of testing for genes, proteins, markers, or mutations in the cancer that might suggest treatment. A testing process that examines a tumor or blood sample for specific genes or mutations that may suggest treatment options, often used to guide cancer staging and treatment decisions. A general term for various types of testing used to assess cancer, including molecular testing, tumor profiling, genomic testing, tumor gene testing, next-generation sequencing (NGS), mutation testing, and comprehensive genomic profiling (CGP). It can be performed on tumor tissue or a sample of blood. A type of medical testing involving the analysis of a piece of tumor tissue in a lab or testing a sample of blood, often used to identify targetable features of a cancer. Recommended for recurrent, advanced, or metastatic cancers that can't be treated with RAI therapy.

nodes.label: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL)
nodes.description: A fast-growing blood cancer that starts in lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell, and is the most common cancer diagnosed in children. It involves the production of too many immature lymphocytes called lymphoblasts, which can crowd out normal bone marrow and lead to less blood being made. There are two main types: B-cell ALL and T-cell ALL. B-cell ALL, or B-ALL, is more common than T-cell ALL and includes a rare subtype called mature B-cell ALL, which is essentially the same as Burkitt lymphoma but treated differently. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is a type of blood cancer that affects the lymphoid progenitor cells, leading to the development of a type of white blood cell called lymphocytes. It is a disease that primarily impacts blood stem cells and their maturation into various blood cell types. A type of cancer, the most common diagnosed in children, that starts in lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell, and has specific treatment depending on various factors. A fast-growing blood cancer that starts in disease-fighting white blood cells of the immune system called lymphocytes. It is the most common cancer diagnosed in children and is characterized by the bone marrow making too many immature lymphocytes called lymphoblasts or blasts. There are two main types of ALL: B-cell or B-ALL and T-cell or T-ALL. B-ALL is more common than T-ALL and includes a rare subtype called mature B-cell ALL, also known as Burkitt leukemia, which is essentially the same as Burkitt lymphoma but treated differently from B-ALL.

nodes.label: PMS2
nodes.description: PMS2 is a gene that, when mutated, can increase the risk of different types of cancer, including prostate, breast, ovarian, pancreatic, and skin cancer (melanoma). Germline mutations in this gene are associated with an increased risk of cancer in general. A gene associated with germline mutations that can put an individual at risk for prostate cancer, colorectal and uterine cancers, and skin cancer (melanoma). PMS2 is a gene that, when mutated, can increase the risk of different types of cancer. It is one of the genes typically looked at in hereditary gene testing for prostate cancer. A gene associated with inherited mutations that can increase the risk of developing certain cancers, including prostate cancer, colorectal cancer, and other cancers.

nodes.label: Radiation
nodes.description: A type of treatment that includes several short sessions given once daily over a few days to weeks. A treatment for cervical cancer that may be administered after non-fertility-sparing treatment or if the cancer is stage 1B3. A type of initial treatment for anal cancer, mentioned as a factor that, if present, may lead to the recommendation of a groin dissection and/or chemotherapy if cancer returns to lymph nodes in the groin but not to the anal area.

nodes.label: Lynch syndrome
nodes.description: A hereditary cancer syndrome associated with an increased risk for different types of cancer, including colorectal cancer, endometrial cancer, and ovarian cancer. It is caused by inherited mutations in the mismatch repair (MMR) genes and increases the risk of developing colon, endometrial, and ovarian cancers. Lynch syndrome is often diagnosed through genetic testing and is linked to an increased risk of developing various types of cancer, including ovarian cancer. It is the most common cause of hereditary colon and uterine cancers but can also cause other cancers. Individuals with Lynch syndrome should be tested for mutations in MMR genes, and those with rectal cancer and a dMMR/MSI-H tumor should be tested for this syndrome.

nodes.label: Endoscopic Submucosal Dissection
nodes.description: A minimally invasive procedure used to remove small rectal cancers in one piece, often curing them. It is recommended for all T1 tumors and involves using an endoscope to locate the tumor, injecting fluid between the tumor and the muscle layer, and cutting off the tumor. Another name for this procedure is Endoscopic Mucosal Resection (EMR).

nodes.label: Myeloid Progenitor Cells
nodes.description: A type of progenitor cell that forms into myeloblasts and other non-lymphoid blood cells. They are involved in the development of myeloid cells, which include red blood cells, platelets, and some white blood cells. Cells in the bone marrow that develop into red blood cells, granulocytes (a type of white blood cell), and platelets. They are affected by AML, which causes the production of abnormal myeloblasts. A type of progenitor cell that forms into myeloblasts and other non-lymphoid blood cells. They are involved in the development of non-lymphoid blood cells. A type of progenitor cell that forms into myeloblasts and other non-lymphoid blood cells. They are involved in the development of white blood cells and platelets.

nodes.label: Physical Exams
nodes.description: An important part of surveillance performed by an oncologist, especially in the first 5 years after treatment. Patients are encouraged to report any changes in their health, such as new or worsening symptoms and other health conditions or concerns, at these follow-up visits. A type of medical examination involving a doctor's hands-on assessment of a patient's body, often part of surveillance and follow-up procedures for thyroid cancer.

nodes.label: Colostomy
nodes.description: A procedure where a part of the colon is connected to the outside of the abdomen, creating an opening (a stoma) on the surface of the abdomen. This is done if the colon can't be connected to the anus or the surgeon delays reattaching the bowel. A surgical procedure involving the attachment of the remaining upper part of the colon to an opening on the surface of the abdomen. This may be done during a colectomy if it is not safe to reconnect the remaining sections of the colon. The colostomy allows waste to be removed from the body through the opening in the abdomen. A surgical procedure where a part of the colon is attached to an opening on the surface of the abdomen, creating a stoma through which stool exits the body and enters a bag attached to the skin. It is often performed to address bowel blockage caused by a large tumor and can be reversed with another operation. Colostomy diverts the flow of stool and is also known as diversion. A surgical procedure where a stoma is created on the abdomen to allow waste to pass outside the body, often performed temporarily or as a first step before a colectomy. A surgical procedure where the remaining colon is connected to the remaining rectum or anus, allowing for near-normal bowel function. A permanent colostomy may not be required in some cases. A surgical procedure involving the creation of an opening in the abdomen for waste to pass into a bag, often required after an abdominoperineal resection (APR). Colostomy is a surgery that allows stool to leave the body after the anus is removed. The end of the bowel is attached to an opening in the surface of the abdomen, and stool is collected in a disposable bag outside of the body.

nodes.label: Blood tests
nodes.description: Diagnostic procedures that involve the collection and analysis of blood samples. Blood tests may be used to identify potential risk factors for ovarian cancer, confirm a diagnosis, or guide treatment decisions. They may include tests for biomarkers, hormones, or other substances that are associated with the disease. A series of medical tests that may be ordered as part of initial testing to provide information about the patient's general health and the health of their liver, kidneys, and other organs before treatment. Laboratory tests that analyze a patient's blood to detect signs of disease or assess their overall health. They are a part of general health tests.

nodes.label: Seminal vesicles
nodes.description: The seminal vesicles are a part of the male reproductive system, responsible for producing seminal fluid that nourishes and transports sperm. They are one of the components that make up the male reproductive system, along with the prostate gland, penis, and testicles. Two glands located above the prostate and behind the bladder, responsible for producing part of the fluid that becomes semen. The seminal vesicles are a part of the male reproductive system that produce a component of semen. Two glands that make and store another part of the fluid that becomes semen, located near the prostate. Two glands that make and store another part of the fluid that becomes semen, located above the prostate and behind the bladder.

nodes.label: Ectocervix
nodes.description: The outer part of the cervix, appearing rounded and extending into the vagina. It can be seen during an examination of the vagina and cervix using a speculum and is lined with squamous cells. The outer part of the cervix that appears rounded and extends into the vagina. It is lined with squamous cells and can be seen during a vaginal examination using a speculum. Most cervical cancers start in the ectocervix portion of the transformation zone. The rounded, bottom part of the cervix, from which small samples of tissue may be taken during a cervical biopsy. The outer part of the cervix, which meets with the endocervix to form the transformation zone.

nodes.label: Squamous cell skin cancer
nodes.description: A type of skin cancer that is the second most common type after basal cell carcinoma. It is highly treatable and often curable, affecting fair-skinned people more commonly. It is characterized by scaly patches that can become solid and misshapen. Also known as cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC). A type of skin cancer that can be treated with various surgical procedures, though the specific details of its treatment are not provided in the text. A type of skin cancer that can be treated using standard surgical excision or Mohs surgery. If lymph nodes near a squamous cell skin cancer tumor are enlarged, the doctor might biopsy them to check for cancer cells. A type of skin cancer that can be treated with surgery, cryotherapy, and radiation therapy. It can spread to nearby lymph nodes and has different risk levels based on the presence of local recurrence and metastasis risks. A type of cancer that can start in damaged skin, especially after radiation therapy, a wound, a scar, or an area of damaged or inflamed skin. It can also form fibrous or connective tissue, indicating a high-risk or very high-risk cancer. Tumors may invade nerves, leading to signs like pain, burning, stinging, loss of feeling or movement, and double or blurred vision. The tumor grade is a rating of how fast the cancer is expected to grow and spread, based on how different the tumor cells look compared to normal cells under a microscope. Certain rare subtypes of squamous cell skin cancer are more likely to return after treatment.

nodes.label: Family history
nodes.description: Information about the health history of a patient's blood relatives, including any instances of cancer, heart disease, or diabetes. Care teams will ask about the patient's family history to help determine their risk for certain conditions and make informed treatment decisions. A family history is a record of the health issues and medical conditions that affect family members, particularly blood relatives, over multiple generations. It is used by care teams to identify potential hereditary risks and inform treatment decisions. A record of the health history of a patient's blood relatives, including information on diseases like heart disease, cancer, and diabetes, and the ages at which they were diagnosed. It is used by care teams to identify potential hereditary health risks. A record of the health histories of blood relatives, used to identify any patterns of cancer or other diseases that may run in families. This information is used by healthcare providers to assess the risk of certain conditions and to determine appropriate screening and prevention strategies. It involves asking about the health issues like heart disease, cancer, and diabetes, and at what age they were diagnosed in family members on both sides of the family. A record of the health histories of a patient's biological family members. It is used as part of treatment planning for NPC and other medical conditions to assess the patient's overall health and identify any potential issues. Family history is important in assessing risk for certain cancers and other diseases, and healthcare providers will ask about the health history of family members who are blood relatives. The health history of blood relatives, including information about heart disease, cancer, and diabetes, and the age at which these conditions were diagnosed. This information helps healthcare providers understand potential genetic risks and make informed treatment decisions. Information about the health history of family members who are blood relatives, which can help determine the risk of certain cancers and other diseases running in families. Healthcare providers will ask about the health history of family members and encourage patients to ask family members about their health issues like heart disease, cancer, and diabetes, and at what age they were diagnosed. It's important to know the specific type of cancer or where the cancer started, if it is in multiple locations, and if they had genetic testing.

nodes.label: Kidneys
nodes.description: Pair of vital organs responsible for filtering waste products and excess fluids from the blood, maintaining fluid and electrolyte balance, and producing hormones. The kidneys are among the organs evaluated for health during AML treatment and recovery through blood tests to ensure their proper functioning. An organ responsible for filtering creatinine out of the blood and maintaining overall kidney function. The level of creatinine in the blood is used as an indicator of kidney health. An organ in the body that can be affected by health problems indicated by protein levels in the blood. Issues with the kidneys can be signaled by abnormal protein levels.

nodes.label: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML)
nodes.description: A type of blood cancer that affects the myeloid lineage of blood cells, characterized by the presence of abnormal, immature cells in the bone marrow. It is caused by the rapid and uncontrolled growth of myeloid cells, leading to the production of abnormal white blood cells. AML can have genetic changes and chromosomes that can be identified through various tests. It is diagnosed when at least 20 percent myeloblasts are present in the bone marrow or blood, and specific gene mutations or abnormal chromosomes can also indicate AML even with fewer blasts. Treatment options include targeted therapies like gemtuzumab ozogamicin (GO) in combination with other drugs.

nodes.label: PET Scan
nodes.description: A medical imaging technique that uses a radioactive drug called a tracer to detect cancer cells and their sugar consumption. It can detect bright spots indicating cancer, but not all tumors or bright spots are cancerous. A PET scan can be combined with CT for a PET/CT scan, which uses a radiotracer called fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG), made of fluoride and a simple form of sugar called glucose. A PET scan appointment can take 1 to 2 hours, including about 30 minutes of actual scanning time. It can be used to detect cancer cells, determine the extent of cancer, monitor treatment, and detect metastasis. A PET scan involves injecting a radioactive substance called a tracer into the bloodstream, which takes about an hour to circulate and is passed out of the body in urine.

nodes.label: Tracer
nodes.description: A radioactive substance injected into a vein to help see cancer cells in the body during a PET scan. A radioactive drug injected into a vein to help the radiologist see certain areas more clearly in imaging procedures like PET scans. A radioactive drug used in PET scans to help visualize certain structures or processes. A radioactive drug injected into a vein to see where cancer cells are in the body and how much sugar is being taken up by the cancer cells in a PET scan. A radioactive sugar-based substance injected into a vein to locate cancer cells and observe their sugar consumption during a PET scan. A radioactive drug injected into a vein to see where cancer cells are in the body and how much sugar is being taken up by the cancer cells, giving an idea about how fast the cancer cells are growing. A radioactive substance injected into the bloodstream for a PET scan, taking about an hour to circulate throughout the body before showing up as bright spots on the scan.

nodes.label: Maintenance Therapy
nodes.description: A type of therapy used to manage ovarian cancer after initial treatment, often guided by tumor's BRCA and HRD status. A type of cancer treatment that is used to prevent the recurrence of cancer after initial treatment. The duration of maintenance therapy depends on the specific drug used. It can last up to 2 years with olaparib alone, up to 15 months with olaparib and bevacizumab together, up to 3 years with niraparib alone, and up to 2 years with rucaparib alone. It is stopped if the cancer grows or spreads, or if the side effects become too harsh. A type of intravesical BCG therapy involving three treatments given in one week at 3 months and again at 6 months after TURBT. It can continue every 6 months for up to 3 years, depending on the risk of recurrence.

nodes.label: Axillary lymph nodes (ALNs)
nodes.description: Axillary lymph nodes (ALNs) are lymph nodes located near the armpit. Lymph from breast tissue drains into lymph vessels and travels to these nodes, where it helps to fight germs. Metastasis can involve cancer cells spreading from the primary tumor to ALNs. Lymph nodes located near the armpit that receive lymph from breast tissue. Lymph is a clear fluid that gives cells water and food and helps to fight germs. Breast cancer can spread to ALNs, indicating that the cancer has metastasized. Axillary lymph nodes (ALNs) are lymph nodes near the armpit that receive lymph fluid from breast tissue. They are part of the lymphatic system, which helps to fight germs and drain fluid from the body. Axillary lymph nodes (ALNs) are lymph nodes located near the armpit. They receive lymph from breast tissue through lymph vessels and are involved in the immune response.

nodes.label: Carcinoma In Situ of the Skin (CSCC)
nodes.description: A type of skin cancer that can grow in a radiated area, usually requiring surgical removal due to weakened tissues from radiation. More common on the scalp and can cause side effects such as non-healing ulcers and cataracts if not treated properly.

nodes.label: Clinical trials
nodes.description: Research studies that investigate the safety and effectiveness of investigational treatments for cancer. They provide an opportunity for patients to access new and potentially more effective treatments, and may be an option for those seeking alternative or additional treatment approaches for their cancer. Clinical trials are research studies evaluating new treatments, therapies, or interventions for prostate cancer, pancreatic cancer, and glioma. They are structured research studies that test new treatments, interventions, or tests in people to evaluate their safety and effectiveness, and are an essential part of advancing cancer treatment and improving patient care. Clinical trials involve human participants and may involve receiving a placebo with a standard treatment, a new drug with a standard treatment, or both. There is no fee to enroll in a clinical trial, but participants may have costs indirectly related to the trial, such as transportation or childcare due to extra appointments.

nodes.label: Smoking
nodes.description: The illegal act of using tobacco products, which is a risk factor for various types of cancer and can negatively impact the effectiveness of cancer treatments and wound healing. A harmful behavior associated with increased risk of developing various types of cancer, including head and neck, lung, and other cancers. It can also limit the effectiveness of cancer treatment and prevent wound healing, as well as increase the risk of side effects during and after surgery. The act of smoking tobacco, a behavior that increases the risk of developing various cancers and negatively impacts the effectiveness of cancer treatment and wound healing. It is also associated with increased side effects during and after surgery. A behavior associated with the greatest risk factor for bladder cancer. The text emphasizes that quitting smoking is a key point in managing bladder cancer risk. The act of inhaling and exhaling the smoke of a burned substance, specifically tobacco, as a harmful behavior that can negatively impact health, particularly in the context of cancer treatment and surgery. A risk factor for anal cancer, involving the habit of smoking tobacco products.

nodes.label: Mucosa
nodes.description: The inner membrane of the esophagus wall that is in contact with food. It has 3 parts: epithelium, lamina propria, and muscularis mucosa. The epithelium is normally made up of flat, thin cells called squamous cells. The inner lining of the esophagus where precancerous changes often occur before cancer develops. The inner lining of the esophagus where precancerous changes often occur before cancer develops. The innermost layer of the colon wall that comes in contact with food, starting where cancer typically begins, as described in the text. The inner membrane of the stomach that is in contact with food. It consists of three layers: surface epithelium, lamina propria, and muscularis mucosae. The mucosa produces mucus, which protects the stomach from the acidic environment. The innermost layer of the stomach wall, where most stomach cancers start. It secretes mucus and is part of the digestive system. The innermost layer of the stomach wall that is often the site of pre-cancerous changes and early-stage stomach cancer.

nodes.label: Family history
nodes.description: A concept referring to the health history of blood relatives, including information about cancer, heart disease, and diabetes diagnoses, their specific types, locations, and whether genetic testing has been done. This information is collected by the care team to help determine the best treatment for an individual. A record or account of the health conditions experienced by an individual's blood relatives, including information about the specific type of cancer, age of diagnosis, and whether genetic testing has been conducted. This information is gathered by healthcare providers during family history assessments to evaluate an individual's risk of developing certain health conditions.

nodes.label: TNM
nodes.description: A system used for assigning cancer a stage based on the size and depth of the main (primary) tumor, if cancer has spread to nearby (regional) lymph nodes, and if cancer has spread (metastasized) to distant parts of the body. An example of a TNM score is T1N0M0 or T1, N0, M0, which might represent a stage 1 cancer.

nodes.label: Lung Cancers
nodes.description: A group of diseases characterized by the formation of cancer cells in the cells that line the airways of the lungs. These cancers can grow through the airway, lung tissue, and lung wall, potentially invading other body parts. A type of cancer that may be affected by smoking or vaping, potentially leading to side effects during and after surgery. A type of cancer associated with a history of smoking or vaping nicotine. They are one of several types of cancer increased by smoking or vaping, along with head and neck and other cancers. A type of cancer affecting the lungs. The text mentions that smoking or vaping increases the risk of developing this type of cancer.

nodes.label: Anal cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer that primarily affects the anal canal or the perianal region, most often starting in squamous cells lining the canal that leads from the skin surface into the rectum. It is characterized by the presence of squamous cell carcinoma, which is different from other types of colorectal cancers such as adenocarcinomas. Risk factors for anal cancer include long-term infection with human papillomavirus (HPV), and people with HIV are at increased risk of developing the condition. Anal cancer can be locally progressive or metastatic, and treatment options may include surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, or immunotherapy. It is a fairly rare condition, and symptoms may include bleeding from the anus. Early detection and treatment are important for managing the condition.

nodes.label: Preventing pregnancy during treatment
nodes.description: An important consideration for cancer patients undergoing treatment. It involves avoiding pregnancy for both the patient and their partner due to potential effects of cancer and its treatment on the ovaries and sperm. Hormonal birth control, intrauterine devices (IUDs), and barrier methods such as condoms, diaphragms, cervical caps, and the contraceptive sponge may be recommended as options.

nodes.label: NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app
nodes.description: A mobile application developed by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) that provides patient guides for various types of cancer, including NSCLC, metastatic breast cancer, distress during cancer care, and fertility and family planning. It offers detailed information about early-stage prostate cancer, metastatic NSCLC, and other cancer-related topics such as polyps, HPV-related cancers, and gallbladder and bile duct tumors. The app is accessible through the NCCN organization and can be used to access NCCN Guidelines for Patients: Bladder Cancer, Early-Stage Prostate Cancer, Colorectal Cancer Screening, and other patient guides.

nodes.label: Systemic therapy
nodes.description: A type of treatment used for high-risk or very high-risk squamous cell skin cancer in non-surgical candidates, along with radiation therapy. A type of cancer treatment administered systemically, which may have common and rare side effects. A type of therapy that affects the whole body, typically given directly into a vein. The most common types of systemic therapy for bladder cancer are chemotherapy and immunotherapy. A treatment that affects the whole body, typically given directly into a vein (intravenously, or IV). The most common types for bladder cancer are chemotherapy and immunotherapy.

nodes.label: Colon Cancer
nodes.description: A common and treatable type of cancer that starts in the colon, often curable when found early. It is the focus of the guide. A type of cancer discussed in the text, often diagnosed through colonoscopy and tested for mismatch repair status. A type of cancer that is being diagnosed more often in young adults, and for which CT scan with contrast is the main imaging test used to determine the extent of the disease in the body. A type of cancer that affects the colon, involving the growth of cancer within the colon wall and potentially requiring chemotherapy after surgery. In some cases, it may necessitate a colostomy procedure during surgery to address bowel blockage caused by a large tumor. A type of cancer that originates in the colon, which can spread to nearby lymph nodes and other areas of the body, such as the liver and lungs.

nodes.label: White blood cells
nodes.description: White blood cells, or leukocytes, are a type of blood cell that play a crucial role in the immune system by defending the body against infections and diseases. They are involved in the body's immune response and their counts are often high at the diagnosis of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). In the context of Hodgkin lymphoma, lymphocytes, which are a type of white blood cell, are the most important cells to understand the disease. White blood cells can be affected by acute myeloid leukemia (AML), leading to a deficiency in their production. Flow cytometry can detect subtle differences between different types of blood cancers, which may not be detectable through white blood cell counts alone.

nodes.label: Targeted Therapy
nodes.description: A type of cancer treatment that uses drugs or other substances to identify and attack specific cancer cells, often used in combination with other therapies and recommended in clinical trials. It may have fewer side effects than chemotherapy and is used for various types of cancer, including primary central nervous system lymphoma, metastatic thyroid cancers, and bladder cancer. Examples include Padcev (enfortumab vedotin-ejfv), Balversa (erdafitinib), and Trodelvy (sacituzumab govitecan-hziy) for bladder cancer.

nodes.label: Clinical trial
nodes.description: A type of medical research study involving human participants that evaluates the safety and effectiveness of new medical treatments, therapies, or preventive measures. Clinical trials may continue to provide standard cancer care to participants, with the standard treatment typically billed and covered by insurance, and patients responsible for copayments and out-of-pocket costs not covered by insurance. Eligibility criteria, informed consent, and a research team are involved in managing clinical trials. Clinical trials may be an option for treatment in addition to standard of care treatments, and may include phases such as dose, safety, and side effects (Phase 1), how well the drug or approach works against a specific type of cancer (Phase 2), test the drug or approach against a standard treatment (Phase 3), and study the long-term safety and benefit of an FDA-approved treatment (Phase 4).

nodes.label: 5-FU
nodes.description: A recommended chemotherapy option for stage 3 colon cancers, typically given for 3 to 6 months, depending on the risk of recurrence. A chemotherapy drug used in the treatment of perianal cancer, administered as an infusion starting when radiation therapy begins and lasting for 4 to 5 days. Another 4- to 5-day infusion is given at the start of week 5 of radiation therapy. A single dose of mitomycin is given on the first day of the first 5-FU infusion and may be given again when the second 5-FU infusion begins. It can cause side effects such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, sores in the mouth and lining of the anus, and low blood cell counts. A chemotherapy drug component of a recommended regimen for treating cancer that returns to lymph nodes, with carboplatin and paclitaxel suggested as a preferred alternative.

nodes.label: Colon
nodes.description: The longest segment of the large bowel, responsible for absorbing water and forming solid waste. It is a part of the large intestine (bowel) located above the rectum and is examined during a colonoscopy by guiding a scope through the rectum. The colon is involved in the removal of waste from the body and can be connected to the outside of the abdomen in a colostomy procedure, creating an opening called a stoma for stool to exit the body. Cancers of the colon may require a colectomy for complete removal, and the two healthy ends of the remaining colon can be attached to each other. Colon cancer often forms in polyps on the lining of the colon, making it an important focus in the prevention and early detection of the disease. The colon is also known as the large intestine and is part of the digestive or gastrointestinal (GI) tract.

nodes.label: Blood
nodes.description: A fluid connective tissue that transports oxygen, nutrients, hormones, and waste products throughout the body. It contains various types of cells, including red blood cells, platelets, and white blood cells. A tissue in the body composed of plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Blood's function is to move oxygen and nutrients throughout the body, carry away waste, play an important role in the immune system, and prevent bleeding. It is a clear, yellowish fluid made up of mostly water. The fluid that circulates in the body, carrying oxygen and nutrients to cells and removing waste products. In AML, abnormal myeloblasts are found in the blood, causing a malfunction of the bone marrow or blood. A clear, yellowish fluid that makes up more than half of the human body's blood. It contains three types of blood cells: red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets, each with specific functions.

nodes.label: Liver cancer
nodes.description: Liver cancer is a type of cancer that originates in the liver, with the most common type being hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). There are also other types, such as intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, which is a cancer of the bile ducts, and rare types of sarcoma that start in the blood vessel cells of the liver. Liver cancer is a type of cancer that originates in the liver, specifically in the blood vessel cells of the liver. It can spread directly through the liver, to distant sites like the lung or bone, or through the blood and lymphatic system. The most common type of liver cancer is hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Risk factors for liver cancer include cirrhosis, hepatitis B or C, alcohol abuse, and exposure to certain toxins. Liver cancer is a medical condition that can develop in individuals with cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis B. It is associated with chronic hepatitis, scarring of the liver (cirrhosis), liver failure, and can be caused by various risk factors including hepatitis B virus or infection, hepatitis C virus or infection, alcohol use, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), genetic hemochromatosis, stage 4 primary biliary cholangitis, alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency, and other causes of cirrhosis. Screening for liver cancer is recommended for those with cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis B, and risk factors for liver cancer include high alcohol use and certain demographic characteristics such as being an Asian male assigned sex at birth 40 years of age or over, an Asian female assigned sex at birth 50 years of age or over, or an African/North American Black person with hepatitis B. Liver cancer is a type of cancer that starts in the liver, often developing in individuals at risk due to chronic liver diseases like HBV, HCV, NAFLD, or genetic hemochromatosis. Screening helps find it early before symptoms occur, when it is more likely to be cured with treatment. Two recommended tests are an ultrasound (US) and an alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) test every 6 months for those at risk. Liver cancer is a medical condition affecting the liver, which can be diagnosed through various tests including blood tests, imaging studies, and biopsies. The goal of liver cancer screening is to identify the disease early in individuals at risk, allowing for more effective treatment and management. Treatment plans are based on the results of these tests, and patients are encouraged to understand their test results and actively engage with their care team.

nodes.label: Pediatric
nodes.description: A demographic category referring to infants, children, and young adults, defined as individuals 18 years of age or under, and certain adolescents and young adults (AYAs) 15 to 39 years of age at the time of initial cancer diagnosis. It is a context for the type of care and treatment recommendations provided in the book. Refers to acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) found in infants, children, and young adults, specifically anyone 18 years of age or under, and certain adolescents and young adults (AYAs) who are 15 to 39 years of age at the time of initial cancer diagnosis.

nodes.label: Cancer Cells
nodes.description: Abnormal cells that can be detected by PET scans through the use of a radioactive tracer, which highlights their sugar consumption. Not all tumors or bright spots are cancerous. Cells that grow and divide abnormally, faster than normal cells, and appear brighter in an MRI or PET scan due to their higher sugar usage. Cells that grow and divide abnormally, using sugar faster than normal cells, and can appear brighter in medical imaging tests like PET. Abnormal cells that grow and divide out of control, which can be detected using a PET scan by showing up as bright spots in the images. Cells that may or may not cause symptoms when found in the spinal fluid and are the subject of a lumbar puncture to check for spread to the spinal cord.

nodes.label: Lobectomy
nodes.description: A surgical procedure involving the removal of a lobe of the thyroid gland, often used in the treatment of thyroid cancer. It may not require lifelong thyroid hormone replacement therapy, potentially with a lower dose needed. Short-term follow-up involves a physical exam and TSH blood test, with a neck ultrasound recommended 6 to 12 months after surgery. It may be a treatment option if the cancer is small and noninvasive, and certain criteria are met, such as no previous radiation therapy and the cancer not spreading beyond the thyroid.

nodes.label: Thyroid
nodes.description: An organ in the body where squamous cells can be found, often associated with squamous cell carcinoma, a type of cancer that originates in squamous cells. An endocrine gland located in the neck that produces hormones regulating metabolism, growth, and development. A butterfly-shaped gland located in the lower front part of the neck, responsible for producing hormones that control blood pressure, metabolism, and other body functions. The thyroid is a butterfly-shaped gland located in the neck that produces hormones to help regulate metabolism and other body functions.

nodes.label: tracer
nodes.description: A radioactive drug injected into a vein to help detect cancer cells and their sugar uptake in a PET scan. A radioactive drug used in PET scans to see where cancer cells are in the body and if they are using sugar produced by your body to grow. It is injected into a vein.

nodes.label: Blood Stem Cells
nodes.description: Early blood-forming cells found in bone marrow that give rise to all types of blood cells, including red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. They are the progenitors of all blood cells. Cells responsible for producing progenitor cells, which eventually develop into red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. They are the initial cells from which all blood cells originate. Early blood-forming cells found in bone marrow that have the ability to develop into different types of blood cells. They are the precursors to red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. In ALL, an increased amount of lymphoid progenitor cells is thought to arise from these stem cells.

nodes.label: Adenocarcinoma
nodes.description: A common type of cancer that forms in an adenoma, a type of polyp, and can spread to areas far from the colon. It is often removed during a colonoscopy using a polypectomy. Adenocarcinoma is the most common type of rectal tumor, cervical cancer, and stomach cancer starting in the cells lining the inside of the stomach and making mucus. It is also the most common subtype of lung cancer, accounting for about 4 out of 10 lung cancers. Adenocarcinoma is less common than squamous cell carcinoma in cervical cancer but more common than adenosquamous carcinoma. It is one of the major types of stomach cancer, with two main types: intestinal and diffuse. Adenocarcinoma is a type of non-urothelial bladder cancer that starts in the gland cells of the bladder lining.

nodes.label: Radiation
nodes.description: A treatment method used alone or in combination with certain systemic therapies to treat or slow the growth of cancer, and may be used as supportive care to help ease pain or discomfort caused by cancer. It involves several short treatment sessions given once daily over a few days to weeks, and may target the chest wall, infraclavicular region, supraclavicular area, or lymph nodes found in the axillary bed. A medical treatment that can damage the ovaries and cause them to stop producing hormones needed for natural pregnancy, often associated with external beam radiation therapy in cervical cancer treatment.

nodes.label: Anal Cancer
nodes.description: An uncommon cancer of the digestive system, most often starting in squamous cells lining the canal that leads from the skin surface into the rectum. It is treated by a team of digestive health experts with experience in chemotherapy, radiation, surgery, and imaging. A type of cancer affecting the anus and nearby areas, including lymph nodes. The most common type is squamous cell carcinoma, which starts in squamous cells found in the tissues that form the surface of the skin and in other areas of the body. Risk factors include long-term infection with HPV, HIV infection, immunosuppressant use, certain cancers or pre-cancers, autoimmune disorders, smoking, and sexually transmitted infections. It is treated with radiation therapy, chemotherapy, and surgery, and may require specific medical treatments and have associated side effects.

nodes.label: Polyps
nodes.description: Non-cancerous growths that form on the inner lining of the colon and rectum. The most common type is called an adenoma, which can become invasive rectal cancer over time. Polyps that rarely turn into cancer include hyperplastic and inflammatory polyps. Removing polyps can prevent cancer before it starts. Polyps are non-cancerous growths that form on the inner lining of the colon and rectum. They can be tested to check for the presence of cancer. Most rectal cancers start in polyps called adenomas, which are called adenocarcinomas. Benign growths that can form in the colon and rectum, associated with familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP). Over time, these polyps can become invasive rectal cancer. Polyps are growths on the lining of the bowel wall, including pedunculated and sessile types, which can sometimes become invasive cancer and are often removed during a colonoscopy using a polypectomy. Benign growths that can form in the colon and rectum, associated with FAP. Over time, these polyps can become invasive colon cancer. Small, benign growths that form on the lining of the colon, which can sometimes develop into cancer. Colon cancer often forms in polyps, making them an important focus in the prevention and early detection of colon cancer.

nodes.label: Papillary Thyroid Cancer
nodes.description: The most common type of thyroid cancer, with the classic type being the most common subtype. Other subtypes, such as follicular variant, tall-cell/columnar cell, hobnail, and diffuse sclerosing, may grow and spread more quickly. A type of thyroid cancer that can be treated with RAI therapy if the cancer takes up iodine. It can also be metastatic and may require other treatments like targeted therapy or monitoring if the cancer doesn't take up iodine or if the tumors are growing slowly.

nodes.label: Prostate cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer that develops when cells in the prostate gland grow out of control. It can develop slowly and stay within the prostate, or spread to other areas of the body.

nodes.label: AML cells
nodes.description: Abnormal white blood cells present in the blood or bone marrow of individuals with acute myeloid leukemia (AML). These cells can disappear in remission, and their genetic changes can determine the type of treatment given. Cells affected by acute myeloid leukemia (AML), which can have changes in genes and chromosomes, including deletions, insertions, inversions, amplifications, translocations, and point mutations.

nodes.label: Supplements
nodes.description: Non-prescription products containing vitamins, minerals, or other substances intended to supplement the diet, often in the form of pills, capsules, or liquids. They can interfere with cancer tests or treatment and should be disclosed to care teams to avoid potential interactions and ensure safe and effective treatment. Supplements may include nutritional or herbal preparations taken to improve health, potentially causing changes in PSA level and requiring the care team to be informed if taken.

nodes.label: Cancer Care Plan
nodes.description: A document outlining the treatment plan for cervical cancer, involving a team of experts including a gynecologic oncologist, a medical oncologist, and a radiation oncologist. Other healthcare providers such as nurses, social workers, and primary care physicians can also be part of the team.

nodes.label: Colorectal Cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer that affects the colon or rectum, increasingly diagnosed in young adults for unknown reasons. A type of cancer that affects the colon or rectum. It is being diagnosed more often in young adults for unknown reasons. A type of cancer that can increase the risk of developing pancreatic cancer. Experts have identified several risk factors for the disease, including close blood relatives with pancreatic, breast, ovarian, or colorectal cancers or melanoma. A type of cancer that can be associated with germline mutations in genes such as MSH2, MSH6, MLH1, and PMS2. A type of cancer that can be associated with inherited mutations in genes like MSH2, MSH6, MLH1, and PMS2. A term used to describe cancers that form in either the colon or rectum, although their treatment is different. A type of cancer that can be screened for, often recommended by a primary care doctor based on patient characteristics.

nodes.label: High-Risk Skin Cancer
nodes.description: A category of skin cancer with an increased risk of local recurrence compared to low-risk skin cancer. It may also have an increased risk of metastasis (spread).

nodes.label: Stoma
nodes.description: An opening created on the surface of the abdomen during a colostomy, through which stool exits the body. An opening created on the surface of the abdomen during a colostomy procedure, through which stool exits the body and enters a bag attached to the skin. A small opening created in the abdominal wall through which urine exits the body in urinary diversion procedures, such as ileal conduit and continent urinary diversion. A small hole created in the abdominal wall during an ileal conduit procedure. One end of the ileal conduit tube is attached to this hole, allowing urine to exit the body. A surgical opening created in the abdomen for the drainage of urine. It can be made in the belly button to make it less noticeable. A small bandage can cover the stoma, and a catheter must be inserted through the valve into the pouch several times a day to drain the urine. An opening created on the surface of the abdomen during a colostomy, through which stool exits the body. Stool goes into a bag attached to the skin.

nodes.label: Anal Canal Cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer affecting the anal canal, with stages I – III. It is treated with chemoradiation, which involves both chemotherapy and radiation therapy during the same time period. Not explicitly mentioned in the text, but inferred as a related type of cancer that is also treated with chemoradiation, like perianal cancer. A type of cancer that is mentioned in the text. Chemoradiation treatment for perianal cancer is the same as for anal canal cancer. A type of anal cancer that is monitored alongside perianal cancer during surveillance.

nodes.label: Human papillomavirus (HPV)
nodes.description: Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a group of viruses that infect the cells on the surface of the skin or on the moist surfaces or inner linings of some organs and body cavities. It is a main cause of squamous cell carcinomas of the throat, particularly cancers of the tonsils and base of the tongue. HPV type 16 is responsible for 9 out of 10 throat cancers. A group of viruses that can cause infections, some of which are associated with an increased risk of throat cancer. A common sexually transmitted infection that is the most frequent cause of cervical cancer. It can lead to long-term infection and subsequent cervical cancer. Human papillomavirus (HPV) is an extremely common sexually transmitted infection (STI) that is the most common cause of cervical cancer. It is a viral infection with more than 100 types (strains), some of which are more likely to lead to cancer than others. Most sexually active people have or had HPV at one point, but most are unaware of their infection. In most people, the immune system gets rid of HPV from the body, but in others, the virus causes long-term cell changes that develop into cancer. The progression to cancer often occurs decades after the initial infection. HPV can also cause abnormal skin growths, called warts, to form on the anus, genitals, or other areas of the body. There are vaccines available that protect against 9 different strains of HPV, including the highest-risk strains, and they work best in younger people (ideally under age 13) because they are less likely to have been exposed to HPV. However, the vaccine does not treat existing HPV infections or HPV-related cancer. Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a sexually transmitted virus that is the most strongly linked risk factor for anal cancer. It is extremely common, affecting almost everyone who has ever been sexually active, and most people are unaware that they are infected. In most people, the immune system clears HPV from the body, but in some cases, it can cause long-term cell changes that develop into cancer. HPV is also associated with other cancers, including cervical, head and neck, penile, vaginal, and vulvar cancers. Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a virus that affects almost everyone who has been sexually active, causing abnormal tissue growth (for example, warts) and other changes to cells. It is almost always the cause of anal cancer. Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a common viral infection that affects almost everyone who has been sexually active. It can cause abnormal tissue growth, such as warts, and other cellular changes. HPV is also the almost always the cause of anal cancer.

nodes.label: MRI scan
nodes.description: A medical imaging technique that uses radio waves and powerful magnets to take pictures of the inside of the body without using x-rays. Contrast might be used in this procedure. A type of scan often combined with a PET scan (PET/MRI) to determine where the cancer cells are located. A medical imaging technique used to provide a highly accurate picture of the cancer in conjunction with an ultrasound image. The MRI scan of the prostate can be combined with the ultrasound image to guide the needle into the prostate during the biopsy procedure.

nodes.label: TNM Staging
nodes.description: A staging system used for squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the mouth, including the mucosa of the lip, to classify tumors based on their size, depth of invasion, and involvement of nearby structures.

nodes.label: Basal Cell Skin Cancer
nodes.description: A type of skin cancer that is the most common form, with about 3 million cases diagnosed annually in the United States. It is treatable and curable, especially if caught early, as it rarely spreads. It typically develops in sun-exposed areas like the face, head, neck, arms, legs, and trunk, but can occur anywhere on the body. It is also known as basal cell carcinoma (BCC). A type of skin cancer that can happen to anyone, but is most common in people with lighter skin, lighter hair, or lighter eyes. It can appear as flat, pale or yellow areas, red patches, small, pink or red, shiny bumps, or open sores that don't heal and might bleed or go away and come back in lighter skin. In darker skin, it can appear as a brown or glossy black bump with a rolled border, which can be mistaken for a normal mole. A type of skin cancer that is highly treatable and curable. It can return to the original area or metastasize to lymph nodes or distant parts of the body. Treatment options include surgery, radiation therapy, and systemic therapy. Early detection and treatment are key. A type of skin cancer that requires testing for diagnosis. The diagnosis involves medical and family history, physical and skin exams, biopsy, and possibly imaging studies. The treatment plan depends on the diagnosis results.

nodes.label: Mohs Surgery
nodes.description: A type of surgery that allows the surgeon to know right away whether all cancer was removed. It involves cutting out the tumor along with a small margin of normal skin. This procedure can be done in a medical office or surgical suite and should be done by a dermatologic surgeon who has special training and experience in this procedure. Most patients remain awake during the procedure. A type of surgery that combines PDEMA with Mohs surgery, allowing for complete testing of the edges of any removed tissue while removing the cancer while sparing as much normal tissue as possible. It should be performed by surgeons who have special training and experience in this procedure. A surgical procedure for treating CSCC, where thin samples of tissue are examined under a microscope to see if there are cancer cells at the margin. A surgical technique used for the treatment of high-risk or very high-risk CSCC, preferred for very high-risk cases, involving the removal of cancerous tissue layer by layer while examining each layer for cancer cells. A surgical procedure mentioned as an alternative to PDEMA for removing cancer. If not possible, a discussion with different cancer doctors is recommended to consider next treatment options. A type of surgery used to treat cancer, specifically mentioned as a possible first treatment option if testing after surgery finds cancer in the margin. A recommended type of surgery for local, high-risk or very high-risk Squamous Cell Skin Cancer, involving the layer-by-layer removal of the tumor with microscopic examination of each layer to ensure complete removal.

nodes.label: Mediastinal gray zone lymphoma (MGZL)
nodes.description: A type of lymphoma with overlapping features of primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma (PMBL) and Hodgkin lymphoma (HL). It is characterized by large cells that can vary in size and may look similar to Reed-Sternberg cells. A type of gray zone lymphoma that is different from primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma (PMBL) and is characterized by the presence of a large mediastinal mass. It is more commonly seen in individuals assigned male at birth between 20 to 40 years of age. Mediastinal lymphomas are growths found behind the breastbone (sternum) in the part of the chest that separates the lungs and holds the heart.

nodes.label: Nicotine
nodes.description: A chemical found in tobacco that causes addiction and makes it challenging for smokers and vapers to quit. It is also associated with an increased risk of developing certain types of cancer. A chemical found in tobacco that causes the desire to continue smoking and vaping. It is the substance responsible for the addictive nature of tobacco products. A chemical found in tobacco that is responsible for the addictive nature of smoking. It is mentioned as the substance in tobacco that makes people want to keep smoking.

nodes.label: Medical history
