nodes.description: A record of a patient's past medical conditions and treatments, used to inform care decisions. The review of a patient's past and current health by the care team during a consult meeting. A medical history is a review of a patient's past and current health, as well as the health history of their close blood relatives, that is conducted by the care team during a consult meeting. It is an important part of the patient assessment process. A record of a person's health and illnesses, used by healthcare providers to make informed decisions about treatment and care; sometimes referred to as a health history. A patient's medical history is collected by healthcare providers to inform their care team about their overall health and guide the best treatment for their cancer. A record of all health issues and treatments a patient has had in their life. It includes a list of illnesses, injuries, and when they occurred, as well as a list of medications, both prescription and over-the-counter, herbs, and supplements the patient takes. A medical history is a record of all health issues and treatments a person has had in their life. It is important to bring a list of old and new medicines, OTC medicines, herbals, or supplements to share with the medical team. A medical history helps determine the best treatment for a patient.

nodes.label: Cervical dysplasia
nodes.description: A condition characterized by areas of abnormal, microscopic cells on the surface of the cervix. It is a precursor to cervical cancer and may be referred to as cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN). If left untreated, cervical dysplasia may become cervical cancer. Cervical dysplasia, also known as cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN), refers to areas of abnormal cells on the lining of the cervix. It can progress to cervical cancer if left untreated, and is graded based on the depth of the abnormal cells on the lining of the cervix, with possible grades of 1, 2, or 3. CIN 1 corresponds to a low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL), while CIN 2 and 3 correspond to high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL), with HSIL being considered a pre-cancer. Areas of abnormal, microscopic cells on the surface of the cervix, also known as cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN). It is an early stage of cervical cancer.

nodes.label: Drug Interaction
nodes.description: A potential adverse effect where certain herbal supplements or medicines can affect the ability of a drug to do its job, potentially impacting the effectiveness of chemotherapy.

nodes.label: Gastrointestinal (GI) tract
nodes.description: A complex system of organs responsible for the digestion and absorption of nutrients from food. The GI tract includes the stomach, small bowel, and large bowel (rectum and colon). Imaging tests, such as endoscopy or colonoscopy, can be used to examine the organs within the GI tract.

nodes.label: PARP inhibitors
nodes.description: PARP inhibitors are a class of drugs used for maintenance therapy after initial treatment of ovarian cancer. They include Olaparib (Lynparza), Niraparib (Zejula), and Rucaparib (Rubraca). Common side effects are similar to chemotherapy and can include fatigue, nausea, vomiting, and low blood cell counts. Rare but serious side effects include myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML). A class of inhibitors that target the PARP protein, which repairs cancer cells and allows them to survive. Blocking PARP can cause cancer cells to die. Olaparib (Lynparza) and talazoparib (Talzenna) are examples. Individuals must have the BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation and their breast cancer must be HER2- for PARP inhibitors to be considered. PARP inhibitors are a class of cancer treatments that require the presence of the BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation and that the breast cancer is HER2-negative to be considered. They are used to treat certain types of breast cancer.

nodes.label: Chemoradiation
nodes.description: A type of cancer treatment that combines chemotherapy and radiation therapy, typically used concurrently to treat locally advanced cervical cancer, anal canal cancer, and perianal cancer. It may include brachytherapy and is often followed by a recommended follow-up physical exam with digital rectal examination (DRE) and anoscopy 8 to 12 weeks after completion. Cisplatin is typically given on a 7-day cycle for 5 to 6 weeks as part of this treatment.

nodes.label: Hodgkin lymphoma
nodes.description: A type of cancer that usually starts in lymph nodes in the upper body and is highly curable. It is diagnosed more commonly in people aged 15 to 30 or after age 50, and is characterized by the uncontrolled growth of white blood cells called lymphocytes. A type of cancer that usually starts in lymph nodes in the upper body, is highly curable, and affects most people between the ages of 15 to 30 or after age 45. It is characterized by abnormally large lymphocytes called Reed-Sternberg cells. A type of cancer that affects the lymphatic system, specifically the lymph nodes. The diagnosis and treatment of Hodgkin lymphoma are discussed in detail in the text, including the use of biopsy and lab testing, health history and physical exam, blood tests, imaging tests, heart and lung tests, and other testing and care. A cancer that can result from Richter transformation in individuals with CLL. It is described as a rare condition leading to a more aggressive cancer. A type of lymphoma that is not mentioned in detail in the text but is contrasted with Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL). It is a cancer of lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell that helps fight and prevent infection. Lymphocytes are found in blood and lymph tissue, and every organ in the body. Lymph tissue includes lymph vessels and lymph nodes. Lymphocytes normally grow in response to infection or inflammation. When they grow on their own without proper regulation, they can develop into lymphoma.

nodes.label: NCCN Guidelines for Patients
nodes.description: Guidelines for understanding cancer care, specifically designed for patients, which include sections on asking questions to help patients get more information on all aspects of their care. Plainly explained cancer care recommendations developed by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network® (NCCN) for people with cancer and caregivers. These guidelines are based on the NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology (NCCN Guidelines®) for various types of Hodgkin Lymphoma and are frequently updated. They are supported by funding from the NCCN Foundation® and corporate supporters like Pfizer Inc. The NCCN independently adapts, updates, and hosts the NCCN Guidelines for Patients, and corporate supporters do not participate in their development or content creation.

nodes.label: Lungs
nodes.description: A pair of organs located in the chest, responsible for moving important gases in and out of the blood. They have sections called lobes, with the left lung having 2 lobes and the right lung having 3 lobes. They are protected by a thin layer of tissue called the pleural membrane. A pair of organs that move important gases in and out of the blood. Lung cancer starts in the cells that line the lungs. A pair of organs that move important gases in and out of the blood, located in the chest cavity. The main organs of the respiratory system, responsible for delivering oxygen to the blood and removing carbon dioxide from the blood. The transfer of these gases is called respiration. A common site for breast cancer metastasis. It is one of the most common locations where breast cancer spreads after the primary tumor. A pair of organs located in the chest, responsible for respiration and gas exchange. Colon cancer can also spread to the lungs, which is another common site for metastasis in stage 4 colon cancer. A less common site for metastasis of nasopharyngeal cancer cells from the primary tumor in the nasopharynx.

nodes.label: Daunorubicin
nodes.description: Daunorubicin is an anthracycline used in the treatment of certain medical conditions. It is an example of an anthracycline that can cause heart issues and has a limit to how much can be received in a lifetime. An anthracycline used in chemotherapy, potentially causing heart issues and having a limit to how much can be received in a lifetime. Daunorubicin is an anthracycline chemotherapy drug used in various treatment regimens. It can cause heart issues and there is a lifetime limit to its dosage. It is combined with cytarabine in the dual-drug liposome CPX-351 or Vyxeos.

nodes.label: Cervical cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer that affects the cervix, the lower part of the uterus that connects to the vagina. It can start as areas of abnormal, microscopic cells on the surface of the cervix, known as cervical dysplasia or cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN). The risk factor most strongly linked with cervical cancer is long-term infection with HPV, a common sexually transmitted infection. There are various types of cervical cancer, including squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, adenosquamous carcinoma, and neuroendocrine carcinoma of the cervix (NECC). Cervical cancer is a type of cancer caused by HPV, and is one of the related cancers associated with this virus. A type of cancer that affects the cervix, the lower part of the uterus. Screening for this cancer is recommended as part of overall health monitoring.

nodes.label: Advanced-stage prostate cancer
nodes.description: A severe form of prostate cancer that has spread to other areas of the pelvis (regional prostate cancer) or the body (metastatic prostate cancer), usually a life-long disease. Treatment can slow down its growth, reduce symptoms, and prolong life.

nodes.label: Family members or relatives
nodes.description: A group of individuals who are related by blood or marriage and may have or had prostate cancer, breast cancer, ovarian cancer, intestinal cancer, and certain other cancers.

nodes.label: Taxanes
nodes.description: A type of chemotherapy, with examples paclitaxel and docetaxel, often given with platinum-based chemotherapy for ovarian cancer. A class of chemotherapy drugs that include docetaxel, paclitaxel, and albumin-bound paclitaxel, and are known to reduce the cells that fight infection.

nodes.label: Cystoscopy
nodes.description: A medical procedure under anesthesia used to look for signs of cancer in the bladder, typically performed when there is a suspicion of cancer in the lower urinary tract. A medical procedure to examine the urethra and bladder for signs of cancer, involving the use of a cystoscope and, if necessary, the removal of tiny tissue samples for testing (biopsy). There are two types of cystoscopes: a flexible one for viewing and biopsy, and a rigid one that is more invasive but can also remove small tumors.

nodes.label: Large bowel
nodes.description: An organ within the gastrointestinal (GI) tract responsible for absorbing water and forming solid waste. The large bowel includes the rectum and colon and is examined using a colonoscopy, which involves inserting a scope into the anus and guiding it through the rectum and colon. The part of the digestive system that includes the colon and rectum, where stool is formed and held until it leaves the body through the anus. It is involved in the formation of colorectal cancer.

nodes.label: Skin Cancer (Melanoma)
nodes.description: A type of cancer that can be associated with germline mutations in genes such as BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, CHEK2, and others. A type of cancer that can be associated with inherited mutations in genes like BRCA1 and BRCA2.

nodes.label: Biomarker-Based Treatment
nodes.description: A type of treatment that considers the presence of specific biomarkers in the cancer. If the cancer has any of the biomarkers listed, targeted therapy or immunotherapy may be an option.

nodes.label: Transabdominal Resection
nodes.description: A surgical procedure recommended for tumors that have invaded the muscle layer of the rectal wall (T2 tumors), or smaller (T1) tumors, and some larger (T3) cancers that haven't spread to lymph nodes. It involves cutting into the abdomen to reach and remove the rectal tumor, some surrounding healthy tissue, and nearby lymph nodes. At least 12 lymph nodes should be removed during all types of transabdominal surgery. A pathologist examines the removed tissue and determines the cancer stage. The type of transabdominal surgery performed depends on the location of the tumor and the extent of the cancer.

nodes.label: Cancer Staging
nodes.description: A process used to reflect prognosis and guide treatment decisions, describing the size and location of the tumor and if cancer has spread to lymph nodes or other parts of the body. The process of determining the stage of breast cancer based on various factors, including tumor size, lymph node involvement, and organ involvement, to guide treatment decisions and reflect prognosis. The process of determining the stage of a cancer based on various factors, including the size and location of the tumor, the presence of cancer in lymph nodes, and the spread of cancer to distant sites, used to reflect prognosis and guide treatment decisions. A process used to determine the stage of perianal cancer, including the invasion of nearby lymph nodes and the grade of the cancer cells.

nodes.label: Surgical Menopause
nodes.description: A medical condition that can occur as a result of surgery, characterized by sudden and more severe symptoms such as hot flashes, sleeping problems, night sweats, weight gain, changes in mood, and vaginal atrophy. A menopause that occurs as a result of surgical procedures, specifically hysterectomy.

nodes.label: Anxiety and depression
nodes.description: Mental health conditions that are common in people with cancer, often requiring support from cancer navigators, social workers, and others, as well as various forms of help such as support groups, talk therapy, exercising, spending time with loved ones, or medication.

nodes.label: Prostate
nodes.description: The prostate is a gland located deep inside the pelvis, just below the bladder and in front of the rectum. It is an important part of the male reproductive system, involved in the production and distribution of seminal fluid. Prostate cancer can develop in the prostate and may spread to nearby areas such as lymph nodes. The prostate can be examined through a digital rectal exam, and its size and texture may be tested using imaging and diagnostic tests. A biopsy may be taken from the prostate to check for cancer, involving the removal of a sample of tissue through the perineum using a needle guided by an ultrasound probe inserted into the rectum. MRI scans can provide a detailed view of the cancer within the prostate and check for cancer spread to nearby lymph nodes or bones in the pelvis.

nodes.label: Stereotactic Biopsy
nodes.description: The standard method for diagnosing primary CNS lymphoma, involving a neurosurgeon removing only enough of the tumor to make a diagnosis with precision targeting and removal.

nodes.label: Hormone therapy
nodes.description: A treatment option for early-stage prostate cancer that involves using medications to block the effects of hormones on cancer cells, often used to slow down tumor growth. Hormone therapy is a treatment for advanced-stage prostate cancer that involves manipulating hormone levels to slow down the growth of cancer cells. Hormone therapy is a treatment for advanced-stage prostate cancer that involves manipulating hormone levels to slow down the growth of cancer cells. It is one of the many treatment options available for advanced-stage prostate cancer, along with chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, radiopharmaceuticals, surgery, and other therapies. Hormone therapy is a type of prostate cancer treatment that aims to reduce the production or block the effects of hormones, such as testosterone, which can stimulate cancer growth. It is used to manage advanced-stage prostate cancer and alleviate symptoms. A type of treatment for prostate cancer that involves depriving the cancer cells of their main fuel, androgens, by reducing testosterone levels. This can be achieved through medication or surgical removal of the testicles (orchiectomy). Hormone therapy can be combined with other therapies to increase their effectiveness. A treatment approach for prostate cancer, often involving medications like LHRH agonists and LHRH antagonists that block testosterone production by the testicles, or anti-androgens, corticosteroids, and androgen synthesis inhibitors taken orally. It has been the main treatment for advanced prostate cancer for several decades and includes medications such as leuprolide (Lupron), degarelix (Firmagon), relugolix (Orgovyx), bicalutamide, flutamide, nilutamide, and others.

nodes.label: FDG-PET/CT
nodes.description: A type of medical imaging test that combines positron emission tomography (PET) and computed tomography (CT) to create detailed images of the body, using a radiotracer called fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG), which is made of fluoride and a simple form of sugar called glucose. It is most helpful when other imaging results are unclear and can be done at the same time as a CT used for diagnosis. It can help find cancer in lymph nodes and distant sites and may indicate the need for a bone scan and sodium fluoride PET/CT if cancer in the bone is clearly shown.

nodes.label: Tumor Size
nodes.description: A factor considered in the AJCC staging system to determine the extent of cancer. The size of the tumor is measured and used to assign a stage to the cancer. A factor used in cancer staging, defined by the size of the tumor and considered in the anatomic TNM staging system. A factor considered in the staging of breast cancer, indicating the extent to which the cancer has grown.

nodes.label: Ovarian cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer that affects the ovaries, a pair of female reproductive organs. It can originate in the surface layer of tissue surrounding the ovaries, called the epithelium, or in the fallopian tube. There are more than 5 types of epithelial ovarian cancer, including high-grade serous carcinoma, high-grade endometrioid carcinoma, low-grade serous carcinoma, low-grade endometrioid carcinoma, carcinosarcoma, clear cell carcinoma, mucinous carcinoma, borderline epithelial tumor, and less common ovarian histologies. Ovarian cancer can also start in tissues that support the ovaries or in the reproductive (egg) cells of the ovary. Less common ovarian cancers are called less common ovarian cancers (LCOCs) or less common ovarian histologies (LCOHs). Primary peritoneal cancer and fallopian tube cancer are also related to ovarian cancer and are treated similarly. Ovarian cancer can cause changes in the body that may not be noticeable until the tumor has grown large or the cancer has spread, with symptoms including bloating, heartburn and indigestion, pelvic or belly pain, difficulty eating, feeling full quickly, frequent or urgent urination, and pain during sex. Treatment for ovarian cancer involves a team of experts, often including gynecologic oncologists and medical oncologists, and may require surgery, chemotherapy, or radiation therapy, depending on the stage and type of cancer. Ovarian cancer can be diagnosed using tumor markers such as CA-125, but a CA-125 test alone cannot diagnose the cancer. Some ovarian cancers may not cause CA-125 to rise, and health problems like endometriosis and diverticulitis can also raise CA-125 levels. Ovarian cancer is a significant health concern for women, and genetic testing is recommended for everyone diagnosed with the disease to determine if they have a mutation in the BRCA genes or other genes that play a role in hereditary cancer. Ovarian cancer is often associated with Lynch syndrome, a genetic disorder caused by inherited mutations in the mismatch repair (MMR) genes. Individuals with Lynch syndrome are at high risk of developing this type of cancer.

nodes.label: Throat cancer
nodes.description: Throat cancer is a type of cancer that starts in the oropharynx, with squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) being the most common type. It is the focus of this book. A form of cancer that affects the oropharynx, including the back of the roof of the mouth (soft palate), the tonsils, the side and back walls of the throat, and the base of the tongue. It is the focus of this book. Throat cancer, also known as oropharyngeal cancer, is a type of cancer that affects the throat area, including the tonsils and base of the tongue. It can be linked to HPV infection, and certain types, such as HPV16, are responsible for a high percentage of cases. Throat cancer is a type of cancer that can be caused by HPV, specifically HPV types 16, 18, 33, and positive strains. It can be targeted during treatment and is associated with the overexpression of p16. Throat cancer is a specific type of cancer that is staged using a system created by the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC). This system helps to determine the extent of the cancer at the time of diagnosis, including the size of the tumor, the spread to nearby lymph nodes, and the presence of metastasis to distant sites. A type of cancer affecting the throat, often related to human papillomavirus (HPV). A type of head and neck cancer most often related to HPV, as stated in the text.

nodes.label: Germline Testing
nodes.description: A type of genetic testing done to look for inherited mutations that occur in every cell in the body, typically using a sample of blood, urine, or saliva. The goal is to identify characteristic changes in genes like BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, CHEK2, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PALB2, PMS2, and others, which can increase the risk of developing certain cancers.

nodes.label: Kidney cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer that affects the kidneys, discussed in the text with information about its symptoms, subtypes, and spread. A type of cancer that originates in the kidneys, characterized by the removal of extra water and waste from the body by filtering blood through the renal artery and vein, and the formation of tumors that can spread to other parts of the body through metastasis.

nodes.label: Risk Factors
nodes.description: Conditions or habits that increase the likelihood of developing lung cancer. They include smoking tobacco, exposure to second-hand smoke, radon, asbestos, arsenic, beryllium, cadmium, chromium, nickel, coal smoke, soot, silica, diesel fumes, and air pollution from fine particulates, ozone, nitrogen oxides, and sulfur dioxide.

nodes.label: Smoking
nodes.description: A harmful behavior involving the inhalation and exhalation of tobacco smoke, which increases the risk of developing various types of cancer, including lung, bladder, and anal cancer, as well as other health issues. It can limit the effectiveness of cancer treatment, increase the risk of surgery side effects, and cause nicotine withdrawal. Quitting smoking is strongly recommended for improved health and reduced cancer risk, especially with the help of healthcare professionals.

nodes.label: Metastatic Cervical Cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer that has spread from the cervix to other parts of the body, typically treated with platinum-based chemotherapy. A severe form of cervical cancer that has spread to other parts of the body. It is characterized by the presence of metastases and requires specialized treatment approaches. Supportive care is a key component of management, focusing on comfort, symptom control, and quality of life improvement.

nodes.label: Radiation Oncologist
nodes.description: A medical professional who specializes in the use of radiation therapy to treat cancer, including discussing possible side effects of whole-brain radiation therapy (WBRT) with patients, and can help determine whether this treatment is appropriate for a patient. They are often involved in the multidisciplinary care team for primary CNS lymphoma and are board-certified experts in the use of radiation to treat cancer.

nodes.label: Lumbar puncture
nodes.description: A type of medical test involving the insertion of a needle into the lumbar region of the spine to withdraw cerebrospinal fluid for examination, used to detect abnormalities or diseases, including AML. A medical procedure in which a needle is inserted into the lower part of the spine to withdraw cerebrospinal fluid for testing. Lumbar punctures are used to diagnose ALL by checking for the presence of cancer cells in the cerebrospinal fluid surrounding the CNS. This test is often performed in conjunction with blood and bone marrow tests. A lumbar puncture, also known as a spinal tap, is a procedure used to examine the cerebrospinal fluid for the presence of leukemia cells. It is one of the possible tests and procedures used to diagnose and treat AML. A medical procedure used to diagnose ALL by examining the cerebrospinal fluid for the presence of lymphoblasts, which can indicate the spread of the disease to the central nervous system (CNS).

nodes.label: Paclitaxel
nodes.description: A chemotherapy drug used in the treatment of ovarian cancer, often in combination with other drugs like carboplatin and bevacizumab. A taxane, a type of chemotherapy, often given with platinum-based chemotherapy for ovarian cancer. A chemotherapy drug used in the preferred regimen for stage 1, 2, 3, and 4 ovarian cancers, often given with carboplatin every 3 weeks. A chemotherapy drug that is a taxane and is known to reduce the cells that fight infection. A chemotherapy medicine used in combination with other medicines, such as cisplatin, carboplatin, or bevacizumab, in the treatment of metastatic cervical cancer. A chemotherapy drug used in the treatment of metastatic cervical cancer, often in combination with other drugs such as cisplatin or bevacizumab. A chemotherapy drug component of a recommended regimen for treating cancer that returns to lymph nodes, often preferred over 5-FU and cisplatin.

nodes.label: Patients
nodes.description: Individuals affected by cancer who may benefit from the clear explanations of current care recommendations provided by the NCCN Guidelines for Patients. Patients are individuals receiving medical treatment for cancer and are encouraged to follow expert recommendations for their care to improve outcomes. NCCN Guidelines for Patients are designed to be trusted by patients and providers alike. Individuals diagnosed with cancer who are seeking treatment and care. Patients can benefit from following expert recommendations for their situation to improve their care and outcomes. Patients are individuals who have been diagnosed with prostate cancer, either in its early or advanced stages, and are receiving treatment for the disease.

nodes.label: Condoms
nodes.description: A type of barrier method used for contraception, particularly recommended during and immediately after cancer treatment to prevent pregnancy. Condoms provide a physical barrier between the penis and vagina or anus, and are often used in conjunction with other forms of birth control like IUDs. They are also effective in preventing sexually transmitted infections.

nodes.label: Systemic Therapy
nodes.description: A type of cancer treatment that affects the entire body, often used in conjunction with surgery or radiation therapy to target cancer cells that may have spread beyond the original tumor site. It includes chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy, and can have side effects. It is given intravenously or taken by mouth as a pill, and may be used for metastatic cancer, cervical cancer, or cancer recurrence. It can also be used after surgery to manage remaining cancer cells.

nodes.label: HER2-targeted therapy
nodes.description: HER2-targeted therapy is a type of cancer treatment that targets the human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) protein. Examples include pertuzumab (Perjeta), trastuzumab (Herceptin), and its substitutes, such as Kanjinti, Ogivri, Herzuma, Ontruzant, and Trazimera. Other HER2-targeted therapies include ado-trastuzumab emtansine (T-DM1) and fam-trastuzumab deruxtecan-nxki (Enhertu). These treatments are used to manage HER2-positive breast cancer. HER2-targeted therapy is a type of drug therapy that treats HER2 breast cancer, often used in combination with chemotherapy or endocrine therapy.

nodes.label: Biomarker
nodes.description: A biological marker used to diagnose and treat CML, identified through testing. A molecular characteristic, such as a genetic mutation, used to identify specific types of gliomas. Each type of glioma has its own biomarker or set of biomarkers. Biomarker is a concept referring to something found in the body that is a sign of a condition, disease, or abnormality. In cancer care, biomarker testing looks for changes in genes, proteins, and other markers, many of which are mutations. A biological marker that can indicate the presence or severity of a disease. Some people with CLL have certain biomarkers that can be targets for chemoimmunotherapy, indicating a more aggressive form of the disease. A biological marker used to predict the results of targeted therapy in CLL, with a specific mention of Beta-2 microglobulin as an example.

nodes.label: Rochoscopy
nodes.description: A medical procedure that allows a doctor to thoroughly examine the mouth, oropharynx, larynx, esophagus, and trachea and bronchi. It is performed under anesthesia for comfort and might be used to look for other tumors or abnormal lymph nodes in the neck. Biopsies can be done with special tools through the scopes.

nodes.label: Blood
nodes.description: A bodily fluid mentioned in the text without further details. A sample type used for genetic germline testing to look for inherited mutations that occur in every cell in the body. A biological sample used for genetic testing, specifically mentioned as a sample type for genetic risk testing of breast cancer. A fluid that enters the liver from the hepatic artery and portal vein and leaves the liver through the hepatic veins before entering the inferior vena cava and returning to the heart. It is a component of the circulatory system. A bodily fluid containing proteins and other substances. The presence or absence of certain substances in the blood can indicate health problems in organs like the kidneys or liver.

nodes.label: Anthracyclines
nodes.description: Anthracyclines are a class of drugs that damage and disrupt the making of DNA, causing cell death of both cancerous and non-cancerous cells. Some anthracyclines can cause heart issues and there is a limit to how much can be received in a lifetime. Anthracycline examples include daunorubicin, idarubicin (Idamycin PFS), and mitoxantrone (Novantrone). Dual-drug liposome of cytarabine and daunorubicin (CPX-351 or Vyxeos) includes an antimetabolite and an anthracycline. Cytarabine is an anthracycline. A type of chemotherapy that damages and disrupts the making of DNA, causing cell death of both cancerous and non-cancerous cells, with some anthracyclines, such as daunorubicin, idarubicin (Idamycin PFS), and mitoxantrone (Novantrone), potentially causing heart issues and having a limit to how much can be received in a lifetime. Anthracyclines are a class of chemotherapy drugs that damage and disrupt the production of DNA, leading to cell death in both cancerous and non-cancerous cells. Some anthracyclines can cause heart issues and there is a lifetime limit to their dosage. Examples include daunorubicin, idarubicin, and mitoxantrone. They are used in various treatment regimens and may be combined with other drugs like cytarabine. A class of chemotherapy drugs that include doxorubicin, doxorubicin liposomal injection, and epirubicin, and are known to reduce the cells that fight infection.

nodes.label: Cutaneous B-Cell Lymphoma (CBCL)
nodes.description: A type of primary cutaneous lymphoma that starts in B cells, a type of white blood cell called a lymphocyte. It appears as a nodule under the skin that might look like small pimples called papules. A type of lymphoma affecting the skin, for which accurate testing is essential for diagnosis and treatment planning. It involves blood and tissue tests, imaging studies, and biopsy to determine treatment.

nodes.label: Imaging Tests
nodes.description: Diagnostic procedures that take pictures of the inside of the body to visualize internal structures and detect abnormalities, used in the context of cancer diagnosis and monitoring. These tests can identify the primary tumor, where cancer started, and check for cancer in other parts of the body. They are performed by a radiologist and the results are interpreted and discussed with the patient by the doctor. Imaging tests may use either the standard 2-dimensional (2D) digital mammogram or 3-dimensional (3D) mammogram known as tomosynthesis. They can also be used to look for leukemia spreading to the lining of the brain and spinal cord, or to check for cancer growth using MRI scans and CT scans. Preparation instructions and sedatives may be provided for patient comfort.

nodes.label: Basal cell skin cancer
nodes.description: A type of skin cancer that is caused by exposure to UV radiation from the sun or other sources like tanning beds, and can be diagnosed by testing methods described in Chapter 2 of a related document. It is more common in people with fair skin, red or blond hair, light eye color, and increases with age. Risk factors also include a history of skin cancer, radiation therapy, and immune suppression. A type of skin cancer, characterized by the growth of abnormal cells in the basal cell layer of the skin. Accurate testing is needed to diagnose and then treat this condition, which involves various tests such as medical and family history review, physical and skin exams, biopsy, and imaging studies.

nodes.label: Liver disease
nodes.description: Liver disease is a broad term referring to various conditions affecting the liver, including cirrhosis, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C. Chronic hepatitis B and hepatitis C can cause scarring of the liver (cirrhosis), liver failure, and liver cancer. Liver disease is a broad category of conditions affecting the liver, including chronic hepatitis, scarring of the liver (cirrhosis), liver failure, and liver cancer. Liver disease is a broad term referring to various conditions that affect the liver, including liver cancer. It can cause physical and emotional challenges for individuals, but with proper management, they can maintain a normal life, engaging in activities such as traveling and having children.

nodes.label: Side effects
nodes.description: Adverse reactions that may occur as a result of treatment, particularly chemotherapy, which can affect various body systems including the bowel, mouth, and blood. They may be managed through communication with the care team and may include common symptoms like nausea, vomiting, and fatigue, as well as more serious but rare conditions such as myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Side effects are managed as a shared effort between the patient and their care team. Adverse reactions that may occur as a result of chemotherapy or radiation therapy, including feeling very tired or weak (fatigue), nausea, and vomiting. These side effects can be managed with medications and other interventions.

nodes.label: Medical oncologist
nodes.description: A board-certified medical expert who specializes in the diagnosis, treatment, and management of cancer using medications, often in collaboration with other specialists. A medical oncologist treats cancer using systemic (drug) therapy, which is one of the types of treatment for AML. They are part of the multidisciplinary team involved in the treatment of AML. A medical professional who treats cancer using systemic (drug) therapy. A medical oncologist is a member of the care team for AML patients. A health care provider specializing in the medical treatment of cancer, often part of a multidisciplinary care team for pancreatic cancer. A health care professional who treats cancer in adults using systemic therapy. They are a member of the multidisciplinary team (MDT) involved in the planning and implementing of treatment for breast cancer. A medical specialist in medical oncology, which involves the use of medications to treat cancer, and is part of the treatment team for thyroid cancer patients. A medical doctor who specializes in the diagnosis and treatment of cancer using medications, often part of the treatment team for thyroid cancer.

nodes.label: Medical History
nodes.description: A record detailing all health issues and treatments experienced throughout an individual's life, used to inform treatment decisions and provide context for medical care. A record of all health issues and treatments a person has had in their life, which includes listing any illness or injury and when it happened, as well as bringing a list of old and new medicines and any over-the-counter (OTC) medicines, herbals, or supplements they take. A record of all health issues and treatments a person has had in their life. This information is used by healthcare providers to understand a patient's medical background and identify potential risk factors for certain conditions, including cancer.

nodes.label: ALL
nodes.description: A type of blood cancer that affects the lymphoid progenitor cells, causing an increased production of lymphoblasts, which mature into lymphocytes. It is the most common diagnosed cancer in children and can start in T-cell or B-cell lymphocytes. Accurate testing is essential for diagnosis, and treatment plans are determined based on test results from blood and bone marrow, and imaging studies. The presence of at least 20 percent lymphoblasts in the bone marrow is required for a diagnosis of ALL, but in some cases, a diagnosis can be made with less. Treatment should be provided at experienced cancer centers.

nodes.label: Lymph nodes
nodes.description: Small, bean-shaped structures that are part of the lymphatic system, responsible for filtering and removing waste from the body. They can be affected by various types of cancer, such as esophageal, pancreatic, colon, anal, and nasopharynx cancer, and can be removed during surgery if they appear abnormal or are larger than normal. Lymph nodes are involved in the body's immune response and can be grouped into categories based on the stage of the tumor.

nodes.label: Health care provider
nodes.description: A medical professional who conducts a physical exam and assesses a patient's health. During a physical exam, a healthcare provider checks various vital signs, examines different parts of the body, and asks the patient about any pain experienced or enlarged lymph nodes. A person mentioned as someone to discuss test results with, along with choosing a friend, family member, or peer for support during diagnosis and treatment. A medical professional involved in the diagnosis, treatment, and care of patients with throat cancer, often consulted to discuss test results and treatment plans. A medical professional responsible for discussing test results and guiding patient care. A medical professional who provides healthcare services, including prevention and treatment. The text lists several types of healthcare providers who may be involved in breast health and cancer screening, such as breast specialists, diagnostic radiologists, gynecologists, lactation consultants, mammogram and imaging technologists, advanced practice providers, obstetricians, pathologists, and primary care providers. A medical professional who provides healthcare services and advice to patients. Users may be referred for genetic testing by their healthcare provider to learn more about their cancer. Users should ask their healthcare provider questions about their cancer diagnosis, treatment options, and next steps.

nodes.label: NCCN Guidelines for Patients
nodes.description: Guidelines for cancer care recommendations made by respected experts in the field. They are based on the latest research and practices at leading cancer centers and are trusted by patients and providers. The guidelines aim to help patients and providers make informed decisions about cancer care. Guidelines developed by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) for patients, which provide information on cancer staging and treatment. NCCN Guidelines for Patients is a resource providing information and treatment options for preserving fertility, and is the subject of an online survey available at NCCN.org/patients/response. NCCN Guidelines for Patients is a resource containing information on fertility and family planning, specifically for adolescent and young adult cancer patients. It is available on the NCCN.org/patientguidelines website. Guidelines designed to help patients understand cancer care. They provide information to improve patients’ understanding, enabling them to discuss their care with their team and share their concerns more effectively. The guidelines include a section called 'Questions to ask' that offers suggested questions for patients to ask their care team. A series of patient guidelines provided by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN), including the guide on immunotherapy side effects for immune checkpoint inhibitors. NCCN Guidelines for Patients are patient education resources developed by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN), providing information on various types of cancer and their treatments.

nodes.label: HPV
nodes.description: Human papillomavirus, a type of virus associated with throat (oropharyngeal) cancer, used in the context of tumor p16 (HPV) testing. Human papillomavirus, a type of virus that can cause infection, abnormal tissue growth (warts), and sometimes cancer; specifically, cancers of the head and neck, including throat cancer, are most often related to HPV, while HPV testing might be done in some cases for nasopharyngeal cancer. Human papillomavirus (HPV) is an extremely common sexually transmitted infection (STI) that is almost always responsible for cervical cancers. It causes long-term cell changes in the body that can develop into cancer, but most people's immune systems clear the virus from the body. Human papillomavirus, a group of viruses that can cause cervical cancer and other health problems. The vaccine is effective in preventing new HPV infections but not in treating existing infections or HPV-related cancer. Human papillomavirus, a common sexually transmitted infection strongly linked with cervical cancer. There is a vaccine available in the United States that protects against 9 different strains of HPV, including the highest-risk strains. A virus that can cause long-term cell changes leading to cancer in some people, with more than 100 types (called strains) that can infect humans. Some strains are more likely to lead to anal cancer and other related cancers, while high-risk forms include HPV16. HPV infection can also cause abnormal skin growths, called warts, to form on the anus or genitals. It can weaken the immune system, making it harder for the body to clear the infection. Certain risk factors, such as a history of cervical, vulvar, or vaginal cancer, a history of anal precancer, a history of blood cancer, autoimmune disorders, smoking, a history of anal sex, or a history of sexually transmitted infection, can increase the risk of anal cancer. A virus that is the cause of almost all cervical cancers and is also the cause of almost all anal cancers.

nodes.label: Epidermis
nodes.description: The top layer of skin mentioned in the text, which provides a waterproof barrier and creates skin color (melanin). It contains three main types of cells: squamous cells, basal cells, and melanocytes. The outermost layer of the skin, providing a waterproof barrier and producing melanin, which gives skin its color. It contains squamous cells, which are thin, flat cells that form the surface of the skin. The top layer of skin, which is removed during a superficial skin shave biopsy along with part of the dermis.

nodes.label: Bone
nodes.description: A common site for breast cancer metastasis, including the spine. It is one of the most common locations where breast cancer spreads after the primary tumor.  A body part, specifically referring to the most common site for metastasis in breast cancer, along with lung. A part of the human body that forms the skeleton and provides support and protection for organs and tissues. Bone cancer is a type of cancer that affects this part of the body. A living tissue made of cells (osteocytes, osteoblasts, and osteoclasts), calcium, phosphate, hydroxyapatite (a bone mineral), and collagen. New bone formation, known as ossification, starts in the womb and ends during adolescence, between 10 and 19 years of age. Once ossification is complete, bone is continuously being replaced by a process called remodeling.

nodes.label: Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL)
nodes.description: A type of fast-growing cancer that NLPHL can transform into over time. A more aggressive type of lymphoma that can be transformed from follicular lymphoma (FL). Tumors are commonly found in lymph nodes, spleen, liver, bone marrow, or other tissues and organs.

nodes.label: Treatment team
nodes.description: A team of medical experts involved in treating thyroid cancer, including an endocrinologist, radiologist, nuclear medicine specialist, surgeon, radiation oncologist, and medical oncologist. The team collaborates to develop a personalized treatment plan for the patient.

nodes.label: Bowel Blockage
nodes.description: A rare condition where a tumor grows large enough to block the flow of stool, potentially requiring surgical intervention such as a colectomy with colostomy or the placement of a mesh metal tube called a stent to keep the colon open.

nodes.label: Cervix
nodes.description: A part of the female reproductive system, where most cervical cancers occur. It is affected by long-term HPV infection and can develop into cervical cancer. The narrow, lower end of the uterus, a part of the female reproductive system where a baby grows and develops before being born. During birth, the cervix opens (dilates) and thins (effaces) to allow the baby to move into the vagina. The lower, narrow end of the uterus that connects to the vagina. It is part of the female reproductive system and includes the ectocervix, endocervix, external os, and inner os. Cervical cancer and dysplasia are mentioned as conditions affecting the cervix. A body part whose tissues can be visualized using an MRI. A part of the female reproductive system that can be viewed using a transvaginal ultrasound. It is located in the pelvis.

nodes.label: Stage 3
nodes.description: The fourth stage in the TNM system for colon cancer, indicating that the cancer has spread from the colon to nearby lymph nodes or there are tumor deposits, which are small tumors in the fat around the colon. A stage of cervical cancer, as determined by surgery, where the cancer has grown beyond the cervix but has not spread to the liver, lungs, or bones. Cancers that are close to spreading beyond the cervix (stage 1B3) are also considered locally advanced. A stage of cervical cancer, for which imaging is recommended 3 to 6 months after treatment and may include an FDG-PET/CT scan or a CT with contrast. A stage of bladder cancer where the cancer has grown through the bladder wall and into the fatty layer surrounding the bladder. It may also have spread to lymph nodes and organs nearby (in the pelvis). It has two subgroups: Stage 3A and Stage 3B. Stage 3A bladder cancer may only be in the fatty tissue surrounding the bladder or have spread to a single nearby lymph node, while Stage 3B has spread to multiple lymph nodes in the pelvis.

nodes.label: Follicular Lymphoma
nodes.description: A slow-growing (indolent) non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) that develops from B lymphocytes, forming clusters (follicles) in the lymph nodes and sometimes other tissues. A type of lymphoma, a cancer affecting the lymphatic system. The text discusses its grading, staging, and treatment based on the types of cells present, with specific details about the relationship between cell types and disease classification.

nodes.label: Medical history
nodes.description: A record of all health issues and treatments a person has experienced throughout their life, including illnesses, injuries, treatments, medications, and previous medical procedures. It is used by healthcare providers to assess a patient's overall health, identify any potential risks or contraindications, and make informed decisions about their current treatment. A medical history is sometimes referred to as a health history.

nodes.label: TNM System
nodes.description: A staging system used to stage throat cancer, where the letters T, N, and M describe different areas of cancer growth based on imaging and pathology results. A staging system used to describe different areas of cancer growth in breast cancer. It uses letters T, N, and M to describe the tumor, node, and metastasis respectively. Scores or numbers are assigned to each letter based on cancer test results, with higher numbers indicating larger tumors or more extensive spread. A staging system used for throat cancer, including nasopharyngeal cancer, where the letters T, N, and M describe different areas of cancer growth based on imaging and pathology results. The higher the number assigned to each letter, the larger the tumor or the more the cancer has spread.

nodes.label: Stage 1
nodes.description: A stage of cancer, specifically stage 1, where the tumor has grown into the second or third (muscle) layer of the rectal wall. The second stage in the TNM system for colon cancer, indicating that the cancer has grown into either the second or third layer of the colon wall, with no cancer in nearby lymph nodes or in areas outside the colon. A stage of cervical cancer, as determined by surgery, where there is no cancer in tissue beyond the cervix or in lymph nodes removed during surgery. A cancer stage in the context of surveillance, where follow-up imaging may include a fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography/computed tomography (FDGPET/CT) scan 3 to 6 months after finishing treatment for those who had radiation or chemoradiation after non–fertility-sparing treatment or cancer is stage 1B3. For those who had fertility-sparing treatment, an MRI of the pelvis (with contrast) may be done 6 months after surgery and then yearly for 2 to 3 years. A stage of bladder cancer where the cancer has grown through the inner lining of the bladder wall and into the layer of connective tissue, but not into the muscle layer of the bladder wall.

nodes.label: Bladder
nodes.description: A muscular organ in the pelvis that stores urine before it is expelled from the body, located above the prostate gland and between the hip bones in the lower abdomen. It has a capacity of up to 2 cups of urine in adults and can develop cancer, which may spread to other parts of the body if not treated properly. The bladder's inner layer is made of urothelial cells and is the site of bladder cancer. It is examined during cystoscopy and CT scans for cancer detection and is the target of various surgical procedures, including tumor removal and complete bladder removal. Medicine is administered directly into the bladder during intravesical therapy using a flexible tube called a catheter.

nodes.label: Myeloblasts
nodes.description: Very immature or most immature cells that are often referred to simply as blasts in CML. They are a type of myeloid progenitor cell. Very immature white blood cells that are abnormal in acute myeloid leukemia (AML), preventing them from becoming mature blood cells. Also known as myeloid blasts. Very immature white blood cells that are abnormal in AML, preventing them from becoming mature blood cells and leading to a buildup in the bone marrow and blood. Synonym for myeloid blasts. Abnormal cells found in the bone marrow or blood in individuals with AML. These cells crowd out other blood cells, leading to impaired function of the bone marrow or blood. Myeloblasts are a type of myeloid blast, very immature white blood cells that do not mature into mature blood cells in AML. They are a key indicator in the diagnosis of AML, with a presence of 20 percent or more in the bone marrow or blood confirming the diagnosis.

nodes.label: NCCN Cancer Centers
nodes.description: A network of comprehensive cancer centers in the United States that provide cancer care and conduct clinical trials, with recognized centers listed on the NCCN.org/cancercenters website and offering resources for finding clinical trials

nodes.label: EBRT
nodes.description: External Beam Radiation Therapy (EBRT) is a type of radiation therapy used to treat cervical cancer. A planning session called simulation is needed before EBRT begins, involving the patient lying on their back, staying still, and getting fitted for a prop to help stay still during radiation sessions. Pictures of the cancer site(s) are obtained with a CT scan, and using CT images and sophisticated computer software, a treatment plan is made specifying the radiation dose(s) and the number of sessions needed. There are several days between simulation and the beginning of treatment sessions to allow for careful treatment planning, dose calculation, and quality assurance. During treatment, the patient lies on a table, devices are used to keep them from moving, and ink marks on their skin help position their body accurately for daily treatments. The technician operates the machine from an adjacent room, and the patient will not see, hear, or feel the radiation. One session can take less than 10 minutes. External beam radiation therapy, a type of cancer treatment used for locally advanced cervical cancers, often in combination with platinum chemotherapy and brachytherapy.

nodes.label: Polypectomy
nodes.description: A minor surgical procedure used to remove polyps, typically during a colonoscopy. Removing polyps can prevent cancer before it starts, as most polyps do not become cancer, but almost all rectal cancers start in a polyp. Ultrasound is an imaging method for prostate cancer, indicating that it is part of the broader imaging category.
Ultrasound is used as a diagnostic tool for Inflammatory Breast Cancer, particularly for guiding a biopsy, as described in the text.
Ultrasound and CT are both imaging techniques that can be used together, with ultrasound sometimes guiding a fine-needle biopsy (FNB) that may be performed alongside a CT scan.
Ultrasound can guide a biopsy, as stated in the text.

Ultrasound, specifically transrectal ultrasound (TRUS) imaging, is used to help guide a biopsy of the prostate, providing a view of the prostate from inside the body to allow for a small sample to be removed without opening the abdomen.

communities.title: Community 26
Community Report on Cancer Treatment and Biomarkers
communities.summary:
Report summary: This report provides key findings on cancer treatment and biomarkers based on the analysis of various entities and their relationships. The report highlights the use of targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and other treatments in cancer management, with a focus on the role of biomarkers in guiding treatment decisions.


Finding summary: The use of targeted therapy in cancer treatment is prevalent, with various drugs targeting specific molecules involved in cancer growth and survival.
Finding explanation: Targeted therapy is a type of systemic therapy that targets specific molecules involved in cancer growth and survival. Examples include epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitors, kinase inhibitors, and HER2-targeted therapy drugs such as trastuzumab, lapatinib, and tucatinib. These drugs are used to treat various types of cancer, including thyroid, prostate, and squamous cell skin cancer, and may be used in combination with other treatments.

Finding summary: Immunotherapy is a preferred treatment for eligible patients with metastatic squamous cell skin cancer, and is often used in combination with other therapies.
Finding explanation: Immunotherapy is a type of systemic therapy that uses the body's immune system to fight cancer cells. Programmed death ligand 1 (PD-1) inhibitors, such as cemiplimab (Libtayo) and pembrolizumab (Keytruda), are a specific type of immunotherapy used to treat squamous cell skin cancer and other cancers. Immunotherapy can be used alone or in combination with other therapies like chemotherapy, targeted therapy, or hormone therapy.

Finding summary: Biomarkers play a crucial role in guiding treatment decisions for cancer, particularly in the context of targeted therapy.
Finding explanation: Biomarkers are specific molecules or genetic markers present in cancer cells that can be targeted by targeted therapy or immunotherapy. They are detected through immunohistochemistry and genetic testing of leukemia cells, and are used to identify cancers that may respond to targeted therapy or immunotherapy. Guide 3 lists specific biomarkers that, if present in cancer cells, may make targeted therapy or immunotherapy an option for treatment.

Finding summary: The use of systemic therapy in cancer treatment is widespread, with various types of systemic therapy available for different types of cancer.
Finding explanation: Systemic therapy is a type of cancer treatment that involves the use of medicines that travel through the bloodstream, reaching and affecting cells throughout the body. It includes chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy. Systemic therapy can affect both cancer cells and normal cells, potentially causing side effects. It is often used in the treatment of AML and is one of the key components of the multidisciplinary team's approach to treating the condition.

Finding summary: Side effects of targeted therapy include body aches, rash, high blood pressure, and abnormal bleeding.
Finding explanation: Targeted therapy is a type of cancer treatment designed to target specific molecules involved in cancer growth and survival. However, it can cause side effects such as body aches, rash, high blood pressure, and abnormal bleeding. These side effects can vary among individuals and should be discussed with the care team.

communities.title: Community Report: Oropharynx Cancer and Head and Neck Cancers

Report summary: This report provides key findings and insights related to oropharynx cancer and head and neck cancers, including their impact on the body, risk factors, and treatment considerations.


Finding summary: Oropharynx cancer is a type of cancer that arises in the oropharynx, including the back of the roof of the mouth, tonsils, side and back walls of the throat, and the base of the tongue.
Finding explanation: Oropharynx cancer is a type of cancer that affects the oropharynx, which is one of the three parts of the pharynx located in the throat. It can cause negative effects on the body, particularly on the jaw, teeth, and gums, and may require special consideration in dental care and treatment.

Finding summary: Head and neck cancer can affect the health of the jaw, teeth, and gums, and may require patients to inform their dentists and maintain regular dental care.
Finding explanation: Head and neck cancer can have negative effects on the health of the jaw, teeth, and gums, and patients are advised to inform their dentists and maintain regular dental care.

Finding summary: Tobacco use is a known risk factor for developing head and neck cancer and can limit the effectiveness of treatment and affect survival rates.
Finding explanation: Tobacco use is a known risk factor for developing head and neck cancer and can limit the effectiveness of treatment and affect survival rates.

Finding summary: Physical activity is a factor that can affect the risk of developing head and neck cancer and treatment outcomes, often involving regular exercise and healthy habits.
Finding explanation: Physical activity is a factor that can affect the risk of developing head and neck cancer and treatment outcomes, often involving regular exercise and healthy habits.

Finding summary: Alcohol is a substance that can increase the risk of developing head and neck cancer and affect treatment outcomes.
Finding explanation: Alcohol is a substance that can increase the risk of developing head and neck cancer and affect treatment outcomes.

communities.title: Community Report on Tumor Testing and Related Entities
communities.summary:
Report summary: This report provides a detailed analysis of the tumor testing process and related entities, including their relationships and impact on cancer diagnosis and treatment. It also highlights key findings and recommendations for further research and clinical practice.


Finding summary: Tumor testing involves a tissue sample from the tumor itself or from a metastasis in a lymph node, bone, liver, lung, or other affected area, or a sample of blood containing the tumor’s DNA. It analyzes the molecular components of the sample to identify molecules released by tumors that can be used as clues for finding and learning about the cancer, helping to determine the likelihood of cancer spread and predict aggressiveness. It also looks for specific abnormalities in genes involved in DNA repair, such as BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, PALB2, FANCA, and others, which can be targeted by therapies like PARP inhibitors.
Finding explanation: Tumor testing is a critical component of cancer diagnosis and treatment, involving a tissue sample from the tumor itself or from a metastasis in a lymph node, bone, liver, lung, or other affected area, or a sample of blood containing the tumor’s DNA. The testing process analyzes the molecular components of the sample to identify molecules released by tumors that can be used as clues for finding and learning about the cancer, helping to determine the likelihood of cancer spread and predict aggressiveness. It also looks for specific abnormalities in genes involved in DNA repair, such as BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, PALB2, FANCA, and others, which can be targeted by therapies like PARP inhibitors.

Finding summary: Biomarker-Based Treatment considers the presence of specific biomarkers in the cancer. If the cancer has any of the biomarkers listed, targeted therapy or immunotherapy may be an option.
Finding explanation: Biomarker-Based Treatment is a type of treatment that considers the presence of specific biomarkers in the cancer. If the cancer has any of the biomarkers listed, targeted therapy or immunotherapy may be an option. This approach allows for personalized treatment based on the molecular features of the tumor, potentially improving treatment efficacy and reducing side effects.

Finding summary: Molecular features of a cancer, such as specific mutations or protein levels, can be tested as part of cancer staging and treatment decisions. In the context of rectal cancer, mismatch repair testing is a type of biomarker analysis.
Finding explanation: Molecular features of a cancer, such as specific mutations or protein levels, can be tested as part of cancer staging and treatment decisions. In the context of rectal cancer, mismatch repair testing is a type of biomarker analysis that involves analyzing a piece of the rectal tumor in a lab to check for mutations in mismatch repair (MMR) genes. An abnormal result is called either mismatch repair deficient (dMMR) or microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H). Tumors without these changes are referred to as microsatellite stable (MSS) or mismatch repair proficient (pMMR). If the cancer is dMMR/MSI-H, the patient is also tested for inherited mutations in the mismatch repair genes.

Finding summary: Precancerous changes in the mucosa of the stomach often occur before cancer develops, serving as a precursor to stomach cancer. These changes can be detected through endoscopy and biopsy samples, allowing for early detection and intervention.
Finding explanation: Precancerous changes in the mucosa of the stomach often occur before cancer develops, serving as a precursor to stomach cancer. These changes can be detected through endoscopy and biopsy samples, allowing for early detection and intervention. Precancerous changes in the mucosa of the stomach often occur before cancer develops, serving as a cause for stomach cancer. These changes can be detected through endoscopy and biopsy samples, allowing for early detection and intervention.

Finding summary: Stomach cancer, often starting in cells that line the inside of the stomach wall and secreting mucus, known as adenocarcinomas, can grow into nearby structures and spread to distant parts of the body through the blood or lymphatic system, such as the liver, abdominal lining, lungs, or bone.
Finding explanation: Stomach cancer, often starting in cells that line the inside of the stomach wall and secreting mucus, known as adenocarcinomas, can grow into nearby structures and spread to distant parts of the body through the blood or lymphatic system, such as the liver, abdominal lining, lungs, or bone. Stomach cancer is a type of cancer that develops in the esophagus, with stages categorized based on how far the cancer has spread, including early-stage, locoregional or locally advanced, and metastatic. It can grow inwards, forming ulcers or masses, and may spread to nearby lymph nodes, other parts of the stomach, or other parts of the body, including the liver, abdominal lining, lungs, or bone.

Finding explanation: Clinical trials are conducted and registered worldwide, including in the United States, through resources such as clinicaltrials.gov and NCCN.org/cancercenters. Clinical trials information can be found in the United States through resources such as NCCN.org/cancercenters and cancer.gov/about-cancer/treatment/clinical-trials/search.

Finding summary: Clinical trials involve the use of research-related costs, including the study drug, which are covered by the study sponsor.
Finding explanation: Clinical trials involve research-related costs, which include the study drug and other associated costs, and these are usually paid for by the study sponsor. Clinical trials may involve the use of a placebo with a standard treatment or a new drug with a standard treatment, as stated in the text.

Finding explanation: Clinical trials are research studies evaluating new treatments, therapies, or interventions for prostate cancer, pancreatic cancer, and glioma.
